1.1.title: General strategies
1.1.summary: A problem becomes manageable when you name one target, draw the setup and choose the physical rule before manipulating symbols.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Choose a positive direction; a negative velocity means motion the other way, not a negative speed.
Two rearrangements of one equation contain only one piece of information.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A problem becomes manageable when you name one target, draw the setup and choose the physical rule before manipulating symbols.

parts.title: The problem-solving loop
parts.body_md: Draw and label the bodies. List the target and givens. Try a simpler version, use symmetry, select a system and coordinates, then count unknowns. Work symbolically until the end. Check dimensions, sign and an easy limit; if stuck, estimate a scale or solve a special case first.

parts.title: Recognition, not formula hunting
parts.body_md: A constant acceleration suggests kinematics; steady motion suggests force balance; a speed after a height change suggests energy. A collision with negligible outside impulse suggests momentum. These are choices to justify, not interchangeable equations.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$N_{\rm equations}=N_{\rm unknowns}$$

Counting independent equations is a diagnostic, not a proof of uniqueness. Track directions and units throughout.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: D,h,x are distances (m); t is time (s); u,v are speeds $(m/s)$; g is acceleration $(m/s^{2})$. Signed velocity needs a chosen positive direction.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Two rearrangements of the same equation are still one fact. Check the final sign, units and a simple limiting case.

examples.title: Meeting halfway is not a rule
examples.setup_md: Two walkers start distance D apart. One walks right at u, the other left at v, both constant and positive.

steps.why: Use one origin and one clock for both walkers.
Meeting means the same position at the same time.
Solve for the common time, then substitute it into one position.

examples.answer_md: They meet after $D/(u+v)$, at $uD/(u+v)$ from the first start.
examples.check_md: If the second walker stands still, the meeting point should be at D. If $u=v$, it should be halfway.

examples.title: Two unknowns, two physical facts
examples.setup_md: A ball is thrown straight up at speed u; air resistance is negligible. Find its maximum height h above release and the time t to get there.

steps.why: Constant downward acceleration changes the upward velocity.
At the highest point, vertical velocity is zero.
Integrate the changing velocity, rather than assuming it remains u.
Substitute the same time into the position equation.

examples.check_md: Doubling launch speed doubles the time but quadruples the height.

practice.question_md: Two cyclists start D apart and approach at speeds 2u and u. Where do they meet, measured from the faster rider?
hints: Write both positions from the faster rider’s start.
Set $2ut=D-ut$; find t before the position.
practice.answer_md: $t=D/(3u)$; the meeting point is $2D/3$.

1.2.title: Units, dimensional analysis
1.2.summary: Units can reveal the shape of an answer before you solve the motion. They cannot supply every number or every dimensionless dependence.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Write length L, mass M and time T as independent powers. A force has dimensions $ML/T^2$.
An angle in radians is dimensionless, so units cannot decide how an answer depends on amplitude.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Units can reveal the shape of an answer before you solve the motion. They cannot supply every number or every dimensionless dependence.

parts.title: Matching powers
parts.body_md: Assume a product of the relevant quantities raised to unknown powers. Match mass, length and time separately. A dimensionless numerical factor remains undetermined.

parts.title: Pendulum, spring and orbit
parts.body_md: For a pendulum use length and gravity; for a spring use mass and stiffness; for an orbit use radius and the gravitational parameter $GM$. Choosing the relevant ingredients is part of the physics. Friction, large angles or another length can introduce extra dimensionless ratios.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$T=C\sqrt{\ell/g}$$

Here $T$ is a pendulum period (s), $\ell$ length (m), $g$ gravitational acceleration $(m/s^{2})$, and $C$ dimensionless. Small-amplitude dynamics gives $C=2\pi$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: T is period (s); $\ell ,r$ are lengths (m); m,M are masses (kg); g is acceleration $(m/s^{2})$; k is spring stiffness $(N/m)$; G is $m^{3}/(\mathrm{kg} s^{2})$. C and angles in radians are dimensionless.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Units cannot determine numerical constants or an unknown function of a dimensionless parameter such as amplitude angle.

examples.title: Pendulum time scale
examples.setup_md: A small bob swings on a light string of length $\ell$ under gravity g. Infer the period scale without solving the equation.

steps.why: Assume length and gravity set the time scale; C is dimensionless.
Replace each quantity by its dimensions.
Match length and time powers independently.
Solve $a=1/2$ and $b=-1/2$. Dynamics gives $C=2\pi$ only for small swings.

examples.answer_md: The period scales as $\sqrt{\ell/g}$; in the small-angle limit it is $2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}$.
examples.check_md: Four times the length gives twice the period; bob mass cannot appear in this ideal model.

examples.title: Spring period
examples.setup_md: A frictionless mass m is attached to a spring of stiffness k, measured in $N/m$.

steps.why: A spring force is k times a displacement.
Write a product with unknown powers.
Match mass and time.

examples.answer_md: The exact ideal-spring period is $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$.
examples.check_md: A stiffer spring should oscillate faster; this formula does.

examples.title: Circular-orbit scale
examples.setup_md: A satellite orbits at radius r about mass M; take its mass as negligible.

steps.why: Read this from gravitational acceleration $GM/r^2$.
The satellite mass does not affect its gravitational acceleration.
Match powers of length and time.
The exponent $3/2$ follows before solving a circle.

examples.answer_md: The exact circular period has $C=2\pi$.
examples.check_md: Eight times $GM$ makes the period smaller by $\sqrt{8}$, at fixed r.

practice.question_md: A spring with mass m and stiffness k has period T. What happens if mass becomes 9m and stiffness becomes 4k?
hints: Use only the ratio of the periods.
The period is proportional to the square root of $m/k$.

1.3.title: Approximations, limiting cases
1.3.summary: An approximation is a controlled way of dropping small effects. First identify a small ratio; then keep enough terms that subtraction does not erase your answer.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Near zero, $(1+\epsilon)^n=1+n\epsilon+O(\epsilon^2)$. State $|\epsilon|\ll1$ before using it.
$\sin\theta\simeq\theta$ and $\cos\theta\simeq1-\theta^2/2$ require radians.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: An approximation is a controlled way of dropping small effects. First identify a small ratio; then keep enough terms that subtraction does not erase your answer.

parts.title: Dropped balls and nearby gravity
parts.body_md: Near Earth, $h/R$ is the small parameter, not h alone. Replacing gravity by a constant is the leading approximation. First-order corrections tell you how much it changes.

parts.title: Mass ratios and symmetry
parts.body_md: In a two-body collision, test equal masses and a very heavy target. Symmetric limits often reveal an algebraic error before calculation. In a circular pendulum, small angle must be applied to both geometry and forces consistently.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$(1+\epsilon)^n\simeq1+n\epsilon,\qquad \sin\theta\simeq\theta$$

Require $\lvert\epsilon\rvert\ll1$ and $\lvert\theta\rvert\ll1$ in radians. Dropped terms begin at second order for the binomial and third order for sine.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $h,R,\ell$ are lengths (m); m,M are masses (kg); g is acceleration $(m/s^{2})$; u,v are speeds $(m/s)$; $\theta$ is an angle in radians. The small quantities are ratios $h/R, m/M$ or $\theta$, not bare lengths or masses.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Small needs a comparison scale. Subtracting nearly equal quantities can make a normally negligible next-order term essential.

examples.title: How constant is gravity?
examples.setup_md: At Earth radius R, gravity is $g_{0}$. Find gravity at height h much smaller than R.

steps.why: Factor out the known surface value and expose a dimensionless ratio.
Apply the binomial expansion through first order.

examples.answer_md: The fractional decrease is approximately $2h/R$.
examples.check_md: The correction is negative and vanishes at $h=0$.

examples.title: A small height from a nearly vertical string
examples.setup_md: A pendulum string of length $\ell$ is displaced through a small angle $\theta$. Find its vertical rise h.

steps.why: Project the string vertically and compare it with its lowest position.
Keeping only $\cos (\theta )=1$ would erase the height entirely.
The leading nonzero height is second order.

examples.answer_md: $h\simeq\ell\theta^2/2$.
examples.check_md: Both positive and negative small angles raise the bob; the square gives the same result.

examples.title: A heavy-target limit
examples.setup_md: In an elastic head-on collision, a moving mass m hits a stationary mass M. The exact first mass velocity is $v=(m-M)u/(m+M)$. Find the heavy-target approximation.

steps.why: Factor M out before expanding.
The small ratio is $m/M$.
Multiply and discard terms of second order in $m/M$.

examples.answer_md: It almost reverses at speed u; finite target motion slightly reduces the rebound speed.
examples.check_md: The exact expression gives zero when $m=M$; the heavy-target expansion is not valid there.

practice.question_md: A circular pendulum has angular frequency $\omega=\sqrt{g/(\ell\cos\theta)}$. Find its first nonzero small-angle correction.
practice.answer_md: $\omega\simeq\sqrt{g/\ell}(1+\theta^2/4)$.

1.4.title: Solving differential equations numerically
1.4.summary: Predict motion by advancing position and velocity through short time steps. A believable animation still needs an error check.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\dot x=v$ means $\Delta x\simeq v\Delta t$ over a short interval.
A second-order motion law needs both starting position and velocity.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Predict motion by advancing position and velocity through short time steps. A believable animation still needs an error check.

parts.title: Explicit Euler
parts.body_md: Calculate acceleration using the old state, then update x and v from that same state. Updating one and using the new value in the other is a different method; name it.

parts.title: Convergence and energy
parts.body_md: Repeat with half the time step over the same physical duration. Compare results and conserved quantities. Near collisions or rapidly changing forces, a step that worked earlier may be too large.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$x_{n+1}=x_n+v_n\Delta t,\qquad v_{n+1}=v_n+a_n\Delta t$$

This is explicit Euler, a first-order method. $x$ is in m, $v$ in $m/s$, $a=F/m$ in $m/s^{2}$ and $\Delta t$ in s.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: x,y,A,H are positions or lengths (m); v is velocity $(m/s)$; a,g are accelerations $(m/s^{2})$; h or $\Delta t$ is a time step (s); N is a step count; $\omega$ is angular frequency $(s^{-1})$; E is energy (J).

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A smooth animation is not an accuracy check. Euler can grow oscillator energy artificially; monitor a conserved quantity and step-size error.

examples.title: Constant acceleration exposes the error
examples.setup_md: Start at $x=0$ and $v=0$ with constant acceleration a. Use explicit Euler with step h.

steps.why: The first position update uses the old zero velocity.
The second position update uses $v_{1}=ah$.
Compare with the exact constant-acceleration result at the same time.
Sum the old velocities 0,ah,...,(N-1)ah.

examples.answer_md: At fixed $t=Nh$, Euler gives $x_N=at^2/2-ath/2$; its error shrinks linearly with h.
examples.check_md: Reducing h while keeping N fixed changes the time; that is not a convergence test.

examples.title: A spring can gain fake energy
examples.setup_md: For $\ddot x=-\omega^2x$, start at $x=A,v=0$ and take one explicit Euler step h.

steps.why: Both updates use the initial state.
Initially all energy is spring potential.
The position stayed at A but the algorithm also created kinetic energy.
The positive drift is numerical, not physical driving.

examples.answer_md: Explicit Euler is unsuitable for long undamped oscillator runs without careful error control; a better integrator is needed.
examples.check_md: A smaller step reduces this error, but does not turn Euler into an energy-conserving method.

practice.question_md: For a constant downward acceleration g, one Euler step begins at $y=H$ and $v=0$ with up positive. What are the next y and v?
hints: Compute acceleration from the current state.
practice.answer_md: $y_1=H$, $v_1=-g\Delta t$. The exact height is already lower by $g\Delta t^2/2$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 11–14; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

2.1.title: Balancing forces
2.1.summary: A resting object has forces, but their vector sum is zero. Identify which object produces each force, then balance components.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An angle measured from the horizontal gives horizontal component $F\cos\theta$ and vertical component $F\sin\theta$.
It adjusts to the required value up to $\mu_sN$; it is not automatically equal to that maximum.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A resting object has forces, but their vector sum is zero. Identify which object produces each force, then balance components.

parts.title: Tension, normal force, friction and gravity
parts.body_md: A taut ideal string pulls along itself; it cannot push. A surface pushes perpendicular to itself and may exert friction parallel to itself. Gravity acts without contact. Equal tension along a string requires the ideal massless-string/frictionless-pulley model; a rough post can change tension.

parts.title: Choose the axes before the trig
parts.body_md: On an incline, use one axis along the surface and one normal to it. The normal component of weight is adjacent to the angle between weight and the inward normal; this gives $mg \cos (\theta )$. The downslope component is $mg \sin (\theta )$.

parts.title: A rope around a pole
parts.body_md: A small curved rope segment needs a normal force approximately $T d(\phi )$. At impending sliding, $dT=\mu T d(\phi )$. Integrating gives a tension ratio, not a constant difference. Below slipping, the static inequality replaces equality.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\sum F_x=0,\qquad\sum F_y=0$$

Forces are in N. Static friction adjusts within $\lvert f_s\rvert\le\mu_sN$; $N$ is the normal force and $\mu_s$ dimensionless.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: N,T,F,f are forces (N); m is mass (kg); g is $m/s^{2}$; $\mu _{s}$ and $\mu$ are dimensionless friction coefficients; $\theta$ and wrap angle $\beta$ are in radians when used in formulas.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Zero net force also allows constant nonzero velocity. Do not automatically set static friction equal to its maximum.

examples.title: Will the block stay put?
examples.setup_md: A block of mass m rests on a fixed ramp at angle $\theta$, with no other applied force.

steps.why: The block has no acceleration perpendicular to the ramp.
Choose upslope as positive for the parallel balance.
The required friction must fit within the static limit.
Cancel positive m,g and $\cos (\theta )$, for an ordinary incline below 90 degrees.

examples.answer_md: Rest is possible when $\tan\theta\le\mu_s$; the actual friction is $mg\sin\theta$.
examples.check_md: At $\theta =0$, friction is zero even if $\mu$ is large.

examples.title: Holding a rope with a smaller force
examples.setup_md: A rope wraps through angle $\beta$ radians around a rough fixed post. Its large-tension end is $T_{high}$ and coefficient is $\mu$. Find the smallest holding tension before slipping.

steps.why: Use the limiting friction on a small rope arc.
Sum fractional tension changes around the contact.
Integrate both sides.
Solve for the required holding force.

examples.answer_md: The minimum holding tension is $T_{high}e^{-\mu\beta}$.
examples.check_md: No wrap or no friction gives equal tensions; $\beta$ must be in radians.

practice.question_md: A block rests on a ramp with $\tan\theta=1/4$ and $\mu_s=1/2$. Is the friction $mg\sin\theta$ or $\mu_sN$?
hints: Find the force required for balance first.
Compare the required friction with the maximum.
practice.answer_md: $f_s=mg\sin\theta$; it is below $\mu_sN$ by a factor of two.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 22–27; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

2.2.title: Balancing torques
2.2.summary: An extended object must balance both force and torque to remain at rest. Choose the torque point to eliminate unknown forces.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\tau=rF\sin\phi$ uses the angle between the position vector and force. Equivalently use force times perpendicular distance.
Zero net force and torque give zero corresponding acceleration; they do not stop existing translation or spin.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: An extended object must balance both force and torque to remain at rest. Choose the torque point to eliminate unknown forces.

parts.title: Taking moments
parts.body_md: Pick an origin at an unknown support so that support contributes no torque. Assign clockwise and counterclockwise signs explicitly. Also write horizontal and vertical force balance; torque alone cannot determine every support force.

parts.title: Leaning ladder
parts.body_md: With a smooth wall, the wall force is horizontal. The floor provides a normal force and friction. The weight acts at the midpoint of a uniform ladder; the horizontal and vertical lever arms differ.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\sum\boldsymbol\tau=0,\qquad\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$$

Torque has units $N\cdot m$. In a planar problem assign clockwise and counterclockwise opposite signs. $\mathbf r$ runs from the chosen pivot to the force application point.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: M is mass (kg); $N_{L},N_{R},N_{f},N_{w},f$ are forces (N); L,a are lengths (m); torque is in N m; $\theta$ is the ladder angle; $\mu _{s}$ is dimensionless.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A force through the pivot has zero torque but still belongs in force balance. Balance both force and torque. Balance alone does not stop existing translation or spin; static equilibrium also requires the object to be at rest.

examples.title: Support loads on a beam
examples.setup_md: A massless horizontal beam length L has supports at both ends. A mass M is placed distance a from the left.

steps.why: The total upward force balances the one downward weight.
Take torques about the left support; its force has zero lever arm.
Solve the torque equation first.
Substitute into force balance.

examples.answer_md: The nearer support carries more load: $N_R=Mga/L$ and $N_L=Mg(L-a)/L$.
examples.check_md: At $a=0$ the right support carries none; at $a=L/2$ the loads match.

examples.title: A ladder needs floor friction
examples.setup_md: A uniform ladder of mass M and length L leans at angle $\theta$ to a rough floor against a smooth wall.

steps.why: Vertical and horizontal force balance determine the directions and relationships.
Take moments about the floor contact: wall force uses the vertical arm, weight the horizontal arm.
Solve for the horizontal forces.
The floor must be able to supply that much static friction.

examples.answer_md: Rest requires $\mu_s\ge\tfrac12\cot\theta$.
examples.check_md: A nearly horizontal ladder needs very large friction; a nearly vertical one needs little.

practice.question_md: The same uniform ladder has $\mu_s=1/2$. Find its smallest angle to the floor.
practice.answer_md: $\theta_{min}=45^\circ$.

visual.description: Uniform ladder against a smooth wall; inspect weight, floor contact and wall reaction separately.

3.1.title: Newton’s laws
3.1.summary: Forces explain changes in motion, not motion itself. Choose one body and an inertial frame, then add only the forces acting on that body.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $a=dv/dt$ measures change of signed velocity. It can oppose the current motion.
Force is measured in $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{kg\,m/s^2}$; mass in kg measures inertia.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Forces explain changes in motion, not motion itself. Choose one body and an inertial frame, then add only the forces acting on that body.

parts.title: First law
parts.body_md: With zero net force, velocity stays constant, including possibly zero. An inertial frame is one where an isolated body follows this rule; an accelerating frame needs additional inertial-force bookkeeping.

parts.title: Second law
parts.body_md: For a fixed collection of particles, $\sum\mathbf F_{ext}=d\mathbf p/dt$. A constant-mass particle gives $\mathbf F_{net}=m\mathbf a$. The term $m\mathbf a$ is the result of real forces, not an additional force.

parts.title: Third law
parts.body_md: The force A exerts on B and the force B exerts on A are equal and opposite, but act on different bodies. Weight and support normal are not a third-law pair. Earth’s gravity is non-contact; the surface supplies the contact force.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\sum\mathbf F=\frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}=m\mathbf a$$

The last equality assumes constant mass. $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v$ $(\mathrm{kg}\cdot m/s)$, $\mathbf a$ $(m/s^{2})$, $m$ (kg), force (N). Newtonian mechanics applies here.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m,M are masses (kg); F,N,T are forces (N); a,g are accelerations $(m/s^{2})$; v,u are velocities or speeds $(m/s)$; momentum is in $\mathrm{kg} m/s$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Weight and normal force on the same block are not a third-law pair. At an instant of zero velocity, acceleration can still be nonzero.

examples.title: An elevator starting upward
examples.setup_md: A person of mass m stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at a.

steps.why: The scale pushes up and Earth pulls down; up is positive.
Solve for the contact force measured by the scale.

examples.answer_md: The scale reads $m(g+a)$, greater than $mg$.
examples.check_md: At $a=0$ it reads $mg$ whether the elevator is stationary or moving steadily.

examples.title: Two carts push one another
examples.setup_md: Two carts of masses m and 3m on a frictionless track are pushed apart by an internal spring exerting force magnitude F at an instant.

steps.why: The interaction forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
Apply the second law separately to each body.
Internal forces cancel when both carts form the system.

examples.answer_md: The lighter cart has three times the acceleration magnitude; equal forces do not imply equal accelerations.
examples.check_md: The center of mass does not accelerate without an external horizontal force.

practice.question_md: A puck slides right on frictionless ice. Someone stops pushing it. What is its acceleration and what happens to its velocity?
hints: List horizontal forces after the push ends.
practice.answer_md: $a_x=0$; its existing rightward velocity remains constant.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 51–55; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

3.2.title: Free-body diagrams
3.2.summary: A free-body diagram turns a complicated machine into one equation per direction for each body. Draw real interactions first, then connect the motions with the rope geometry.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $mg\sin\theta$ is the downslope component of weight; $mg\cos\theta$ is the inward normal component. They replace weight in component equations, not supplement it.
A massless rope over a frictionless massless pulley has equal tension along it. A massive pulley generally does not.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A free-body diagram turns a complicated machine into one equation per direction for each body. Draw real interactions first, then connect the motions with the rope geometry.

parts.title: Plane and masses
parts.body_md: Isolate the mass on the plane and the hanging mass separately. Normal force follows the perpendicular equation. Along the rope, choose compatible positive directions so the common acceleration has one sign.

parts.title: Platform and movable pulleys
parts.body_md: Count the rope segments whose length changes. A platform supported by two parallel segments can have upward force 2T, while its displacement may be half the motion of a free rope end. Forces and acceleration constraints are separate facts.

parts.title: Atwood’s machine
parts.body_md: For two hanging masses, subtract the two force equations to eliminate tension. A negative answer tells you the true motion is opposite your initial sign choice.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$N=mg\cos\theta,\qquad ma=mg\sin\theta-\mu_kN$$

For this relation the ramp is fixed, the block slides downward, and positive is down the ramp. $\theta$ is its angle, $g$ $(m/s^{2})$, $\mu_k$ dimensionless, $N$ (N).

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m,M are masses (kg); T,N are forces (N); a,g are $m/s^{2}$; $\theta$ is the incline angle; s,y are lengths (m). Rope constraints relate signed displacements and their derivatives.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Do not draw $m\mathbf a$ as another force. Taut strings constrain total length; derive the actual pulley relation instead of assuming all accelerations match.

examples.title: Two hanging masses
examples.setup_md: Masses M and m, with $M>m$, hang over an ideal fixed pulley.

steps.why: Choose the heavier mass downward as positive.
The lighter mass moves upward with the same acceleration magnitude.
Add the equations so the internal tension cancels.
Solve a, then substitute it back into either body equation.

examples.answer_md: $a=(M-m)g/(M+m)$ and $T=2Mmg/(M+m)$.
examples.check_md: For $M=m, a=0$ and $T=mg$; as m tends to zero, the heavy mass approaches free fall.

examples.title: One hanging mass pulls another along a ramp
examples.setup_md: Mass m is on a frictionless ramp of angle $\theta$; mass M hangs over an ideal pulley at its top. Choose M downward and m upslope positive.

steps.why: Write the hanging body equation.
Use only the ramp-parallel component of the other weight.
Add the two equations and solve.
The ramp prevents perpendicular acceleration.

examples.answer_md: The sign of the computed a decides the direction; the normal force is not generally $mg$.
examples.check_md: At $\theta=90^\circ$ this becomes the ordinary Atwood setup.

examples.title: A slowly lifted movable pulley
examples.setup_md: A load of mass M hangs from a light movable pulley supported by two vertical rope segments. One end is fixed; the other is pulled slowly.

steps.why: The two upward rope tensions support the load in the slow-motion limit.
The required pull is half the load’s weight.
Raising the pulley shortens two segments, so the free end must move twice as far.

examples.answer_md: The force advantage costs distance: work is $T\Delta s=Mg\Delta y$.
examples.check_md: Do not use the same acceleration for the free end and movable pulley in a dynamic version.

practice.question_md: In the ramp-and-hanging-mass setup, choose $M=m\sin\theta$. What are a and T?
hints: Use the net force along the rope.
practice.answer_md: $a=0$ and $T=Mg=mg\sin\theta$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 55–60; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

3.3.title: Solving differential equations
3.3.summary: An equation of motion becomes solvable once you choose the right variable. Velocity-dependent forces suggest integrating in time; position-dependent forces often suggest using velocity as a function of position.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An equation $dv/dt=f(v)$ becomes $dv/f(v)=dt$ where the division is valid.
$dv/dt=(dv/dx)(dx/dt)=v\,dv/dx$ along a one-dimensional trajectory.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: An equation of motion becomes solvable once you choose the right variable. Velocity-dependent forces suggest integrating in time; position-dependent forces often suggest using velocity as a function of position.

parts.title: Initial conditions and constants
parts.body_md: Integrating creates constants. Use the specified position and velocity to determine them; do not discard the negative branch of a velocity without a direction argument.

parts.title: Dropped ball with drag
parts.body_md: Take downward as positive to keep gravity simple. Linear drag has force -bv and a terminal speed $mg/b$. The solution approaches terminal speed gradually rather than reaching it at a finite time.

parts.title: Gravity depending on position
parts.body_md: For inverse-square gravity, use $v dv/dr$ to integrate acceleration over radius. This yields a speed-position relation without first finding the full clock-time motion.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$a=\frac{dv}{dt}=v\frac{dv}{dx}$$

For constant mass, $m\dot v=F$. Use $dt$ for $F(t)$, $v\,dv/dx$ for $F(x)$, and separate $dv/F(v)=dt/m$ for $F(v)$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $x,r,r_{0}$ are lengths (m); t is time (s); v,u are velocities $(m/s)$; m,M are masses (kg); b is linear-drag coefficient $(\mathrm{kg}/s)$; $\alpha$ is a decay rate $(s^{-1})$; G is $m^{3}/(\mathrm{kg} s^{2})$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A constant of integration is not optional. Division by $v$ can lose a stationary solution, so check it separately.

examples.title: Fall with linear drag
examples.setup_md: A mass m is released from rest. Downward speed is v; drag magnitude is bv.

steps.why: Gravity accelerates down; drag opposes downward motion.
Put the equation into first-order linear form.
Choose the integration constant so $v(0)=0$.
Integrate velocity and enforce $x(0)=0$.

examples.answer_md: $v$ tends to $mg/b$ on the time scale $m/b$.
examples.check_md: For small t, expand the exponential to recover $v\approx gt$ and $x\approx gt^2/2$.

examples.title: Radial fall toward a planet
examples.setup_md: A particle is released from rest at radius $r_{0}$ outside a spherical mass M. Ignore drag; r is outward-positive.

steps.why: Use the exterior inverse-square gravitational acceleration.
Replace the time derivative using the chain rule.
Use definite integrals to impose the initial condition immediately.
Choose the inward, negative branch.

examples.answer_md: The speed is the positive square-root magnitude; signed radial velocity is negative.
examples.check_md: At $r=r_{0}$ it is zero; it grows as radius decreases.

practice.question_md: A cart obeys $\dot v=-\alpha v$ with $v(0)=u>0$. Find v(t) and total distance traveled.
hints: Integrate the resulting velocity from zero to infinity.
practice.answer_md: $v=ue^{-\alpha t}$ and total distance $u/\alpha$, for $\alpha>0$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 60–65; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

3.4.title: Projectile motion
3.4.summary: Horizontal and vertical motion share the same clock. Gravity changes only the vertical velocity, so find the event time vertically and use it horizontally.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $v_{0x}=u\cos\theta$, $v_{0y}=u\sin\theta$ when $\theta$ is measured above horizontal.
At the top $v_{y}=0$; at the ground $y=0$. These are different events.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Horizontal and vertical motion share the same clock. Gravity changes only the vertical velocity, so find the event time vertically and use it horizontally.

parts.title: Trajectory and assumptions
parts.body_md: With constant g and negligible drag, $x=u\cos\theta\,t$ and $y=y_0+u\sin\theta\,t-gt^2/2$. Eliminating t gives a parabola. These equations use an inertial frame and a locally flat ground.

parts.title: Throwing a ball
parts.body_md: A maximum-range angle depends on release and landing heights. Forty-five degrees is the equal-height result; it is not universal. The nonnegative root of the landing-time equation matters.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$x=x_0+v_{0x}t,\qquad y=y_0+v_{0y}t-\tfrac12gt^2$$

Positions are in m, velocities in $m/s$ and time in s. $v_{0x}=v_0\cos\theta$, $v_{0y}=v_0\sin\theta$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: u,v are speeds $(m/s)$; H,y,R,x are lengths (m); t is time (s); g is $m/s^{2}$; $\theta$ is the angle above horizontal. R denotes horizontal range here.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The equal-height range formula does not apply to a cliff landing. Horizontal speed does not slow vertical falling in this approximation.

examples.title: Return to the launch height
examples.setup_md: Launch at speed u and angle $\theta$ above level ground.

steps.why: Set landing height equal to initial height.
Discard the trivial $t=0$ root corresponding to launch.
Use the same flight time in horizontal motion.
The maximum of $\sin (2\theta )$ is one.

examples.answer_md: Equal-height range is $u^2\sin(2\theta)/g$.
examples.check_md: Angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ-\theta$ give the same range but different flight times.

examples.title: A horizontal launch from a ledge
examples.setup_md: A ball leaves a ledge height H horizontally at speed u.

steps.why: Initial vertical velocity is zero.
Choose the positive future time.
Multiply horizontal speed by flight time.
Combine perpendicular velocity components at impact.

examples.answer_md: The range is $u\sqrt{2H/g}$ and impact speed is $\sqrt{u^2+2gH}$.
examples.check_md: Flight time does not depend on u in this ideal model.

practice.question_md: At fixed launch speed and equal landing height, compare the ranges at 30 and 60 degrees.
practice.answer_md: The ranges match; the 60-degree throw stays in the air longer.

visual.description: Representative level-ground projectile; its default45-degree launch illustrates the equal-height maximum-range case.

3.5.title: Motion in a plane, polar coordinates
3.5.summary: In polar coordinates, the directions themselves rotate. Acceleration contains terms from changing speed and from changing the basis.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\hat{\mathbf r}$ points outward; $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ points toward increasing $\theta$. Their lengths stay one while their directions change.
$v_{tangent}=r\dot\theta$ converts radians per second into metres per second.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: In polar coordinates, the directions themselves rotate. Acceleration contains terms from changing speed and from changing the basis.

parts.title: Differentiate the arrows
parts.body_md: $\dot{\hat{\mathbf r}}=\dot\theta\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ and $\dot{\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}}=-\dot\theta\hat{\mathbf r}$. Thus $\mathbf v=\dot r\hat{\mathbf r}+r\dot\theta\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$. Differentiate both coefficients and unit vectors to obtain acceleration.

parts.title: Two acceleration components
parts.body_md: $a_r=\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2$ and $a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$. The inward circular term can exist at constant speed. The second tangential term appears when radius and angle both change.

parts.title: Circular pendulum
parts.body_md: The horizontal radius is $\ell \sin (\theta )$, not $\ell$. Vertical tension balances weight, while the horizontal tension produces inward acceleration. Use the same angle convention in both equations.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\mathbf a=(\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2)\hat{\mathbf r}+(r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta)\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$$

$r$ is in m and $\theta$ in rad. $\dot{\hat{\mathbf r}}=\dot\theta\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ and $\dot{\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}}=-\dot\theta\hat{\mathbf r}$. Each acceleration component is in $m/s^{2}$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $r,R,\ell$ are lengths (m); $\theta$ is an angle in radians; $\omega$ or $\dot\theta$ is angular speed $(s^{-1})$; u,v are linear speeds $(m/s)$; T is string tension (N) in the force equations.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Constant speed is not constant velocity. The turning basis is precisely why circular motion accelerates.

examples.title: Uniform circular motion
examples.setup_md: A particle moves on radius R at angular speed $\omega$.

steps.why: The radius and angular speed are constant.
Insert those values into the polar acceleration equations.
Connect angular speed to the familiar centripetal-acceleration form.

examples.answer_md: The acceleration points toward the center even though speed is constant.
examples.check_md: A zero tangential acceleration does not mean zero total acceleration.

examples.title: A conical pendulum
examples.setup_md: A bob on string length $\ell$ moves in a horizontal circle; the string makes $\theta$ with downward vertical.

steps.why: There is no vertical acceleration.
The horizontal force supplies circular acceleration, and geometry determines the radius.
Substitute T and $v=r \omega$.
Cancel $\sin (\theta )$ for a nonzero circular motion.

examples.answer_md: The circular period is $2\pi\sqrt{\ell\cos\theta/g}$.
examples.check_md: For very small $\theta$ it approaches the small-angle pendulum period.

practice.question_md: A bead moves outward at constant speed u along a line rotating at constant angular speed $\omega$. At radius r, find its polar acceleration components.
hints: Retain the term containing both changing radius and angle.
practice.answer_md: $a_r=-r\omega^2$, $a_\theta=2u\omega$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 68–70; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

4.1.title: Linear differential equations
4.1.summary: Linear equations let you combine simple solutions into a general one. Exponentials are useful because differentiation keeps their shape.

prerequisites.refresher_md: If $x=e^{rt}$, then $\dot x=re^{rt}$ and $\ddot x=r^2e^{rt}$.
$e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ packages two real oscillatory solutions; the physical displacement is real.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Linear equations let you combine simple solutions into a general one. Exponentials are useful because differentiation keeps their shape.

parts.title: Homogeneous and driven equations
parts.body_md: For $a\ddot x+b\dot x+cx=0$, sums of solutions remain solutions. With a drive f(t), a particular solution plus any homogeneous solution is general. Two driven solutions cannot simply be added without also adding their drives.

parts.title: Roots tell the motion
parts.body_md: Substituting $e^{rt}$ gives $ar^2+br+c=0$. Distinct real roots give two exponentials; complex conjugate roots give oscillation with an exponential envelope. A repeated root requires $(A+Bt)e^{rt}$, not two identical exponentials.

parts.title: Initial data
parts.body_md: For a second-order equation, use x(0) and $\dot x(0)$ to determine two constants. A guessed solution must be substituted into the original equation before it is trusted.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$x=e^{\lambda t}\ \Longrightarrow\ a\lambda^2+b\lambda+c=0$$

For $a\ddot x+b\dot x+cx=0$, $\lambda$ has units $s^{-1}$. Two distinct roots give $x=Ae^{\lambda_1t}+Be^{\lambda_2t}$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: x,A,C are displacements (m) in the oscillator example; u,v are speeds $(m/s)$; $r,\alpha ,\gamma ,\omega$ are rates $(s^{-1})$; t is in s. Coefficients in a differential equation must make all its terms share units.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Superposition applies to homogeneous linear equations. Repeated roots need $te^{\lambda t}$; a driven equation needs one particular solution too.

examples.title: A decaying velocity
examples.setup_md: A cart obeys $\dot v+\alpha v=0$ with $v(0)=u$ and $\alpha$ positive.

steps.why: The exponential turns differentiation into multiplication by r.
The root gives the time dependence.
Use the initial velocity.

examples.answer_md: $v(t)=ue^{-\alpha t}$.
examples.check_md: Substitution gives $\dot v=-\alpha v$; the exponent is dimensionless.

examples.title: An oscillator with both initial position and velocity
examples.setup_md: Solve $\ddot x+\omega^2x=0$ with $x(0)=A$ and $\dot x(0)=u$.

steps.why: The exponential roots are imaginary.
Combine the complex pair into a real displacement.
The sine vanishes initially.
Differentiate before imposing the initial velocity.
Both independent initial facts now appear.

examples.answer_md: The amplitude is $\sqrt{A^2+(u/\omega)^2}$, not necessarily A.
examples.check_md: Putting $u=0$ gives release from rest; putting $A=0$ gives a launch through equilibrium.

practice.question_md: Why is $x=Ae^{-\gamma t}$ alone insufficient for every solution of $\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x+\gamma^2x=0$?
hints: A second-order equation still needs two independent constants.
practice.answer_md: The general solution is $(A+Bt)e^{-\gamma t}$; the extra $t$ supplies the second independent solution.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 101–105; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

4.2.title: Simple harmonic motion
4.2.summary: A stable restoring force pulls toward equilibrium and, for small displacements, is often proportional to displacement. That produces simple harmonic motion.

prerequisites.refresher_md: The x in a spring’s restoring law is measured from its equilibrium position; a constant load can shift that position.
Angular frequency $\omega$ has units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$; ordinary frequency is $f=\omega/(2\pi)$ and period $T=2\pi/\omega$.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A stable restoring force pulls toward equilibrium and, for small displacements, is often proportional to displacement. That produces simple harmonic motion.

parts.title: The restoring sign
parts.body_md: $m\ddot x=-kx$ means a positive displacement has negative acceleration. Matching $\ddot x=-\omega^2x$ identifies $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$; the amplitude comes from initial conditions, not from $k/m$.

parts.title: Energy and phase
parts.body_md: $x=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)$ gives $v=-A\omega\sin(\omega t+\phi)$. Energy swaps between $kx^2/2$ and $mv^2/2$ while their sum stays fixed. Speed is largest at equilibrium.

parts.title: Simple pendulum
parts.body_md: The tangential restoring force is $-mg \sin (\theta )$. The small-angle replacement $\sin\theta\approx\theta$ makes it harmonic; the full pendulum is not exactly sinusoidal at large angles.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$m\ddot x=-kx,\qquad x=A\cos(\omega_0t+\phi),\qquad\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$$

$x,A$ (m), $k$ $(N/m)$, $m$ (kg), $\omega_0$ $(\mathrm{rad}/s)$, $\phi$ (rad). This is an ideal undamped linear spring.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m is mass (kg); k is $N/m$; $x,A,\ell$ are lengths (m); $\theta$ is in radians; $\omega$ is $s^{-1}$; period T is s; energy is J.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: At the center the force is zero but speed is greatest; at a turning point speed is zero but acceleration is greatest.

examples.title: A displaced spring
examples.setup_md: A mass m is released from rest at displacement A on a frictionless horizontal spring of stiffness k.

steps.why: Identify the coefficient multiplying the restoring displacement.
Release from rest fixes the phase at an extremum.
Differentiate to obtain velocity.
The sine magnitude can reach one.

examples.answer_md: The period is $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ and maximum speed is $A\sqrt{k/m}$.
examples.check_md: At release acceleration is largest in magnitude but speed is zero.

examples.title: A small pendulum swing
examples.setup_md: A bob on a light string length $\ell$ is released at small angle theta0 from vertical.

steps.why: Use tangential acceleration $\ell$ times angular acceleration.
Use the small-angle approximation in radians.
Match the oscillator and impose zero initial angular velocity.
Convert angular speed back to tangential speed.

examples.answer_md: $T\simeq2\pi\sqrt{\ell/g}$; this is only the small-angle period.
examples.check_md: The bob mass cancels, but string length does not.

practice.question_md: A spring mass passes equilibrium at speed u. What is its amplitude?
hints: At equilibrium all oscillator energy is kinetic.
Equate that energy to the potential at maximum displacement.
practice.answer_md: $\tfrac12mu^2=\tfrac12kA^2$, so $A=u\sqrt{m/k}$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 105–107; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

4.3.title: Damped harmonic motion
4.3.summary: Damping removes mechanical energy. Whether the mass oscillates on the way back depends on damping relative to its natural frequency.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $F_d=-b\dot x$ opposes velocity; b has units $\mathrm{kg}/s$.
$\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$ and $\gamma=b/(2m)$ both have units $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Damping removes mechanical energy. Whether the mass oscillates on the way back depends on damping relative to its natural frequency.

parts.title: Three damping regimes
parts.body_md: $\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x+\omega_0^2x=0$ has roots $-\gamma\pm\sqrt{\gamma^2-\omega_0^2}$. Underdamped: $\gamma <\omega _{0}$, with oscillation frequency $\omega_d=\sqrt{\omega_0^2-\gamma^2}$. Critical: equality. Overdamped: two real decay rates, generally no repeated crossings.

parts.title: Energy accounting
parts.body_md: $dE/dt=-b\dot x^2\le0$. The underdamped amplitude envelope decays as $e^{-\gamma t}$; cycle-averaged energy follows $e^{-2\gamma t}$. Instantaneous energy need not equal a perfectly smooth exponential.

parts.title: Return without overshoot
parts.body_md: Critical damping gives the boundary between oscillatory and nonoscillatory response. A very large b can return slowly because the slow root is approximately $-k/b$; more damping is not always a quicker return.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\ddot x+2\gamma\dot x+\omega_0^2x=0,\qquad\gamma=\frac{b}{2m}$$

$F_d=-b\dot x$, $b$ $(\mathrm{kg}/s)$, $\gamma,\omega_0$ $(s^{-1})$. Underdamped: $\gamma<\omega_0$; critical: equal; overdamped: greater.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m is kg; k is $N/m$; b is $\mathrm{kg}/s$; $\gamma =b/(2m), \omega _{0}$ and $\omega _{d}$ are $s^{-1}$; x,A are m; energy E is J; damping time is $1/\gamma$ in s.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: This drag is not constant-magnitude dry friction. At critical damping the solution is $(A+Bt)e^{-\gamma t}$, not two identical exponentials.

examples.title: Underdamped release from rest
examples.setup_md: Release a damped spring at $x=A$ with $v=0$; assume $\gamma <\omega _{0}$.

steps.why: Use the complex characteristic roots.
Apply the initial displacement.
Differentiate the whole product before applying zero initial velocity.
The sine term is necessary for a true release from rest.

examples.answer_md: The envelope shrinks while the oscillation proceeds at $\omega _{d}$, below the undamped frequency.
examples.check_md: Simply using $A \exp (-\gamma t) \cos (\omega _{d} t)$ would give nonzero initial velocity.

examples.title: Critical return
examples.setup_md: For $\gamma =\omega _{0}$, release at $x=A$ with $v=0$.

steps.why: A repeated root needs two independent solutions.
Apply position and velocity at $t=0$.
Substitute $D=\gamma A$.
Differentiate to check the direction for $t>0$.

examples.answer_md: For $A>0$ it decreases toward equilibrium without crossing it.
examples.check_md: The initial derivative is zero and the long-time position tends to zero.

practice.question_md: If damping b is quadrupled while mass stays fixed, how does the underdamped amplitude decay time $2m/b$ change?
hints: Take the ratio before assuming the motion stays underdamped.
practice.answer_md: It becomes one quarter as long if the system remains underdamped; otherwise the oscillatory-envelope description no longer applies.

visual.description: A damped spring mass; use displacement and velocity to see that damping opposes motion, not displacement.

4.4.title: Driven (and damped) harmonic motion
4.4.summary: A repeated push can sustain motion against damping. The response size and phase depend on how the push frequency compares with the oscillator’s own frequency.

prerequisites.refresher_md: The full solution is a decaying transient plus a driven steady response. Steady-state formulas do not automatically satisfy arbitrary initial conditions.
In $x=A\cos(\Omega t-\delta)$, positive $\delta$ means displacement lags the driving force.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A repeated push can sustain motion against damping. The response size and phase depend on how the push frequency compares with the oscillator’s own frequency.

parts.title: Response amplitude and phase
parts.body_md: For $m\ddot x+b\dot x+kx=F_0\cos\Omega t$, use $A=F_0/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+b^2\Omega^2}$ and $\delta=\operatorname{atan2}(b\Omega,k-m\Omega^2)$. The two-argument phase keeps the correct quadrant.

parts.title: Resonance
parts.body_md: The displacement-amplitude peak occurs at $\Omega^2=\omega_0^2-2\gamma^2$ when this is positive. At strong damping the amplitude decreases from its zero-frequency value. Maximum average absorbed power occurs at omega0, a different criterion.

parts.title: The phase phi and the power
parts.body_md: At low frequency displacement follows force; at omega0 it lags by $\pi /2$; at high frequency it nearly opposes force. Average power is $\langle P\rangle=bA^2\Omega^2/2$. With zero damping at exact resonance, there is no bounded steady-state amplitude.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$A=\frac{F_0/m}{\sqrt{(\omega_0^2-\Omega^2)^2+(2\gamma\Omega)^2}}$$

Drive is $F_0\cos\Omega t$ (N); $A$ (m), $\Omega,\omega_0,\gamma$ $(s^{-1})$. Lag is $\delta=\operatorname{atan2}(2\gamma\Omega,\omega_0^2-\Omega^2)$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $F_{0}$ is driving-force amplitude (N); m is kg; b is $\mathrm{kg}/s$; k is $N/m$; A is displacement amplitude (m); $\Omega ,\omega _{0},\gamma$ are $s^{-1}$; $\delta$ is a phase in radians; average power is $W=J/s$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The displacement-amplitude peak is at $\sqrt{\omega_0^2-2\gamma^2}$ when real; do not call every resonance peak exactly $\omega_0$.

examples.title: Driven exactly at the natural frequency
examples.setup_md: A damped spring with $b>0$ is driven at $\Omega=\omega_0=\sqrt{k/m}$. Consider the settled response.

steps.why: The spring and inertial terms cancel in the steady-response denominator.
Only the damping term remains, and the phase is a quarter-cycle lag.
Convert cosine minus $\pi /2$ into sine.
Substitute the amplitude into the average dissipated power.

examples.answer_md: The force is in phase with velocity, supplying the energy lost to drag.
examples.check_md: This amplitude formula diverges as b tends to zero; the steady-state assumption fails at exact undamped resonance.

examples.title: Undamped resonant growth
examples.setup_md: Set $b=0$, drive at omega0, and start at $x=0,v=0$.

steps.why: State the exact resonant equation.
Multiply the resonant trial shape by time to avoid a homogeneous solution.
Differentiate twice; the terms proportional to t cancel.
Match the drive coefficient.

examples.answer_md: $x=F_0t\sin(\omega_0t)/(2m\omega_0)$ has a linearly growing envelope.
examples.check_md: It satisfies both zero initial conditions. Real systems eventually violate the ideal linear, undamped model.

practice.question_md: A drive varies very slowly compared with omega0. What are the approximate amplitude and phase?
hints: Think of a slowly loaded spring.
practice.answer_md: $A\simeq F_0/k$ and $\delta\simeq0$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 109–115; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

4.5.title: Coupled oscillators
4.5.summary: A coupling spring responds to the difference between two displacements. Normal modes are special motions that preserve a fixed shape while the whole pattern oscillates.

prerequisites.refresher_md: If the right endpoint moves by $x_{2}$ and the left by $x_{1}$, the spring extension changes by $x_2-x_1$.
A linear system can superpose independent mode motions. The mode amplitudes are determined by the initial displacements and velocities.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A coupling spring responds to the difference between two displacements. Normal modes are special motions that preserve a fixed shape while the whole pattern oscillates.

parts.title: Start with the physical pattern
parts.body_md: For two equal masses and three equal springs, moving both masses together leaves the middle spring unchanged. Moving them oppositely stretches it strongly. Therefore the opposite-motion mode must be faster.

parts.title: Turn equations into modes
parts.body_md: For equal masses m and all three springs k, $m\ddot x_1=-2kx_1+kx_2$, $m\ddot x_2=kx_1-2kx_2$. Adding gives a separate equation for $x_1+x_2$; subtracting gives one for $x_1-x_2$. In a larger system, the same idea becomes an eigenvector problem.

parts.title: General coupling and beats
parts.body_md: If the outside springs have k and the middle spring has stiffness $\kappa$, the squared frequencies are $k/m$ and $(k+2\kappa)/m$. Weak coupling makes these close and produces slow energy exchange. These coefficients belong to this explicitly defined three-spring setup; they must not be transferred to a differently arranged example.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md: For the equal-three-spring setup, $m\ddot x_1=-2kx_1+kx_2$ and $m\ddot x_2=kx_1-2kx_2$. If sums and differences are not obvious, try $x_1=Ae^{i\omega t}$, $x_2=Be^{i\omega t}$. A nonzero amplitude pair requires $(2k-m\omega^2)^2-k^2=0$. The two roots give frequencies; substitute each into either original algebra equation to find $B/A$. A mode is a displacement pattern such as (1,-1); a normal coordinate such as $x_{1}-x_{2}$ isolates that pattern. For unequal coefficients, the correct combinations need not be simple sums and differences. Morin’s opening example instead uses $2\ddot x+\omega_0^2(5x-3y)=0$ and $2\ddot y+\omega_0^2(5y-3x)=0$: its sum frequency is omega0 and its difference frequency is 2omega0. That illustrates the same method with different coefficients; it is not the identical-spring scene’s equation.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m is each mass (kg); k is each outside spring stiffness $(N/m)$; $\kappa$ is middle stiffness when different $(N/m)$; $x_{1},x_{2},A$ are displacements (m); $\omega _{+},\omega _{-}$ are $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A normal mode has a fixed displacement ratio. Releasing just one mass combines modes; it is not by itself a pure in-phase or out-of-phase mode.

examples.title: Find the two fixed-shape motions
examples.setup_md: Two equal masses m lie between walls on a frictionless line, with three identical springs k. Coordinates measure displacement from equilibrium.

steps.why: In-phase motion leaves the middle spring unstretched.
Match the single-oscillator form.
Opposite motion doubles the middle-spring extension in addition to the outside spring.
The stronger restoring force gives the larger frequency.

examples.answer_md: The mode shapes are (1,1) and (1,-1), with frequencies $\sqrt{k/m}$ and $\sqrt{3k/m}$.
examples.check_md: A mode shape is a ratio and relative sign, not a requirement that every displacement equal one metre.

examples.title: Release only the left mass
examples.setup_md: Use the same three-spring apparatus. Initially $x_{1}=A,x_{2}=0$ and both velocities vanish.

steps.why: Decompose the initial shape into the two mode shapes.
The left component is positive in both modes.
The right component changes sign in the opposite mode.
Check the initial displacements after recombining.

examples.answer_md: Each mass generally combines both frequencies; neither motion is one simple sinusoid.
examples.check_md: Both derivatives vanish initially because both contributions are cosines.

practice.question_md: Both masses are displaced by the same A and released. Which mode is present, and what does the middle spring do?
hints: Compare the initial vector with (1,1) and (1,-1).
practice.answer_md: Only the in-phase mode occurs: $x_1=x_2=A\cos(\sqrt{k/m}\,t)$; the middle spring has no changing extension.

visual.description: Exact equal-mass, three-identical-spring apparatus used in both worked examples.

5.1.title: Conservation of energy in one dimension
5.1.summary: Work tells you how a force changes kinetic energy. For a conservative force, the same transfer can be tracked as a change in potential energy.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $dW=F_x\,dx$ in one dimension. A force opposite the displacement does negative work.
Kinetic and potential energy are in joules: $1\,\mathrm J=1\,\mathrm{N\,m}$.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Work tells you how a force changes kinetic energy. For a conservative force, the same transfer can be tracked as a change in potential energy.

parts.title: From force to potential
parts.body_md: $\Delta K=\int F_xdx$ follows from $ma=mv\,dv/dx$. Define $V(b)-V(a)=-\int_a^bF_xdx$ for a conservative force, so $K+V$ is constant. Only differences in V matter.

parts.title: Gravitational potential and near-Earth gravity
parts.body_md: With zero potential at infinity, $V=-GMm/r$. For a small height h above a large radius R, the change is approximately mgh, with $g=GM/R^2$. Do not combine the negative inverse-radius potential and an unrelated zero point without taking a difference.

parts.title: Work versus potential; raising a book
parts.body_md: If you count gravity through potential energy, do not also add its work to the same side of the energy balance. A slowly raised book receives positive work from your hand and negative work from gravity; its kinetic energy stays constant while gravitational potential rises.

parts.title: Constraints and the unwinding-string method
parts.body_md: Energy can relate speed to geometry while a perpendicular tension does no work. It may not determine the geometry alone: the thin-pole unwinding-string example also needs horizontal circular-motion balance. Count unknowns after writing energy; a second physical equation may still be essential.

parts.title: Connecting energy to circular balance
parts.body_md: For Morin’s thin-pole idealization, let the unwound string length be $\ell$ and its angle to vertical be $\theta$. The drop is $\ell \cos (\theta )$, so energy gives $v^2=2g\ell\cos\theta$. Nearly horizontal circular motion gives $T\cos\theta=mg$ and $T\sin\theta=mv^2/(\ell\sin\theta)$. Eliminating T gives $v^2=g\ell\sin\theta\tan\theta$. Equating the two speed expressions gives $\tan^2\theta=2$. The important method is that energy supplies one relation while the constrained circular motion supplies the other; the slow lowering and thin pole are essential assumptions.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$E=\tfrac12mv^2+V(x),\qquad F(x)=-\frac{dV}{dx}$$

$E,V$ (J), $m$ (kg), $v$ $(m/s)$, $x$ (m). Mechanical energy is constant for this time-independent conservative force.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: K,V,E,W are energies or work (J); m,M are kg; k is $N/m$; x,A,h,R are lengths (m); g is $m/s^{2}$; G is $m^{3}/(\mathrm{kg} s^{2})$; v is $m/s$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Energy determines speed, not its sign. Turning points have $E=V$; equilibrium requires $V'=0$, a different condition.

examples.title: Spring compression becomes speed
examples.setup_md: A frictionless mass m is released from a spring compression A. Find speed at displacement x from equilibrium.

steps.why: At release the speed is zero.
The conservative spring transfers energy between kinetic and potential forms.
Isolate the speed squared.

examples.answer_md: $|v|=\sqrt{(k/m)(A^2-x^2)}$, valid for $|x|\le A$. Direction must be supplied separately.
examples.check_md: At the turning points the speed vanishes; outside the allowed interval the squared speed would be negative.

examples.title: Gravity over a finite height
examples.setup_md: A mass falls from radius R+h to radius R outside a spherical planet of mass M, starting at rest.

steps.why: Use the same zero of potential in both states.
Cancel m and isolate speed.
Express the result using surface g.

examples.answer_md: The exact speed is $\sqrt{2gh/(1+h/R)}$; for h much smaller than R it approaches $\sqrt{2gh}$.
examples.check_md: Constant surface gravity slightly overestimates the speed because gravity is weaker above the surface.

practice.question_md: A hand raises a book of mass m through height h at constant speed. Give the work by the hand, work by gravity and change in kinetic energy.
hints: Constant speed means zero net work.
Upward displacement makes gravitational work negative.
practice.answer_md: $W_{hand}=mgh$, $W_g=-mgh$, $\Delta K=0$; gravitational potential increases by mgh.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 138–147; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.2.title: Small oscillations
5.2.summary: Near a stable minimum, even a complicated potential looks like a spring. Its curvature gives the effective stiffness.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $V(x_0+\eta)=V(x_0)+V\prime(x_0)\eta+V\prime\prime(x_0)\eta^2/2+\cdots$.
Equilibrium needs $V\prime(x_0)=0$; positive curvature gives a restoring force for small departures.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Near a stable minimum, even a complicated potential looks like a spring. Its curvature gives the effective stiffness.

parts.title: Find the minimum before expanding
parts.body_md: First solve for the equilibrium position. Then define displacement $\eta$ from that position. Expanding about an arbitrary origin can leave a constant force and conceal the oscillator.

parts.title: What curvature measures
parts.body_md: $k_{eff}=V\prime\prime(x_0)$ has units $N/m$ for a Cartesian length coordinate; $\omega^2=k_{eff}/m$. A maximum gives negative $\omega^2$ and instability. Zero curvature requires higher-order analysis.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$V(x)\simeq V(x_0)+\tfrac12V''(x_0)(x-x_0)^2,\qquad\omega=\sqrt{V''(x_0)/m}$$

Require $V'(x_0)=0$ and $V''(x_0)>0$. Curvature has units $N/m$; $\omega$ is $\mathrm{rad}/s$. Displacement must be small enough for higher terms to be negligible.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $x,x_{0},\eta$ are lengths (m); V is J; $V^{\prime}$ is N; $V^{\prime\prime}$ is $N/m$; m is kg; k and b in the quartic example are $N/m$; a in that example is $J/m^{4}$; $\omega$ is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: If the quadratic coefficient vanishes, this formula does not prove finite-frequency harmonic motion; inspect higher terms.

examples.title: A vertical spring shifts its center
examples.setup_md: A mass m hangs on a spring of stiffness k. Let x be downward extension from its unstretched length.

steps.why: Downward movement lowers gravitational potential.
Find equilibrium before describing oscillation.
The constant gravity term cancels at equilibrium.
Curvature remains k; gravity changes the center, not this frequency.

examples.answer_md: Oscillations occur about $x_0=mg/k$ with period $2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$.
examples.check_md: Measuring x from the unstretched spring without shifting would not give the homogeneous oscillator equation.

examples.title: Two wells, one unstable middle
examples.setup_md: A particle has potential $V=ax^4-bx^2$, where $a,b>0$.

steps.why: Differentiate to locate stationary points.
Set the force to zero.
Differentiate again to test stability.
The middle is a maximum; the outer points are minima.
Use the curvature of either well.

examples.answer_md: Small oscillations about either minimum have the same frequency; small deviations from $x=0$ grow instead.
examples.check_md: b has units $N/m$, so $4b/m$ has units inverse seconds squared.

practice.question_md: For $V=\tfrac12kx^2+cx$ with $k>0$, find the equilibrium and small-oscillation frequency.
practice.answer_md: $x_0=-c/k$, $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 147–148; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.3.title: Conservation of energy in three dimensions
5.3.summary: A potential energy landscape assigns one energy to each position. If the work depends on the route, one such potential cannot describe the whole force.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=F_xdx+F_ydy+F_zdz$ keeps only the force component along a small displacement.
When differentiating V with respect to x, hold y and z fixed.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A potential energy landscape assigns one energy to each position. If the work depends on the route, one such potential cannot describe the whole force.

parts.title: Gradient and work
parts.body_md: $\mathbf F=-\nabla V$ gives each component from a partial derivative. Then $\Delta K=W$ and $K+V$ is conserved for a time-independent potential. A force perpendicular to velocity does zero instantaneous work.

parts.title: Conservative forces in three dimensions
parts.body_md: Path independence is equivalent to zero work around every closed loop. On a simply connected smooth region, $\nabla\times\mathbf F=0$ is a local test that implies a potential. Singularities and holes in the domain require care.

parts.title: Central force
parts.body_md: A force depending only on radius and directed radially has potential $V(r)$ with $F_r=-dV/dr$. Tangential displacement does no work. This prepares the later reduction of orbits to radial motion.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$W=\int\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=-\Delta V,\qquad\mathbf F=-\boldsymbol\nabla V$$

Work and potential are in J. For a smooth field in a simply connected region, zero curl ensures a potential. Mechanical energy is conserved when the potential has no explicit time dependence.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: V,W,K are J; x,y,a,b are lengths (m); $k,\kappa ,c$ in these examples are $N/m$; force components are N; v is $m/s$; m is kg.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Position dependence alone does not guarantee a conservative force. Check the field and its domain; friction is not recovered from a single position potential.

examples.title: A two-direction spring landscape
examples.setup_md: A particle has $V=\tfrac12kx^2+\tfrac12\kappa y^2$. Find force and speed change from (a,0) to (0,b).

steps.why: Take a separate partial derivative in each direction.
Evaluate potential at the two endpoints.
Conservative work changes kinetic energy by the negative potential difference.
Solve for the final speed squared.

examples.answer_md: The speed relation depends on endpoints, not on the route, if the point is dynamically reachable.
examples.check_md: A negative predicted squared speed means the proposed endpoint cannot be reached with that initial energy.

examples.title: A rotating force field has no single potential
examples.setup_md: Let $\mathbf F=\kappa(-y,x)$ in a plane. Compare paths from (0,0) to (a,b), with $a,b>0$.

steps.why: The first horizontal segment has $y=0$; the second has $x=a$.
Reversing the order changes which component does work.
Different work for the same endpoints rules out a global potential here.

examples.answer_md: This field is nonconservative; its circulation around the rectangle is $2 \kappa ab$.
examples.check_md: Kappa has units $N/m$, so $\kappa ab$ is energy.

practice.question_md: For $V(x,y)=cxy$, find the force components and compare the cross derivatives.
hints: Differentiate while holding the other coordinate fixed.
Compare partial F_y/partial x with partial F_x/partial y.
practice.answer_md: $F_x=-cy$, $F_y=-cx$; both cross derivatives equal -c, consistent with a conservative force.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 148–152; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.4.title: Gravity
5.4.summary: Newtonian gravity adds the attractions from all mass elements. Spherical symmetry makes that sum simple; a torsion balance lets a small attraction measure G.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $G$ has units $\mathrm{m^3/(kg\,s^2)}$ and $F=GMm/r^2$ is the magnitude for point masses.
Replace a mass sum with $dm=\rho\,dV$ for volume density $\rho$.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Newtonian gravity adds the attractions from all mass elements. Spherical symmetry makes that sum simple; a torsion balance lets a small attraction measure G.

parts.title: Universal law and superposition
parts.body_md: Each pair attracts along the line joining it. Sum forces as vectors, not magnitudes. Outside a spherically symmetric body, its field equals a point mass at its center. Inside a spherical shell the field is zero; inside a solid body only enclosed mass contributes.

parts.title: Supporting a tube
parts.body_md: In a uniform sphere, g(r) increases linearly from zero to its surface value. A thin uniform radial column therefore has average gravitational acceleration equal to half the surface value. Integrate its weight slice by slice; multiplying all its mass by surface g would overestimate the support force.

parts.title: Cavendish measurement
parts.body_md: A torsion fibre converts a tiny gravitational torque into a measurable angle. Calibrate its stiffness, account for both force arms and the actual separations, then infer G. The experiment measures G, rather than assuming Earth’s mass from its weight.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$F_r=-\frac{GMm}{r^2},\qquad V=-\frac{GMm}{r}$$

$G$ $(m^{3}/(\mathrm{kg}\cdot s^{2}))$, masses (kg), separation $r$ (m), force (N), potential (J). Choose $V=0$ at infinity. Outside a spherical mass distribution use its total mass.

parts.title: A radial column feels changing gravity
parts.body_md: For a narrow uniform column of cross-section A extending from the center to radius R inside a uniform sphere, $dm=\rho A\,dr$ and $g(r)=g_s r/R$. Its support force is $F=\int_0^R g(r)\,dm=(\rho A g_s/R)\int_0^R r\,dr=\rho ARg_s/2=M_{column}g_s/2$. This is an application of summing local weights, not a new constant-gravity law. The ideal narrow hole is assumed not to disturb the sphere’s gravitational field appreciably.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: G is $m^{3}/(\mathrm{kg} s^{2})$; M,m are kg; r,R,d are m; $\rho$ is $\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$; $\phi$ is twist in radians; torsional $\kappa$ is $N m/\mathrm{rad}$; torque is N m; oscillation frequency is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The point-mass exterior formula cannot use total enclosed-plus-exterior mass unchanged inside a sphere.

examples.title: Gravity inside a uniform sphere
examples.setup_md: A spherical body of radius R and uniform density $\rho$ contains a test mass m at radius $r<R$. Neglect the test mass’s disturbance.

steps.why: Only the mass interior to r contributes to the radial gravitational field; outer shells cancel.
Insert the enclosed mass into the spherical gravitational law.
Along a straight tunnel through the center, use a signed coordinate for the same restoring acceleration.

examples.answer_md: Along an ideal central tunnel the motion is harmonic, with $\omega^2=4\pi G\rho/3$.
examples.check_md: The field goes to zero at the center and matches $GM/R$ squared at the surface; real Earth density is not uniform.

examples.title: Infer G from a torsion balance
examples.setup_md: Two small masses m sit at opposite ends of a light rod, distance d from its suspension axis. Two nearby masses M each exert approximately transverse attraction at center separation r. Cross-attractions are neglected.

steps.why: Use the pairwise gravitational force for each nearby pair.
Both attractions twist the rod in the same sense, with equal lever arms.
At equilibrium the torsion fibre’s restoring torque balances gravity.
Solve for the unknown gravitational constant.

examples.answer_md: G follows from the measured twist and calibrated torsional stiffness $\kappa$.
examples.check_md: The torque coefficient has units N m per radian; geometry and background gravitational torques matter in a real experiment.

practice.question_md: At radius $R/2$ inside a uniform sphere, compare gravity with its surface value.
hints: Find the fraction of enclosed mass.
Then divide by the squared radius fraction.
practice.answer_md: The enclosed mass is $M/8$, so $g(R/2)=(1/8)/(1/4)\,g(R)=g(R)/2$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 152–156; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.4.1.title: Newton’s universal law of gravitation
5.4.1.summary: Use pairwise attraction for arbitrary masses and the shell theorem only when the source distribution is spherical.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Add gravitational vectors from different sources. Opposing contributions can cancel even though every pairwise force is attractive.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Use pairwise attraction for arbitrary masses and the shell theorem only when the source distribution is spherical.

parts.title: Shells and a solid sphere
parts.body_md: Outside a spherical shell, $F_r=-GMm/r^2$; inside it, zero. A solid spherical distribution is a stack of shells, so $g(r)=GM(<r)/r^2$. Uniform density is an additional assumption, not part of the shell theorem.

parts.title: Potential and zero point
parts.body_md: Choosing zero at infinity gives $V=-GMm/r$ outside. Inside a shell the potential is constant, not zero: its gradient vanishes there.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$F_r=-\frac{GmM(<r)}{r^2}$$

$M(<r)$ is mass inside radius $r$ (kg). Exterior spherical shells contribute zero net field inside them, although their potential need not vanish.

parts.title: A radial column feels changing gravity
parts.body_md: For a narrow uniform column of cross-section A extending from the center to radius R inside a uniform sphere, $dm=\rho A\,dr$ and $g(r)=g_s r/R$. Its support force is $F=\int_0^R g(r)\,dm=(\rho A g_s/R)\int_0^R r\,dr=\rho ARg_s/2=M_{column}g_s/2$. This is an application of summing local weights, not a new constant-gravity law. The ideal narrow hole is assumed not to disturb the sphere’s gravitational field appreciably.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: G is $m^{3}/(\mathrm{kg} s^{2})$; M,m are kg; r,R,d are m; $\rho$ is $\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$; $\phi$ is twist in radians; torsional $\kappa$ is $N m/\mathrm{rad}$; torque is N m; oscillation frequency is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Shell results require spherical symmetry. Zero force inside a shell means constant potential, not necessarily zero potential.

examples.title: Gravity inside a uniform sphere
examples.setup_md: A spherical body of radius R and uniform density $\rho$ contains a test mass m at radius $r<R$. Neglect the test mass’s disturbance.

steps.why: Only the mass interior to r contributes to the radial gravitational field; outer shells cancel.
Insert the enclosed mass into the spherical gravitational law.
Along a straight tunnel through the center, use a signed coordinate for the same restoring acceleration.

examples.answer_md: Along an ideal central tunnel the motion is harmonic, with $\omega^2=4\pi G\rho/3$.
examples.check_md: The field goes to zero at the center and matches $GM/R$ squared at the surface; real Earth density is not uniform.

practice.question_md: Two equal masses M are fixed at $x=+a$ and $x=-a$. What is the gravitational force on a test mass at $x=0$?
practice.answer_md: The net force is zero by vector cancellation; the potential is negative, not zero.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 152–154; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.4.2.title: The Cavendish experiment
5.4.2.summary: A torsion balance measures a tiny force by allowing it to twist a calibrated fibre. The angle is the readout, and force-to-torque geometry connects it to G.

prerequisites.refresher_md: A perpendicular force F at distance d contributes torque dF.
$\tau=-\kappa\phi$ is the rotational analogue of Hooke’s law for a small twist.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A torsion balance measures a tiny force by allowing it to twist a calibrated fibre. The angle is the readout, and force-to-torque geometry connects it to G.

parts.title: Calibrate before inferring gravity
parts.body_md: If the suspended assembly has known moment of inertia I and free period T, $\kappa=4\pi^2I/T^2$ for small, weakly damped torsional oscillations. Then use the static deflection under the source masses.

parts.title: Model the geometry
parts.body_md: Both test masses and both source masses contribute. The simple two-equal-torque formula below assumes the nearby force dominates and is transverse. A real measurement sums all pairwise torques, subtracts backgrounds and controls vibration.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\kappa\theta=\tau_g,\qquad F=\frac{GMm}{r^2}$$

$\kappa$ is torsional stiffness $(N\cdot m/\mathrm{rad})$, $\theta$ twist (rad), $\tau_g$ gravitational torque $(N\cdot m)$, and masses/separations are measured independently.

parts.title: Calibration quantities
parts.body_md: I is the suspended assembly’s moment of inertia $(\mathrm{kg} m^{2}), T$ is its small-oscillation period (s), and $\kappa$ is torsional stiffness $(N m/\mathrm{rad})$. The letter T denotes period here, not rope tension.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: G is $m^{3}/(\mathrm{kg} s^{2})$; M,m are kg; r,R,d are m; $\rho$ is $\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$; $\phi$ is twist in radians; torsional $\kappa$ is $N m/\mathrm{rad}$; torque is N m; oscillation frequency is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
