parts.body_md: Measuring surface gravity determines $GM_{\rm Earth}$, not $G$ by itself. Account for all source masses and lever arms.

examples.title: Infer G from a torsion balance
examples.setup_md: Two small masses m sit at opposite ends of a light rod, distance d from its suspension axis. Two nearby masses M each exert approximately transverse attraction at center separation r. Cross-attractions are neglected.

steps.why: Use the pairwise gravitational force for each nearby pair.
Both attractions twist the rod in the same sense, with equal lever arms.
At equilibrium the torsion fibre’s restoring torque balances gravity.
Solve for the unknown gravitational constant.

examples.answer_md: G follows from the measured twist and calibrated torsional stiffness $\kappa$.
examples.check_md: The torque coefficient has units N m per radian; geometry and background gravitational torques matter in a real experiment.

practice.question_md: If the torsion fibre stiffness doubles and all gravitational geometry stays fixed, what happens to the equilibrium twist?
practice.answer_md: The twist halves.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 154–156; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.5.title: Momentum
5.5.summary: Momentum tracks how motion is redistributed between interacting bodies. Choose a system whose external impulse is known before declaring momentum conserved.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\mathbf p=m\mathbf v$ has units $\mathrm{kg} m/s$. Impulse $\int\mathbf Fdt$ has the same units.
A fixed collection of particles can include fuel that later leaves or material that later joins a cart.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Momentum tracks how motion is redistributed between interacting bodies. Choose a system whose external impulse is known before declaring momentum conserved.

parts.title: Conservation of momentum
parts.body_md: Internal action-reaction pairs cancel in the total momentum equation. Momentum is conserved in each direction with negligible external impulse, even if kinetic energy becomes heat.

parts.title: Snow on a sled
parts.body_md: Capturing material at a different velocity transfers momentum into the chosen moving subsystem. Write momentum before and after including that parcel; using $F=ma$ on a changing mass without the flux term gives wrong results.

parts.title: Rocket motion
parts.body_md: For a rocket with backward relative exhaust speed u, $M\dot v=-u\dot M+F_{ext}$. Since mass loss has $\dot M<0$, the thrust term points forward. With gravity, integrate its contribution too; the force-free logarithm alone is incomplete.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\mathbf P=\sum_i m_i\mathbf v_i,\qquad\Delta\mathbf P=\int\mathbf F_{\rm ext}\,dt$$

Momentum is $\mathrm{kg}\cdot m/s$, impulse $N\cdot s$. For rockets, include expelled fuel while applying conservation over each short interval.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $M,M_{0},M_{f},q$ are masses (kg); v,u are speeds $(m/s)$; P is momentum $(\mathrm{kg} m/s)$; $dM/dt$ is a mass-change rate $(\mathrm{kg}/s)$; F is N; impulse is N s.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Momentum conservation concerns the whole chosen system. A rocket alone loses mass and exchanges momentum with its exhaust.

examples.title: A cart gathers falling material
examples.setup_md: A frictionless cart initially has mass M and horizontal speed u. It catches mass q of material with zero initial horizontal speed.

steps.why: The falling material brings no horizontal momentum.
After capture all the collected mass moves with the cart.
Negligible external horizontal impulse conserves total horizontal momentum.

examples.answer_md: The cart slows as it collects mass, even without an external horizontal force.
examples.check_md: This is not a fixed-mass system if you draw the boundary around the cart alone; include the incoming material.

examples.title: A rocket coasting in space
examples.setup_md: A rocket ejects fuel backward at constant speed u relative to itself. Its mass decreases from $M_{0}$ to $M_{f}$, with no external force.

steps.why: Include the ejected parcel; dM is negative and its mass is -dM.
Drop the product dM dv and cancel the initial momentum.
Integrate the infinitesimal momentum balance.
Mass ratio, rather than burned mass alone, controls the ideal speed gain.

examples.answer_md: $\Delta v=u\ln(M_0/M_f)$ in the force-free, constant-exhaust-speed model.
examples.check_md: $M_{f}<M_{0}$ gives positive forward acceleration; the exhaust speed is measured relative to the rocket, not the ground.

practice.question_md: A cart of mass M moving at u catches another mass M dropped with zero horizontal speed. Find final speed and the fraction of initial kinetic energy left.
hints: Conserve horizontal momentum, not kinetic energy.
Compute final kinetic energy with the combined mass.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 156–161; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.5.1.title: Conservation of momentum
5.5.1.summary: An internal collision can redistribute momentum but cannot change the total without an external impulse.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\Delta\mathbf P=\int\mathbf F_{ext}dt$. Small duration alone does not guarantee small impulse if the external force is huge.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: An internal collision can redistribute momentum but cannot change the total without an external impulse.

parts.title: Choosing the closed system
parts.body_md: Include every body exchanging important momentum. For a cart catching snow, the cart-plus-incoming-snow system has conserved horizontal momentum even though the cart’s mass changes.

parts.title: What conservation does not promise
parts.body_md: Kinetic energy, each individual velocity and momentum in the presence of external forces are not automatically conserved. Momentum is a vector; write components.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\frac{d\mathbf P}{dt}=\mathbf F_{\rm ext}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbf P={\rm constant}$$

This classical statement assumes the full isolated material system and appropriate internal action-reaction balance. Momentum is a vector in $\mathrm{kg}\cdot m/s$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $M,M_{0},M_{f},q$ are masses (kg); v,u are speeds $(m/s)$; P is momentum $(\mathrm{kg} m/s)$; $dM/dt$ is a mass-change rate $(\mathrm{kg}/s)$; F is N; impulse is N s.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Zero initial momentum does not mean each particle stays motionless. Also check whether external forces deliver appreciable impulse during the event.

examples.title: A cart gathers falling material
examples.setup_md: A frictionless cart initially has mass M and horizontal speed u. It catches mass q of material with zero initial horizontal speed.

steps.why: The falling material brings no horizontal momentum.
After capture all the collected mass moves with the cart.
Negligible external horizontal impulse conserves total horizontal momentum.

examples.answer_md: The cart slows as it collects mass, even without an external horizontal force.
examples.check_md: This is not a fixed-mass system if you draw the boundary around the cart alone; include the incoming material.

practice.question_md: Two initially stationary people on frictionless skates push apart. One has mass m and moves right at u; the other has mass 2m. Find the other velocity.
practice.answer_md: $mu+2mv=0$, so the heavier person moves left at speed $u/2$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 156–159; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.5.2.title: Rocket motion
5.5.2.summary: A rocket accelerates by giving exhaust backward momentum. No air or external surface is needed to push against.

prerequisites.refresher_md: If M is the remaining rocket mass, $dM<0$ during burning. The ejected parcel has positive mass -dM.
If the rocket moves at v and exhaust leaves backward at relative speed u, its inertial velocity is approximately v-u.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A rocket accelerates by giving exhaust backward momentum. No air or external surface is needed to push against.

parts.title: Derive one parcel at a time
parts.body_md: Write total momentum before and after a tiny ejection, retain first-order terms, and only then take a derivative. This avoids confusing exhaust-relative speed with its ground-frame speed.

parts.title: External forces and burn time
parts.body_md: $\dot v=-u\dot M/M-g$ for a vertical ascent with constant g and negligible drag. Over burn time $t_{b}$, $\Delta v=u\ln(M_0/M_f)-gt_b$; gravity losses depend on time as well as mass ratio.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$m\,dv=-u\,dm,\qquad\Delta v=u\ln\frac{m_i}{m_f}$$

$u>0$ is exhaust speed $(m/s)$, $dm<0$ rocket mass change, and $m_i,m_f$ are initial/final rocket masses. Formula assumes constant $u$ and no external force.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $M,M_{0},M_{f},q$ are masses (kg); v,u are speeds $(m/s)$; P is momentum $(\mathrm{kg} m/s)$; $dM/dt$ is a mass-change rate $(\mathrm{kg}/s)$; F is N; impulse is N s.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Do not apply $F=d(mv)/dt$ to the shrinking rocket alone without the outgoing momentum flux.

examples.title: A rocket coasting in space
examples.setup_md: A rocket ejects fuel backward at constant speed u relative to itself. Its mass decreases from $M_{0}$ to $M_{f}$, with no external force.

steps.why: Include the ejected parcel; dM is negative and its mass is -dM.
Drop the product dM dv and cancel the initial momentum.
Integrate the infinitesimal momentum balance.
Mass ratio, rather than burned mass alone, controls the ideal speed gain.

examples.answer_md: $\Delta v=u\ln(M_0/M_f)$ in the force-free, constant-exhaust-speed model.
examples.check_md: $M_{f}<M_{0}$ gives positive forward acceleration; the exhaust speed is measured relative to the rocket, not the ground.

practice.question_md: A force-free rocket has exhaust speed u and burns from mass 4M to M. What speed gain does it get? What if it burns from 8M to 2M?
practice.answer_md: Both gains equal $u\ln4$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 159–161; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.6.title: The center of mass frame
5.6.summary: The center-of-mass frame removes the shared drift of a system. What remains is the motion of its parts relative to one another.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\mathbf R=\sum m_i\mathbf r_i/\sum m_i$ weights each position by mass.
$\mathbf v_i\prime=\mathbf v_i-\mathbf V$ for a frame moving at constant velocity V.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: The center-of-mass frame removes the shared drift of a system. What remains is the motion of its parts relative to one another.

parts.title: Definition and acceleration
parts.body_md: $\mathbf V_{CM}=\mathbf P/M$ and $M\mathbf a_{CM}=\mathbf F_{ext}$. A fixed inertial CM frame is available when the external total force vanishes. The origin need not coincide with a material particle.

parts.title: Kinetic-energy split
parts.body_md: $K=MV_{CM}^2/2+\sum m_iv_i\prime{}^2/2$. The cross terms vanish because the CM-frame total momentum is zero. For two bodies, the second term is $\mu v_{rel}^2/2$.

parts.title: Two-body collisions
parts.body_md: For an elastic one-dimensional collision the CM velocities reverse. Transform to the CM frame, reverse the two velocities, then transform back. Reversal requires elasticity and actual collision; it is not a rule for sticking.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\mathbf V_{\rm CM}=\frac{\mathbf P}{M},\qquad\mathbf v_i'=\mathbf v_i-\mathbf V_{\rm CM}$$

$M=\sum m_i$ (kg), velocities $(m/s)$, and total CM-frame momentum is zero. This is an inertial frame when external net force is zero.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $m,m_{1},m_{2},M,\mu$ are masses (kg); $R_{\mathrm{CM}}$ is a position (m); $V_{\mathrm{CM}},v,u$ are velocities $(m/s)$; K is J; P is $\mathrm{kg} m/s$. A prime labels a different frame, not a derivative, in these collision formulas.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The CM need not lie on material. Changing frame changes kinetic energy, while the interaction physics remains consistent.

examples.title: Find the frame with zero total momentum
examples.setup_md: Mass m moves right at speed u, while mass 3m is initially at rest.

steps.why: The center-of-mass velocity is total momentum divided by total mass.
Subtract the frame velocity from the first body’s lab velocity.
Transform the second body using the same frame velocity.
Verify that the transformed total momentum vanishes.

examples.answer_md: The CM frame moves right at $u/4$; the bodies approach with opposite momenta.
examples.check_md: The relative velocity remains u in both Galilean frames.

examples.title: Separate shared travel from relative motion
examples.setup_md: Two masses m and 3m have lab velocities u and zero. Find the kinetic energy associated with center-of-mass travel and relative motion.

steps.why: Only the first mass moves in the lab initially.
Treat the total mass as moving at the CM velocity.
The reduced mass packages the relative degree of freedom.
Use relative speed u.
The two contributions recover the lab energy.

examples.answer_md: One quarter of the lab kinetic energy is CM travel; three quarters is relative motion.
examples.check_md: If the masses stick with no external impulse, only the relative part can become internal energy.

examples.title: Solve the collision by changing frames
examples.setup_md: A mass m moving at u hits a stationary mass 3m elastically in one dimension. Use the CM frame instead of solving a quadratic energy equation.

steps.why: Subtract the shared CM velocity from each initial lab velocity.
In an actual one-dimensional elastic collision, both CM-frame velocities reverse.
Transform the first outgoing velocity back to the lab.
Add the same frame velocity to the other outgoing velocity.

examples.answer_md: The light body rebounds and the heavy body moves forward, both at speed $u/2$ in the lab.
examples.check_md: The relative speed reverses from +u to -u while total momentum remains $m u$.

practice.question_md: Two equal masses move with velocities +u and -u. What is $V_{\mathrm{CM}}$, and is their kinetic energy zero?
hints: Add momenta before dividing by total mass.
Kinetic energy uses squares, not signed velocities.
practice.answer_md: $V_{CM}=0$, but $K=mu^2$; all of it is relative motion.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 161–164; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.6.1.title: Definition
5.6.1.summary: Find a system’s average motion by dividing total momentum by total mass. Subtract this velocity to see the internal motion clearly.

prerequisites.refresher_md: The heavier body contributes more to the center-of-mass position and velocity.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Find a system’s average motion by dividing total momentum by total mass. Subtract this velocity to see the internal motion clearly.

parts.title: Position and motion
parts.body_md: $\mathbf R_{CM}=(m_1\mathbf r_1+m_2\mathbf r_2)/(m_1+m_2)$. Differentiate to obtain velocity, and differentiate again to relate acceleration to external forces.

parts.title: Lab versus CM
parts.body_md: Neither frame is automatically more real. Choose the CM frame when symmetric incoming/outgoing momenta simplify the collision, then return to the frame requested in the question.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\mathbf R=\frac{\sum m_i\mathbf r_i}{M},\qquad M\ddot{\mathbf R}=\mathbf F_{\rm ext}$$

$\mathbf R$ is in m, $M$ in kg and external force in N, for a fixed collection of constant masses.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $m,m_{1},m_{2},M,\mu$ are masses (kg); $R_{\mathrm{CM}}$ is a position (m); $V_{\mathrm{CM}},v,u$ are velocities $(m/s)$; K is J; P is $\mathrm{kg} m/s$. A prime labels a different frame, not a derivative, in these collision formulas.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A simple midpoint works only for equal masses or matching symmetry. Do not confuse CM velocity with each particle's velocity.

examples.title: Find the frame with zero total momentum
examples.setup_md: Mass m moves right at speed u, while mass 3m is initially at rest.

steps.why: The center-of-mass velocity is total momentum divided by total mass.
Subtract the frame velocity from the first body’s lab velocity.
Transform the second body using the same frame velocity.
Verify that the transformed total momentum vanishes.

examples.answer_md: The CM frame moves right at $u/4$; the bodies approach with opposite momenta.
examples.check_md: The relative velocity remains u in both Galilean frames.

practice.question_md: Mass m sits at $x=0$ and mass 2m at $x=L$. Find the center-of-mass position.
hints: Use mass times position in the numerator.
practice.answer_md: $X_{CM}=2L/3$, closer to the heavier mass.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 161–163; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.6.2.title: Kinetic energy
5.6.2.summary: Kinetic energy includes a frame-dependent shared drift and energy of relative motion. The CM frame removes the first part.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Write $\mathbf v_i=\mathbf V+\mathbf v_i\prime$ before squaring; the cross term matters until summed.
$\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ has units of mass and describes two-body relative kinetic energy.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Kinetic energy includes a frame-dependent shared drift and energy of relative motion. The CM frame removes the first part.

parts.title: Why the cross term vanishes
parts.body_md: $\sum m_i\mathbf v_i\prime=0$ in the CM frame, so the summed term $\mathbf V\cdot\sum m_i\mathbf v_i\prime$ is zero. This yields $K=MV^2/2+K_{relative}$.

parts.title: Energy loss in a sticking collision
parts.body_md: With no external impulse, shared CM motion cannot change. Sticking removes the relative motion, so its kinetic energy becomes deformation, heat or other internal energy.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$K=\tfrac12MV_{\rm CM}^2+K_{\rm CM},\qquad K_{\rm CM}=\sum_i\tfrac12m_i{v_i'}^2$$

All energies are in J; $V_{\rm CM},v_i'$ are in $m/s$. This classical decomposition is exact for constant masses.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $m,m_{1},m_{2},M,\mu$ are masses (kg); $R_{\mathrm{CM}}$ is a position (m); $V_{\mathrm{CM}},v,u$ are velocities $(m/s)$; K is J; P is $\mathrm{kg} m/s$. A prime labels a different frame, not a derivative, in these collision formulas.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Zero CM momentum does not mean zero CM kinetic energy. Oppositely moving particles still carry energy.

examples.title: Separate shared travel from relative motion
examples.setup_md: Two masses m and 3m have lab velocities u and zero. Find the kinetic energy associated with center-of-mass travel and relative motion.

steps.why: Only the first mass moves in the lab initially.
Treat the total mass as moving at the CM velocity.
The reduced mass packages the relative degree of freedom.
Use relative speed u.
The two contributions recover the lab energy.

examples.answer_md: One quarter of the lab kinetic energy is CM travel; three quarters is relative motion.
examples.check_md: If the masses stick with no external impulse, only the relative part can become internal energy.

practice.question_md: Masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ approach with relative speed u and stick. How much kinetic energy is lost?
hints: There is no final relative motion.
practice.answer_md: $\Delta K_{lost}=\tfrac12\mu u^2$, with $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 163–164; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.7.title: Collisions
5.7.summary: Momentum constrains every isolated collision; kinetic energy supplies an extra equation only for an elastic one. Directional geometry decides how many unknowns remain.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Elastic means total translational kinetic energy is conserved in the ideal model. Sticking is maximally inelastic for the given masses and momentum.
In a plane, momentum provides separate x and y equations; an angle or impact geometry may still be needed.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Momentum constrains every isolated collision; kinetic energy supplies an extra equation only for an elastic one. Directional geometry decides how many unknowns remain.

parts.title: One-dimensional motion
parts.body_md: For elastic impact, $(v_2-v_1)=-(u_2-u_1)$ together with momentum conservation is often easier than two quadratic energy terms. With coefficient of restitution e, replace reversal by relative separation speed e times approach speed, where $0\le e\le 1$ for a passive collision.

parts.title: Two-dimensional motion and billiards
parts.body_md: Resolve momentum along chosen axes. For equal masses with one initially at rest, elastic energy and vector momentum force perpendicular nonzero outgoing velocities. In general, conservation alone may leave a scattering angle free; contact geometry supplies it.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\sum\mathbf p_i=\sum\mathbf p_f,\qquad K_i=K_f\ \text{(elastic)}$$

Momentum has units $\mathrm{kg}\cdot m/s$ and kinetic energy J. Inelastic collisions convert some organized kinetic energy to internal energy.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m is mass (kg); $u,v_{1},v_{2}$ are velocities $(m/s)$; K is J; e is a dimensionless coefficient of restitution; scattering angles are dimensionless radians or clearly marked degrees.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Sticking is perfectly inelastic, not elastic. Conservation laws alone may need geometric or impact information to determine all outgoing directions.

examples.title: An unequal-mass elastic impact
examples.setup_md: A mass m moving right at u hits a stationary mass 3m in one dimension; the collision is elastic.

steps.why: Conserve total momentum.
Elastic one-dimensional collisions reverse the relative velocity.
Use the relative-velocity relation to eliminate one unknown.
Substitute into momentum conservation.
Recover the first velocity: it rebounds.

examples.answer_md: The light mass rebounds at $u/2$ and the heavy mass moves forward at $u/2$.

examples.title: Why equal billiard balls separate at a right angle
examples.setup_md: An equal-mass elastic collision occurs on a frictionless plane. Initially one ball moves at velocity u-vector and the other rests. Ignore spin.

steps.why: Cancel the common mass in vector momentum conservation.
Cancel the common half-mass in kinetic-energy conservation.
Square the vector momentum equation.
Compare the two expressions for u squared.

examples.answer_md: The two nonzero outgoing velocities are perpendicular; a head-on exchange with one ball stopped is a degenerate case.
examples.check_md: This relies on equal masses, elasticity and one initially stationary ball; it is not a universal collision angle.

practice.question_md: A mass m moving at u sticks to a stationary mass 3m. Find final velocity and the fraction of initial kinetic energy retained.
hints: Conserve momentum for the combined mass.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 164–167; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.7.1.title: One-dimensional motion
5.7.1.summary: In one dimension, an elastic collision is fixed by momentum conservation and reversal of relative velocity.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Keep rightward positive for every mass; a negative final velocity means a rebound.
$K_i=K_f$ is additional information; momentum conservation alone does not determine two final velocities.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: In one dimension, an elastic collision is fixed by momentum conservation and reversal of relative velocity.

parts.title: A reusable route
parts.body_md: Write momentum, write the elastic relative-velocity relation, solve the resulting linear pair, then verify energy and easy mass-ratio limits.

parts.title: Special cases
parts.body_md: Equal masses exchange velocities. A light mass hitting a very heavy stationary target nearly reverses. A very heavy moving mass changes little while a light stationary target can leave near twice the heavy mass’s initial speed.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$v_{1f}=\frac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}v,\qquad v_{2f}=\frac{2m_1}{m_1+m_2}v$$

These formulas assume particle 1 initially moves at signed velocity $v$ and particle 2 is initially at rest. Masses are in kg, velocities in $m/s$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m is mass (kg); $u,v_{1},v_{2}$ are velocities $(m/s)$; K is J; e is a dimensionless coefficient of restitution; scattering angles are dimensionless radians or clearly marked degrees.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A negative result is a direction, not a negative speed. These particular formulas cannot be used unchanged for two moving incoming particles.

examples.title: An unequal-mass elastic impact
examples.setup_md: A mass m moving right at u hits a stationary mass 3m in one dimension; the collision is elastic.

steps.why: Conserve total momentum.
Elastic one-dimensional collisions reverse the relative velocity.
Use the relative-velocity relation to eliminate one unknown.
Substitute into momentum conservation.
Recover the first velocity: it rebounds.

examples.answer_md: The light mass rebounds at $u/2$ and the heavy mass moves forward at $u/2$.

practice.question_md: Two equal masses have initial velocities 3u and -u and collide elastically in one dimension. Find their final velocities.
hints: For equal masses an elastic head-on collision exchanges velocities.
Check both momentum and energy afterward.
practice.answer_md: The first leaves with -u and the second with 3u.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 164–166; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.7.2.title: Two-dimensional motion
5.7.2.summary: In a planar collision, conserve momentum as a vector. Energy controls speed magnitudes but cannot by itself choose a direction.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=ab\cos\phi$; a zero dot product means perpendicular nonzero vectors.
A vector equality gives one scalar equation for each independent axis.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: In a planar collision, conserve momentum as a vector. Energy controls speed magnitudes but cannot by itself choose a direction.

parts.title: Recognize the billiards pattern
parts.body_md: Equal masses, one initially at rest, and an elastic collision imply perpendicular outgoing paths when both move. Real balls with spin, friction or deformation can depart from this idealization.

parts.title: Determining speeds from an angle
parts.body_md: If one outgoing equal-mass ball makes angle $\theta$ to the initial direction, its speed is $u\cos\theta$ and the other’s is $u\sin\theta$ in this ideal right-angle geometry.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\mathbf v=\mathbf v_1'+\mathbf v_2',\qquad v^2={v_1'}^2+{v_2'}^2$$

These relations are for equal masses, an initially stationary target and an elastic collision. Velocities are in $m/s$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m is mass (kg); $u,v_{1},v_{2}$ are velocities $(m/s)$; K is J; e is a dimensionless coefficient of restitution; scattering angles are dimensionless radians or clearly marked degrees.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The right-angle result is a special case, not every elastic collision. Unequal masses or a moving target change it.

examples.title: Why equal billiard balls separate at a right angle
examples.setup_md: An equal-mass elastic collision occurs on a frictionless plane. Initially one ball moves at velocity u-vector and the other rests. Ignore spin.

steps.why: Cancel the common mass in vector momentum conservation.
Cancel the common half-mass in kinetic-energy conservation.
Square the vector momentum equation.
Compare the two expressions for u squared.

examples.answer_md: The two nonzero outgoing velocities are perpendicular; a head-on exchange with one ball stopped is a degenerate case.
examples.check_md: This relies on equal masses, elasticity and one initially stationary ball; it is not a universal collision angle.

practice.question_md: In that ideal equal-ball collision, one outgoing ball makes 30 degrees with the original direction. Find both speeds.
hints: Resolve the initial speed along the two final directions.
practice.answer_md: The 30-degree ball has speed $\sqrt3u/2$; the other has speed $u/2$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 166–167; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

5.8.title: Inherently inelastic processes
5.8.summary: When material joins or leaves a stream, momentum transfer can demand a force while mechanical energy is irreversibly lost. Track the moving mass and the momentum flux separately.

prerequisites.refresher_md: A rate $\sigma$ in $\mathrm{kg}/s$ differs from a line density $\lambda$ in $\mathrm{kg}/m$. For a line moving at speed v, the passing mass rate is $\lambda v$.
$P=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v$ is the rate at which a force transfers energy at its point of action.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: When material joins or leaves a stream, momentum transfer can demand a force while mechanical energy is irreversibly lost. Track the moving mass and the momentum flux separately.

parts.title: Sand on a conveyor
parts.body_md: The motor supplies momentum to new grains. Its work is not all stored as the grains’ kinetic energy; the velocity mismatch becomes heat. Slowing the frictional transfer does not remove this loss for the same initial and final velocities.

parts.title: Chain on a scale
parts.body_md: The scale both supports deposited weight and stops arriving links. For an ideal freely falling flexible chain with links stopping inelastically, add the momentum flux to the supported weight. Do not conserve mechanical energy for the entire chain.

parts.title: The chain model matters
parts.body_md: A chain making a smooth bend can transfer energy through tension, unlike a sequence of links stopping abruptly with slack between them. Different limiting procedures for link spacing and bend size can give different motion; an “ideal chain” label alone does not choose the model.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$K_i-K_f=\tfrac12\mu(v_1-v_2)^2,\qquad\mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2}$$

For two masses sticking in 1D with negligible external impulse; $\mu$ (kg), velocities $(m/s)$, lost kinetic energy (J).

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $\sigma$ is incoming mass rate $(\mathrm{kg}/s)$; $\lambda$ is line density $(\mathrm{kg}/m)$; V,u,v are speeds $(m/s)$; x is deposited length (m); F,N are N; power and heat rate are W.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Total energy is still conserved. The loss is from the kinetic-energy account, not disappearance of energy; material collection needs momentum flux.

examples.title: A conveyor catches moving grains
examples.setup_md: A belt moves at fixed speed V and receives grains at mass rate $\sigma$ with incoming horizontal speed $u<V$. The grains end moving at V.

steps.why: The motor supplies the horizontal momentum increase per second.
The belt contact moves at speed V.
Subtract incoming from outgoing kinetic-energy flux.
The difference is the unavoidable conversion into internal energy.

examples.answer_md: Heat production is $\sigma(V-u)^2/2$.
examples.check_md: It vanishes when grains already match the belt speed; vertical-impact losses are excluded from this horizontal calculation.

examples.title: A chain reaches a scale with an initial speed
examples.setup_md: An ideal uniform chain of line density $\lambda$ reaches a scale already moving downward at speed u. After length x has landed, the still-falling part has fallen distance x and links stop abruptly.

steps.why: The moving part falls freely in this particular inelastic-link model.
A length v dt arrives during time dt.
Each arriving parcel loses its downward momentum.
Add weight of deposited length x to the stopping force.

examples.answer_md: Before the last link arrives, the reading exceeds deposited weight because momentum $m u$ st also be stopped.
examples.check_md: After all material has settled, the flux term vanishes and the reading is just the total weight.

practice.question_md: A belt of speed V receives stationary grains at rate $\sigma$. What fraction of the motor’s horizontal work rate becomes heat?
practice.answer_md: One half: $\dot Q=\sigma V^2/2$ while $P_{motor}=\sigma V^2$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 167–173; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.1.title: The Euler–Lagrange equations
6.1.summary: The Lagrangian method describes motion through energies and convenient coordinates. It often removes constraint forces that would clutter a force diagram.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For ordinary conservative mechanics, $L=T-V$; both T and V are in joules.
Treat q and $\dot q$ as independent inputs when taking partial derivatives of L; take the total time derivative afterward.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: The Lagrangian method describes motion through energies and convenient coordinates. It often removes constraint forces that would clutter a force diagram.

parts.title: Choose independent coordinates
parts.body_md: Use enough coordinates to specify the configuration, after applying geometrical constraints. A rigid pendulum needs one angle; a spring pendulum needs both length and angle. Write position in terms of those coordinates to calculate speed.

parts.title: The Euler–Lagrange recipe
parts.body_md: For each coordinate q, calculate $\partial L/\partial\dot q$, differentiate it in time, calculate $\partial L/\partial q$, then equate them. A generalized coordinate may be an angle; its conjugate momentum is then often angular momentum, not linear momentum.

parts.title: Spring pendulum
parts.body_md: A bob attached to an extensible light spring has two coupled motions. Radial extension changes angular inertia, so the angular equation contains a term proportional to radial speed. Omitting that term breaks angular-momentum accounting.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$L=T-V,\qquad\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}$$

$L,T,V$ are in J. $q_i$ may be length (m) or angle (rad); its conjugate momentum has corresponding units. Ideal holonomic constraints fit this formulation.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: L,T,V are energies (J); $r,\ell ,\ell _{0}$ are m; $\theta$ is an angle in radians; m is kg; k is $N/m$; g is $m/s^{2}$. A dot is a time derivative; angular conjugate momentum is $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Treat $q$ and $\dot q$ as independent during partial differentiation. Only then take the total time derivative.

examples.title: Recover the pendulum equation from energies
examples.setup_md: A bob of mass m is held a fixed distance $\ell$ from a pivot. $\theta$ is measured from downward vertical.

steps.why: Use tangential speed $\ell \dot\theta$ and height above the lowest point.
Subtract potential from kinetic energy.
The length is constant, so only angular velocity differentiates.
Differentiate the position-dependent term.
Equate the two expressions and divide by $m \ell$ squared.

examples.answer_md: The exact pendulum equation emerges without first solving for tension.
examples.check_md: For small angles it becomes the harmonic equation; the full sine remains necessary for large swings.

examples.title: Let the pendulum stretch
examples.setup_md: A bob m hangs from a light spring of stiffness k and relaxed length ℓ₀. Its instantaneous length is r and angle $\theta$ is measured from downward vertical.

steps.why: Combine radial and tangential speeds; the vertical coordinate is $-r \cos (\theta )$.
Apply Euler–Lagrange to r.
Apply it separately to $\theta$.
Expand the derivative before dividing by mr.

examples.answer_md: These two equations describe coupled stretching and swinging; neither coordinate is generally a separate oscillator.
examples.check_md: At a static vertical equilibrium, $r=\ell _{0}+mg/k$; holding r constant recovers the rigid-pendulum angular equation.

practice.question_md: For $L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-\tfrac12kx^2$, write the two derivatives needed for Euler–Lagrange and the resulting motion equation.
hints: Differentiate with respect to $\dot x$ before taking a time derivative.
The x derivative of L is $-kx$.
practice.answer_md: $d(\partial L/\partial\dot x)/dt=m\ddot x$, $\partial L/\partial x=-kx$; hence $m\ddot x=-kx$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 218–221; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.2.title: The principle of stationary action
6.2.summary: The actual path makes the first-order change of action vanish when nearby paths have the same endpoints. This is a stationarity statement, not always a minimum.

prerequisites.refresher_md: A function takes a number to a number. The action takes a whole candidate path q(t) to a number.
$\int f\dot\eta\,dt=[f\eta]-\int\dot f\eta\,dt$ moves the derivative off a small path variation.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: The actual path makes the first-order change of action vanish when nearby paths have the same endpoints. This is a stationarity statement, not always a minimum.

parts.title: Vary the path
parts.body_md: Set $q_\epsilon=q+\epsilon\eta$, with $\eta(t_i)=\eta(t_f)=0$. To first order, $\delta S=\int[(\partial L/\partial q)\eta+(\partial L/\partial\dot q)\dot\eta]dt$. Integrating by parts removes the endpoint term and leaves the Euler–Lagrange equation because $\eta$ is otherwise arbitrary.

parts.title: What is held fixed
parts.body_md: Both endpoint positions and endpoint times are fixed in this basic derivation. Initial-value motion still needs initial position and velocity; the variational proof is a way to derive the equations, not a claim that a particle consciously chooses a destination.

parts.title: Stationary versus least
parts.body_md: A first derivative of zero can describe a minimum, maximum or saddle of an action functional. Also, adding a total time derivative of a coordinate function changes the action only by fixed endpoint values and leaves the motion unchanged.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$S=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}L\,dt,\qquad\delta S=0$$

Action $S$ has units $J\cdot s$. The varied path has $\delta q(t_1)=\delta q(t_2)=0$. Stationary means first-order change vanishes.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: L is J and action S is J s; x,D are m; t,T are s; F is N; m is kg. Eta is a small path variation with the same units as its coordinate; $\epsilon$ can be chosen dimensionless.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Stationary does not always mean a minimum. Do not vary endpoint times in this fixed-endpoint derivation.

examples.title: Why a free particle travels uniformly
examples.setup_md: A free particle must go from $x=0$ at $t=0$ to $x=D$ at $t=T$, with $T>0$.

steps.why: There is no potential energy.
Euler–Lagrange follows from stationary action.
Zero acceleration makes position linear in time.
Use the fixed endpoints.

examples.answer_md: The stationary path is $x=Dt/T$.
examples.check_md: Uneven speed adds a positive integral of squared speed deviations to this free-particle action, so this particular stationary path is also a minimum.

examples.title: Stationarity with a constant force
examples.setup_md: A particle experiences constant force F along x and has endpoints $x(0)=0,x(T)=D$.

steps.why: Choose $V=-Fx$ so the force is +F.
The action variation produces a constant acceleration.
Apply the initial position to the integrated equation.
Use the final endpoint to determine the initial velocity.

examples.check_md: For $F=0$ this reduces to the free-particle straight line in time.

practice.question_md: Does adding $d(c x)/dt$ to a Lagrangian, with constant c, change its equations of motion for fixed endpoint positions?
hints: Integrate the added term over time.
Ask whether its endpoint difference changes under the allowed path variations.
practice.answer_md: No. It adds $c[x(T)-x(0)]$ to the action, a fixed endpoint quantity.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 221–227; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.3.title: Forces of constraint
6.3.summary: Constraint forces keep a body on its allowed geometry. Eliminating a coordinate hides that force; retaining the constraint with a multiplier lets you recover it.

prerequisites.refresher_md: A holonomic constraint is a relation $f(q,t)=0$ between coordinates and possibly time.
An ideal fixed constraint force is perpendicular to every allowed infinitesimal displacement, so its virtual work vanishes.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Constraint forces keep a body on its allowed geometry. Eliminating a coordinate hides that force; retaining the constraint with a multiplier lets you recover it.

parts.title: Multiplier convention
parts.body_md: Use $d(\partial L/\partial\dot q_i)/dt-\partial L/\partial q_i=\lambda\,\partial f/\partial q_i$ together with $f=0$. The physical constraint-force components are the multiplier times the gradient; $\lambda$ alone depends on how f is normalized.

parts.title: What the reduced equations omit
parts.body_md: A fixed-length pendulum’s one-angle equation determines motion but not tension directly. Introduce r temporarily and impose $r=\ell$ afterward. Moving constraints can do work, so absence of friction does not automatically imply conserved particle energy.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}=\lambda\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}$$

Constraint is $f(q,t)=0$. $\lambda$ units depend on how $f$ is defined; the product on the right is the generalized constraint force.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $r,\ell ,x,y$ are m; m is kg; $\theta ,\alpha$ are angles; T,N are forces (N). $\lambda$ has units determined by the constraint f: for $f=r-\ell$ or $y-x \tan (\alpha ), \lambda$ is N.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The multiplier is not automatically a force in N for every constraint normalization. Interpret its coefficient in the actual coordinate equation.

examples.title: Recover pendulum tension
examples.setup_md: For a bob m, use polar coordinates $r,\theta$ from downward vertical and impose $f=r-\ell =0$.

steps.why: Keep r as a coordinate long enough to expose its radial force.
Apply the stated multiplier convention to r.
Set $r=\ell$ and $\ddot r=0$ after deriving the equation.
Positive r points outward, while tension points inward.

examples.answer_md: The string tension contains both a gravitational component and the force needed for circular acceleration.
examples.check_md: At the bottom T exceeds $mg$ while the bob moves. A computed negative T means a string cannot enforce the assumed path.

examples.title: Find a ramp’s normal force using a constraint
examples.setup_md: A mass slides on the line $y=x \tan (\alpha )$, with x right and y up. The ramp is fixed and frictionless.

steps.why: Describe the ramp algebraically without rotating coordinates.
The gradient of f supplies the constraint-force direction.
Differentiate the fixed constraint twice and substitute into the equations.
The multiplier is the vertical component, not the normal-force magnitude.

examples.answer_md: $N=mg\cos\alpha$ for an ordinary incline between 0 and 90 degrees.
examples.check_md: Rescaling f would rescale $\lambda$ but leave $\lambda$ times grad f unchanged.

practice.question_md: For a bob at the bottom of a taut pendulum with speed v, write the tension.
practice.answer_md: $T=mg+mv^2/\ell$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 227–229; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.4.title: Change of coordinates
6.4.summary: Changing coordinates changes the algebra, not the physical trajectory. Transform the kinetic energy carefully; nonlinear coordinates can make the effective inertia depend on position.

prerequisites.refresher_md: If $x=x(q)$, then $\dot x=(dx/dq)\dot q$. Transform velocities before writing kinetic energy.
Use an invertible coordinate transformation in the region of interest; coordinate singularities need separate care.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Changing coordinates changes the algebra, not the physical trajectory. Transform the kinetic energy carefully; nonlinear coordinates can make the effective inertia depend on position.

parts.title: From Cartesian to polar
parts.body_md: $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$ give $\dot x^2+\dot y^2=\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2$. The factor r squared is essential; treating $\dot\theta$ as a linear speed loses the geometry.

parts.title: Euler–Lagrange keeps its form
parts.body_md: After expressing L in the new coordinates and their velocities, use the same Euler–Lagrange procedure. Generalized force and momentum need not be Cartesian components. A transformation that depends explicitly on time can introduce time dependence even when the old L had none.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$T=\tfrac12m(\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2)$$

For planar polar coordinates, $r$ is in m, $\theta$ in rad and $T$ in J. The extra factor $r^2$ comes from tangential speed $r\dot\theta$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $x_{1},x_{2},R,q,r$ are lengths (m); $\theta$ is in radians; $m_{1},m_{2},M,\mu$ are kg; L,T,V are J. Angular momentum $mr^{2} \dot\theta$ is $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Do not just relabel $x$ as $r$ while leaving Cartesian kinetic energy unchanged.

examples.title: A free particle viewed in polar coordinates
examples.setup_md: A particle m moves freely in a plane; use r and $\theta$ instead of x,y.

steps.why: Insert the polar expression for speed squared.
Apply Euler–Lagrange to r.
$\theta$ does not occur explicitly in L.
Expand the angular equation.

examples.answer_md: The resulting radial and tangential acceleration components are both zero, as required for straight-line inertial motion.
examples.check_md: $\ddot r$ can be positive even for a free particle because the polar origin is fixed while the particle passes it.

examples.title: Coordinates that separate shared and relative motion
examples.setup_md: Two particles with masses $m_{1},m_{2}$ have positions $x_{1},x_{2}$. Define R as their center of mass and $q=x_{1}-x_{2}$.

steps.why: Solve the definitions for the original coordinates.

steps.math: \dot x_1=\dot R+\frac{m_2}{M}\dot q,\quad\dot x_2=\dot R-\frac{m_1}{M}\dot q
steps.why: Differentiate each expression.
Expand both squares; the cross terms cancel.
The remaining coefficient is the reduced mass.

examples.answer_md: For a potential depending only on q, R is a free coordinate and q contains the interaction.
examples.check_md: Equal masses give $\mu =m/2$, not the total mass 2m.

practice.question_md: A mass moves only along a circle of fixed radius R. What is its kinetic energy in the angle $\theta$ coordinate?
practice.answer_md: $T=\tfrac12mR^2\dot\theta^2$; the angular inertia is $mR^2$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 229–232; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.5.title: Conservation laws
6.5.summary: Missing coordinates and missing time dependence reveal conserved quantities before you solve the full motion.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $p_i=\partial L/\partial\dot q_i$. Its units depend on the coordinate: a length gives linear momentum, an angle often gives angular momentum.
L can vary along a trajectory through q(t) without having explicit dependence on the clock t.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Missing coordinates and missing time dependence reveal conserved quantities before you solve the full motion.

parts.title: Cyclic coordinates
parts.body_md: If $\partial L/\partial q_i=0$, then $p_i$ is constant. A free Cartesian coordinate gives a conserved linear momentum. In cylindrical coordinates a cyclic azimuth gives $mr^2\dot\phi$; in spherical coordinates it gives $mr^2\sin^2\theta\dot\phi$, the z angular momentum.

parts.title: Energy conservation
parts.body_md: Define $\mathcal E=\sum_i\dot q_i p_i-L$. Along the motion, $d\mathcal E/dt=-\partial L/\partial t$. For time-independent L it is constant. It equals T+V under the usual quadratic kinetic-energy and time-independent-coordinate assumptions, not in every generalized formulation.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$p_i=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i},\qquad E=\sum_i\dot q_i p_i-L$$

If $\partial L/\partial q_i=0$, then $p_i$ is conserved. If $\partial L/\partial t=0$, then $E$ is conserved. $E$ has units J.

parts.title: Which angular momentum?
parts.body_md: In cylindrical coordinates $(r,\phi ,z), \phi$ is the azimuth around z. If L has no $\phi$ or z dependence, $p_\phi=mr^2\dot\phi$ and $p_z=m\dot z$ are conserved. In spherical coordinates, $\theta$ is the angle from the positive z axis and $\phi$ is again azimuth, so $p_\phi=mr^2\sin^2\theta\dot\phi$. This is the z component of angular momentum, not generally its full magnitude.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: L and the energy function are J; q may be a length or angle; $p_{q}$ has units J s per unit of q. Thus Cartesian momentum is $\mathrm{kg} m/s$ while angular momentum is $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Absent coordinate and absent coordinate velocity are different conditions. The conserved $E$ equals $T+V$ under the usual time-independent-coordinate, quadratic-kinetic assumptions.

examples.title: A central potential conserves angular momentum
examples.setup_md: A mass m moves in a plane with a potential V(r).

steps.why: Neither the kinetic geometry nor the potential depends on the absolute angle $\phi$.
$\phi$ is cyclic.
Apply Euler–Lagrange to the missing coordinate.
Compute the conserved conjugate momentum.

examples.answer_md: Angular momentum is conserved even while radius and angular speed change.
examples.check_md: It is r squared times angular speed that stays fixed, not angular speed alone.

examples.title: Recognize the conserved energy
examples.setup_md: For a spring mass use $L=m\dot x^2/2-kx^2/2$.

steps.why: First compute the conjugate momentum.
Use the energy-function definition, not simply minus L.
Substitute and simplify.
There is no explicit time dependence.

examples.answer_md: The energy function equals the usual total mechanical energy for this ordinary time-independent-coordinate system.
examples.check_md: If coordinates or external constraints depend on time, the energy function need not be the particle’s ordinary T+V.

practice.question_md: For $L=\tfrac12m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)-mgy$, which Cartesian momentum is conserved?
hints: Look for a coordinate absent from L itself.
practice.answer_md: $p_x=m\dot x$ is conserved; $p_y$ changes because $\partial L/\partial y=-mg$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 232–236; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.5.1.title: Cyclic coordinates
6.5.1.summary: A cyclic coordinate is absent from L, although its velocity may appear. Its conjugate momentum then stays constant.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Test whether the coordinate itself appears while holding the other inputs fixed; do not confuse absence of q with absence of $\dot q$.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A cyclic coordinate is absent from L, although its velocity may appear. Its conjugate momentum then stays constant.

parts.title: Linear and angular versions
parts.body_md: For a translational coordinate x, cyclicity commonly gives $m\dot x$. For an azimuth $\phi$ in a central potential, it gives $mr^2\dot\phi$. In spherical coordinates the corresponding z component includes $\sin^2\theta$.

parts.title: The coordinate can still move
parts.body_md: Cyclic does not mean constant. A freely moving particle has changing x and constant $p_{x}$. Radius changes can make angular speed change while its conjugate momentum stays fixed.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}=0$$

Conjugate momentum is $\mathrm{kg}\cdot m/s$ for a length coordinate and $\mathrm{kg}\cdot m^{2}/s$ for an angle. It need not equal mass times coordinate speed.

parts.title: Which angular momentum?
parts.body_md: In cylindrical coordinates $(r,\phi ,z), \phi$ is the azimuth around z. If L has no $\phi$ or z dependence, $p_\phi=mr^2\dot\phi$ and $p_z=m\dot z$ are conserved. In spherical coordinates, $\theta$ is the angle from the positive z axis and $\phi$ is again azimuth, so $p_\phi=mr^2\sin^2\theta\dot\phi$. This is the z component of angular momentum, not generally its full magnitude.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: L and the energy function are J; q may be a length or angle; $p_{q}$ has units J s per unit of q. Thus Cartesian momentum is $\mathrm{kg} m/s$ while angular momentum is $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Cyclic does not mean the motion is periodic. It describes the Lagrangian's dependence on a coordinate.

examples.title: A central potential conserves angular momentum
examples.setup_md: A mass m moves in a plane with a potential V(r).

steps.why: Neither the kinetic geometry nor the potential depends on the absolute angle $\phi$.
$\phi$ is cyclic.
Apply Euler–Lagrange to the missing coordinate.
Compute the conserved conjugate momentum.

examples.answer_md: Angular momentum is conserved even while radius and angular speed change.
examples.check_md: It is r squared times angular speed that stays fixed, not angular speed alone.

practice.question_md: In a central orbit, radius halves. By what factor does angular speed change if angular momentum is fixed?
hints: Compare r squared before and after.
practice.answer_md: Angular speed becomes four times as large.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 232–234; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.5.2.title: Energy conservation
6.5.2.summary: Time-translation symmetry gives a conserved energy function. Compute it from L rather than assuming that every generalized L makes it equal T+V.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For each coordinate, multiply its velocity by its conjugate momentum, add the results, then subtract L.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Time-translation symmetry gives a conserved energy function. Compute it from L rather than assuming that every generalized L makes it equal T+V.

parts.title: Derivation in one sentence
parts.body_md: Differentiate the energy function, use the chain rule on L, and cancel coordinate-force terms with Euler–Lagrange; only minus the explicit time derivative remains.

parts.title: Time-dependent apparatus
parts.body_md: A moving rail, driven support or time-varying spring can exchange energy with the particle. A conserved quantity in a reduced coordinate description need not be ordinary mechanical energy in the lab frame.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$E=\sum_i\dot q_i\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}-L,\qquad\frac{dE}{dt}=-\frac{\partial L}{\partial t}$$

$E$ is in J. The partial derivative means explicit time dependence while coordinates and velocities are held fixed.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: L and the energy function are J; q may be a length or angle; $p_{q}$ has units J s per unit of q. Thus Cartesian momentum is $\mathrm{kg} m/s$ while angular momentum is $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A moving constraint can make the Lagrangian explicitly time-dependent and exchange energy with the system.

examples.title: Recognize the conserved energy
examples.setup_md: For a spring mass use $L=m\dot x^2/2-kx^2/2$.

steps.why: First compute the conjugate momentum.
Use the energy-function definition, not simply minus L.
Substitute and simplify.
There is no explicit time dependence.

examples.answer_md: The energy function equals the usual total mechanical energy for this ordinary time-independent-coordinate system.
examples.check_md: If coordinates or external constraints depend on time, the energy function need not be the particle’s ordinary T+V.

practice.question_md: A spring’s stiffness is externally changed: $L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-\tfrac12k(t)x^2$. What is the rate of change of its energy function?
hints: Use minus the explicit partial derivative of L with respect to t.
Hold x and $\dot x$ fixed while taking that partial derivative.
practice.answer_md: $d\mathcal E/dt=\tfrac12\dot k(t)x^2$. The actuator can add or remove energy.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 234–236; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.6.title: Noether’s theorem
6.6.summary: A continuous change that leaves the physics unchanged produces a conserved quantity. Find the symmetry first, then calculate its momentum.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Write $\delta q_i=\epsilon K_i(q)$ and retain first-order terms in the small parameter $\epsilon$.
A uniform shift of a coordinate missing from L is the simplest symmetry, but more general changes can mix coordinates.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A continuous change that leaves the physics unchanged produces a conserved quantity. Find the symmetry first, then calculate its momentum.

parts.title: The conserved combination
parts.body_md: If a time-independent infinitesimal coordinate transformation leaves L unchanged to first order, $Q=\sum_i p_iK_i$ is constant. Euler–Lagrange turns the first-order change of L into $dQ/dt$. Scaling every $K_{i}$ rescales Q but does not alter its conservation.

parts.title: Translation and rotation
parts.body_md: A common translation of interacting particles conserves their total momentum when the potential depends only on separation. A common rotation in an isotropic plane conserves angular momentum. Rotational symmetry requires both kinetic and potential terms to respect the transformation.

parts.title: Scope of the rule
parts.body_md: This is the coordinate-symmetry form used here. Time translations yield the energy function; transformations that change L by a total derivative require an additional boundary-term correction. Do not apply the simple Q formula indiscriminately.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\delta q_i=\epsilon K_i(q)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q=\sum_i p_iK_i\ \text{constant}$$

This form assumes $\delta L=0$ for the coordinate symmetry. A total-derivative change adds a boundary-term correction. Units of $Q$ follow the chosen symmetry parameter.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: L is J; $p_{i}$ is conjugate momentum; $K_{i}$ describes the coordinate change per chosen $\epsilon$. Q inherits units from that choice: translation gives linear momentum, rotation gives angular momentum.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A symmetry shifts the entire physical configuration in a specified way, not just one term of the formula.

examples.title: Two interacting carts can slide together without changing L
examples.setup_md: Two masses $m_{1},m_{2}$ interact via a potential $V(x_{1}-x_{2})$ on a frictionless line.

steps.why: Translate both by the same amount.
Their separation and velocities do not change.
Read the symmetry coefficients from the coordinate changes.
Multiply each conjugate momentum by its coefficient and add.

examples.answer_md: The conserved quantity is total linear momentum, even though the individual momenta change.
examples.check_md: A fixed external wall potential would break this common-translation symmetry.

examples.title: An isotropic spring has rotational symmetry
examples.setup_md: A mass moves in a plane with $L=\tfrac12m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)-\tfrac12k(x^2+y^2)$. Use a small counterclockwise rotation.

steps.why: These are the first-order changes under rotation.
The potential depends only on a rotation-invariant radius.
Identify the symmetry coefficients; the kinetic term is invariant too.
Form the conserved momentum combination.

examples.answer_md: The z angular momentum is conserved.
examples.check_md: If the x and y spring constants differ, the potential is not rotationally symmetric and this conclusion no longer follows.

practice.question_md: A two-coordinate system has potential V(2x-y) and ordinary kinetic energy. Which simultaneous constant shifts leave the potential unchanged, and what momentum combination is conserved?
hints: Make $2 \delta x$ minus $\delta y$ equal zero.
practice.answer_md: $\delta x=\epsilon$, $\delta y=2\epsilon$; the conserved combination is $p_x+2p_y$, provided the kinetic term is also invariant under these shifts.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 236–239; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

6.7.title: Small oscillations
6.7.summary: Small oscillations come from linearizing the motion around a stable equilibrium. The relevant inertia depends on the coordinate and on any other conserved motion.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Solve the unperturbed equations first. Then write $q=q_{0}+\eta$ and keep only first-order changes in $\eta$.
If $T=\tfrac12A(q)\dot q^2$, the small-oscillation inertia at rest is $A(q_{0})$, not automatically the particle mass.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Small oscillations come from linearizing the motion around a stable equilibrium. The relevant inertia depends on the coordinate and on any other conserved motion.

parts.title: Linearization
parts.body_md: For an ordinary one-coordinate equilibrium at rest, $A(q_0)\ddot\eta+V\prime\prime(q_0)\eta=0$. Terms proportional to $\dot\eta$ squared are second order. Positive curvature gives stability; zero curvature does not decide it.

parts.title: Conserved motion changes the problem
parts.body_md: If a second coordinate keeps rotating, first use its conservation law correctly or expand the full coupled equations. The bare gravitational potential alone may miss the effective restoring term and even predict zero frequency incorrectly.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\omega^2=\frac{K}{M},\qquad L\simeq\tfrac12M\dot\eta^2-\tfrac12K\eta^2$$

$\eta=q-q_0$. The units of $M,K$ follow the coordinate; their ratio is $s^{-2}$. For several coordinates solve $\det(K-\omega^2M)=0$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $q,\eta$ may be lengths or angles; $A(q_{0})$ is the associated inertia and $V^{\prime\prime}$ the associated stiffness. Their ratio has units $s^{-2}$. For the hoop, m is kg, R is m, and $\Omega$ and $\omega _{\mathrm{small}}$ are $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Do not use the bare mass with angular-coordinate curvature. First identify the kinetic-energy coefficient in the same coordinate.

examples.title: Small oscillations in an angle coordinate
examples.setup_md: A rigid pendulum of length $\ell$ has bob mass m and small departures $\theta$ from its lowest point.

steps.why: The angular inertia is $m \ell$ squared.
Expand the potential about the stable equilibrium.
Use the angular inertia and angular stiffness.
Divide stiffness by inertia, not by m alone.

examples.answer_md: $\omega=\sqrt{g/\ell}$.
examples.check_md: The $\theta$ stiffness has units of energy per radian squared, not $N/m$.

examples.title: A bead on a rotating hoop
examples.setup_md: A light vertical hoop of radius R rotates at prescribed angular speed $\Omega$ about its vertical diameter. A bead m slides frictionlessly; $\theta$ is measured from the bottom.

steps.why: Include speed caused both by sliding and by the externally driven hoop.
Apply Euler–Lagrange in $\theta$.
Find a nonzero equilibrium when rotation is fast enough.
Differentiate the right-hand side at the equilibrium and retain its linear term.
Read off the stable oscillation frequency.

examples.answer_md: At slow rotation the bottom is stable with squared frequency $g/R-\Omega^2$; above the threshold stable off-bottom equilibria appear.
examples.check_md: The motor can exchange lab-frame energy with the bead, so this is not a free isolated pendulum.

practice.question_md: For $T=\tfrac12A\dot q^2$ and $V=\tfrac12B(q-q_0)^2$, where $A,B>0$ are constants, find the frequency.
hints: Compare its equation with $\ddot\eta$ plus $\omega^2 \eta$ equals zero.
practice.answer_md: $\omega=\sqrt{B/A}$.

visual.description: Exact effective-potential graph for the rotating-hoop example, parameterized by Omega²R/g. This is a graph of equilibria and stability, not a claim of a finished bead-motion simulation.

6.8.title: Other applications
6.8.summary: The same variation method can choose a curve rather than a motion. Replace time by a curve parameter and extremize the quantity the problem actually asks for.

prerequisites.refresher_md: A small curve segment has length $ds=\sqrt{1+y\prime{}^2}\,dx$ when $y=y(x)$.
Euler–Lagrange finds stationary candidates. Boundary conditions and stability decide which candidate is a minimum.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: The same variation method can choose a curve rather than a motion. Replace time by a curve parameter and extremize the quantity the problem actually asks for.

parts.title: A general geometric functional
parts.body_md: For $J=\int F(y,y\prime,x)dx$, use $d(\partial F/\partial y\prime)/dx=\partial F/\partial y$. Here x is a parameter, not time. A constant multiplier in J does not affect its stationary curve.

parts.title: Minimal surface of revolution
parts.body_md: Rotating $y(x)>0$ around the x axis gives area $A=2\pi\int y\sqrt{1+y\prime{}^2}\,dx$. With no explicit x dependence, $F-y\prime F_{y\prime}$ is constant. This produces a catenary generating curve, hence a catenoid surface.

parts.title: The reusable first integral
parts.body_md: For $F=f(y)\sqrt{1+y\prime{}^2}$, the invariant is $f(y)/\sqrt{1+y\prime{}^2}=C$. Thus $1+y\prime{}^2=f(y)^2/C^2$. Boundary values determine the integration constants. A local inverse x(y) may simplify the cyclic-coordinate calculation, but can be multivalued globally.

parts.title: Existence matters
parts.body_md: For sufficiently separated rings there is no connecting catenoid of the required shape; even when stationary candidates exist, not all are stable minima. A broken surface can have less area. Stationarity is not a universal existence or minimum guarantee.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\frac{\partial f}{\partial y'}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$$

For a functional $J=\int f(y,y',x)dx$, $y'=dy/dx$. Units follow the quantity being extremized rather than a mechanical Lagrangian.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: x,y,a,b,c,R are lengths (m); $y^{\prime}=dy/dx$ is dimensionless. Arc length J is m; surface area A is $m^{2}$. The integrand F is chosen for the geometric quantity, and is not necessarily energy.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: A stationary surface may not be the global minimum for the chosen boundary rings. Check admissible alternatives and boundary conditions.

examples.title: The shortest planar path
examples.setup_md: Connect (0,0) to (a,b), with $a>0$, by a curve y(x) and minimize its length.

steps.why: Use arc length as the quantity to minimize.
The integrand has no y dependence.
The displayed expression is a one-to-one function of finite slope.
Apply the two endpoint conditions.

examples.answer_md: The stationary shortest path is the straight segment joining the endpoints.
examples.check_md: The length is $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, consistent with the triangle inequality.

examples.title: The neck of a symmetric soap-film surface
examples.setup_md: Two equal coaxial rings are at $x=\pm a$ with radius R. Find the stationary connecting surface-of-revolution form.

steps.why: Drop the constant factor 2pi from the area functional.
Use the first integral from absent explicit x dependence.
Rearrange the constant relation.
Symmetry puts the neck at $x=0$; this form satisfies the differential relation.
The endpoint radius determines the possible neck radii c.

examples.answer_md: The candidate surface is a catenoid; the boundary equation can have two, one or no positive solutions depending on separation.
examples.check_md: At $x=0, y=c$ and $y^{\prime}=0$. One must still compare stability and competing surfaces.

practice.question_md: For a functional with integrand $F=f(y)\sqrt{1+y\prime{}^2}$ and no explicit x, what quantity is constant?
hints: Use F minus $y^{\prime}$ times its derivative with respect to $y^{\prime}$.
Simplify after differentiating the square root.
practice.answer_md: $f(y)/\sqrt{1+y\prime{}^2}$ is constant along a stationary curve.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 242–246; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

7.1.title: Conservation of angular momentum
7.1.summary: A central force points along the line to one fixed center. It therefore produces no torque about that center, so angular momentum stays fixed.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times m\mathbf v$ has magnitude mr times the velocity perpendicular to r.
The position vector and torque must be measured from the same specified center.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: A central force points along the line to one fixed center. It therefore produces no torque about that center, so angular momentum stays fixed.

parts.title: Why the orbit is planar
parts.body_md: $d\mathbf L/dt=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=0$ for a central force. Both r and v stay perpendicular to the fixed nonzero L, so motion stays in one plane. Zero angular momentum is the special radial-motion case.

parts.title: Area as angular-momentum bookkeeping
parts.body_md: A small swept triangle has area $dA=r^2d\theta/2$. Thus $dA/dt=L/(2m)$. Equal areas in equal times follow from any central force, not only inverse-square gravity.

parts.title: Radial force can still do work
parts.body_md: Zero torque does not mean zero force or constant speed. A radial force can change radial velocity and kinetic energy while conserving angular momentum.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times m\mathbf v,\qquad\dot{\mathbf L}=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=0$$

$\mathbf r$ is measured from the force center (m), $\mathbf L$ is $\mathrm{kg}\cdot m^{2}/s$. For nonzero $L$, the orbital plane is fixed.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: m is kg; $r,R,r_{p},r_{a}$ are lengths (m); v is $m/s$; L is angular momentum $(\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s)$; torque is N m; area rate is $m^{2}/s$. L here is not the Lagrangian.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Conserved angular momentum does not mean constant angular speed. The origin must be the force center for the zero-torque argument.

examples.title: Moving inward increases tangential speed
examples.setup_md: A particle subject only to a central force has tangential speed v at radius R. Later its radius is $R/3$.

steps.why: Initially angular momentum uses the perpendicular, tangential velocity.
Write the same conserved quantity at the new radius.
Equate the two expressions.
Angular speed changes by an additional radius factor.

examples.answer_md: Tangential speed triples and angular speed increases ninefold; the radial speed is not determined by angular momentum alone.
examples.check_md: Do not conclude that total kinetic energy stays constant under an arbitrary central force.

examples.title: A fast periapsis sweeps the same area
examples.setup_md: An orbit has closest and farthest radii $r_{p}$ and $r_{a}$. At these turning points radial velocity vanishes.

steps.why: All velocity is tangential at a radial turning point.
Cancel the mass and angular momentum.
The skinny swept triangles have equal area per time.

examples.answer_md: The object moves faster near the center, exactly enough to preserve the areal rate.
examples.check_md: If $r_a=r_p$, the speed is the same all around a circular orbit.

practice.question_md: For a nonzero central-force orbit, can angular momentum change direction? Can the velocity direction change?
hints: A radial force can bend the path while its torque about the center is zero.
practice.answer_md: Angular momentum stays fixed in magnitude and direction; velocity generally changes direction.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 281–283; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

7.2.title: The effective potential
7.2.summary: Fixed angular momentum lets you replace a planar orbit with one-dimensional radial motion in an effective potential.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $v^2=\dot r^2+r^2\dot\theta^2$ and $L=mr^2\dot\theta$.
A radial turning point has $\dot r=0$, but tangential motion can remain nonzero.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Fixed angular momentum lets you replace a planar orbit with one-dimensional radial motion in an effective potential.

parts.title: Eliminate the angular speed
parts.body_md: Substitute $\dot\theta=L/(mr^2)$ into energy to obtain $E=m\dot r^2/2+V_{eff}$, with $V_{eff}=V+L^2/(2mr^2)$. Allowed radii have $E\ge V_{eff}$.

parts.title: Read the graph
parts.body_md: Intersections $E=V_{\mathrm{eff}}$ give turning radii. A minimum gives a stable circular orbit; a maximum gives an unstable one. A horizontal energy line below the entire potential has no allowed motion.

parts.title: Do not double-count
parts.body_md: The barrier term represents angular kinetic energy, not extra potential from a new physical interaction. It is useful in the radial reduction; retain the original central force when drawing the real inertial-frame force diagram.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$E=\tfrac12m\dot r^2+V_{\rm eff}(r),\qquad V_{\rm eff}=V(r)+\frac{L^2}{2mr^2}$$

$E,V_{\rm eff}$ are in J; $L$ is fixed angular momentum $(\mathrm{kg}\cdot m^{2}/s)$. Turning radii satisfy $E=V_{\rm eff}$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $E,V,V_{\mathrm{eff}}$ are J; m,M are kg; r,b are m; L is angular momentum $(\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s)$; G is $m^{3}/(\mathrm{kg} s^{2})$; $\omega _{r}$ is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The extra term is tangential kinetic energy, not a new physical potential interaction. Stability needs $V_{\rm eff}''>0$.

examples.title: The centrifugal barrier of a free flyby
examples.setup_md: A free particle approaches at speed v along a line whose perpendicular distance from the origin is $b>0$.

steps.why: Evaluate constants far from the closest point.
Separate radial kinetic energy from tangential kinetic energy.
At closest approach the radius stops decreasing.
Substitute the initial constants.

examples.answer_md: Even without a force, nonzero angular momentum prevents the trajectory from passing through the chosen origin.
examples.check_md: The effective barrier is coordinate bookkeeping for tangential kinetic energy, not an added physical outward force in the inertial frame.

examples.title: A stable circular gravitational orbit
examples.setup_md: A test mass m moves around a fixed spherical mass M with nonzero angular momentum L.

steps.why: Add the angular kinetic-energy barrier to gravitational potential.
A circular radius is an equilibrium of radial motion.
Solve for the equilibrium radius.
Substitute $L^2=GMm^2r_0$ into the curvature.
Small radial disturbances oscillate instead of growing.

examples.answer_md: The circular orbit is radially stable, with radial oscillation frequency equal to the circular angular frequency.
examples.check_md: The minimum energy at this L is negative: $-GMm/(2r_{0})$.

practice.question_md: For $V=0$ and nonzero L, can a finite-energy particle reach $r=0$?
hints: Inspect the L squared divided by r squared term.
Allowed radii require E at least $V_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
practice.answer_md: No. The effective potential diverges as r approaches zero, so there is a positive closest radius.

visual.description: Prepared Newtonian gravitational effective-potential plot, with m=1 kg, adjustable angular momentum, gravitational strength and energy. It illustrates the circular-orbit example; the separate free-flyby example has V=0 and is not this plot.

7.3.title: Solving the equations of motion
7.3.summary: Energy gives the radial speed, angular momentum gives the angular speed, and a change of variable can give the orbit shape directly.

prerequisites.refresher_md: If $\dot r=f(r)$, then $dt=dr/f(r)$ on a branch where the sign is fixed.
For nonzero $L, \theta$ changes monotonically with a chosen orientation, allowing r to be described as a function of $\theta$.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Energy gives the radial speed, angular momentum gives the angular speed, and a change of variable can give the orbit shape directly.

parts.title: Finding r(t) and theta(t)
parts.body_md: $\dot r=\pm\sqrt{2[E-V_{eff}(r)]/m}$. Integrate its reciprocal to obtain t(r), invert if possible, then integrate $\dot\theta=L/(mr^2)$. At a turning point switch the radial branch; one sign cannot describe the entire oscillation.

parts.title: Finding r(theta)
parts.body_md: Put $u=1/r$. With primes denoting angle derivatives, the central-force equation becomes $u\prime\prime+u=-mF_r(1/u)/(L^2u^2)$. It is often easier than separately finding r(t) and $\theta (t)$.

parts.title: What the constants mean
parts.body_md: Energy, angular momentum and orientation encode the initial state. A formal integral is a valid solution even if it lacks an elementary inverse; numerical quadrature can then provide the clock-time motion.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
