$$\dot r=\pm\sqrt{\frac{2}{m}(E-V_{\rm eff})},\qquad\dot\theta=\frac{L}{mr^2}$$

$r$ is in m, time in s, $\theta$ in rad, $E$ in J. The radial sign distinguishes inward and outward parts of a trajectory.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: r,b,p are lengths (m); $u=1/r$ is reciprocal length $(m^{-1})$, not speed; v is speed $(m/s)$; $\theta$ is in radians; L is angular momentum; k in $F=-k/r^{2}$ has units J m. Primes here mean $\theta$ derivatives.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: An orbit's shape does not tell you its timing. The sign of $\dot r$ changes at a turning point.

examples.title: Recover time and angle for a straight flyby
examples.setup_md: A free particle has Cartesian path $x=b,y=vt$, with $b,v>0$; closest approach occurs at $t=0$ and $\theta =0$.

steps.why: Use the distance from the fixed origin.
The perpendicular lever arm of the momentum is b.
Use conserved angular momentum to recover angular speed.
Integrate with $\theta (0)=0$, choosing the continuous branch for this $x=b$ path.

examples.answer_md: Both r and $\theta$ vary although the Cartesian velocity is constant.
examples.check_md: The angle runs from $-\pi /2$ to $+\pi /2$ over the complete flyby; r never falls below b.

examples.title: The inverse-square orbit equation
examples.setup_md: A particle m feels radial force $F_r=-k/r^2$ with $k>0$ and fixed L nonzero. Define $u=1/r$; primes below mean $\theta$ derivatives.

steps.why: Use $r=1/u$ and $\dot\theta=L u^2/m$.
Differentiate in time and substitute $\dot\theta$ again.
Insert the radial force into the radial equation.
Solve a constant-driven oscillator equation in angle, with constants set by the orbit.
Invert u to recover radius.

examples.answer_md: The orbit shape is a conic with eccentricity e; this equation gives shape, not yet its time schedule.
examples.check_md: $e=0$ gives constant radius. A denominator approaching zero can correspond to infinity on an unbound branch.

practice.question_md: Why does knowing $r(\theta )$ not by itself tell you when the particle reaches a point?
hints: A clock law still needs $\dot\theta$ from angular momentum.
practice.answer_md: Use $dt=mr^2\,d\theta/L$ to attach times to points on the orbit.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 285–287; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

7.3.1.title: Finding r(t) and θ(t)
7.3.1.summary: Reduce radial motion to an energy integral, then reconstruct the angular clock. Keep track of which way the radius is moving.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $V_{eff}=V+L^2/(2mr^2)$ includes the tangential kinetic energy at fixed L.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Reduce radial motion to an energy integral, then reconstruct the angular clock. Keep track of which way the radius is moving.

parts.title: Radial quadrature
parts.body_md: $t-t_0=\pm\int_{r_0}^{r}\sqrt{m/[2(E-V_{eff}(s))]}\,ds$. Choose the sign to agree with inward or outward motion. The integrand may diverge at a simple turning point while the elapsed time remains finite.

parts.title: Angular reconstruction
parts.body_md: Once r(t) is known, $\theta(t)-\theta_0=\int_{t_0}^{t}L/[mr(s)^2]\,ds$. A radial orbit $L=0$ is a separate simple case and should not be processed by dividing by L.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$t-t_0=\pm\int_{r_0}^{r}\frac{d\rho}{\sqrt{2[E-V_{\rm eff}(\rho)]/m}}$$

$\rho$ is an integration radius (m), $t$ in s, and $V_{\rm eff}=V+L^2/(2m\rho^2)$. Use the sign consistent with radial motion.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: r,b,p are lengths (m); $u=1/r$ is reciprocal length $(m^{-1})$, not speed; v is speed $(m/s)$; $\theta$ is in radians; L is angular momentum; k in $F=-k/r^{2}$ has units J m. Primes here mean $\theta$ derivatives.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Many integrals have no elementary inverse; numerical integration is valid. Match branches at turning points instead of keeping one sign forever.

examples.title: Recover time and angle for a straight flyby
examples.setup_md: A free particle has Cartesian path $x=b,y=vt$, with $b,v>0$; closest approach occurs at $t=0$ and $\theta =0$.

steps.why: Use the distance from the fixed origin.
The perpendicular lever arm of the momentum is b.
Use conserved angular momentum to recover angular speed.
Integrate with $\theta (0)=0$, choosing the continuous branch for this $x=b$ path.

examples.answer_md: Both r and $\theta$ vary although the Cartesian velocity is constant.
examples.check_md: The angle runs from $-\pi /2$ to $+\pi /2$ over the complete flyby; r never falls below b.

practice.question_md: At radius r a particle has energy E and effective potential $V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)$. Write the magnitude of its radial velocity.
hints: Subtract the effective potential from energy.
The remainder is radial kinetic energy.
practice.answer_md: $|\dot r|=\sqrt{2(E-V_{eff})/m}$ in an allowed region.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 286–286; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

7.3.2.title: Finding r(θ )
7.3.2.summary: Describe an orbit directly with reciprocal radius. The angular-momentum relation removes time derivatives from the shape equation.

prerequisites.refresher_md: If $u=1/r$, then $dr/d\theta=-u\prime/u^2$.
$\dot\theta=Lu^2/m$ cancels those inverse-square factors.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Describe an orbit directly with reciprocal radius. The angular-momentum relation removes time derivatives from the shape equation.

parts.title: Derive before substituting the force
parts.body_md: First obtain $\dot r=-(L/m)u\prime$ and $\ddot r=-(L^2/m^2)u^2u\prime\prime$. Insert them into $m(\ddot r-r\dot\theta^2)=F_r$ to get Binet’s equation. $F_{r}$ is signed outward-positive.

parts.title: Test a free path
parts.body_md: When $F_{r}=0$, the equation is $u^{\prime\prime}+u=0$. Choosing $u=\cos (\theta )/b$ yields $r \cos (\theta )=b,$ a straight line. The coordinate oscillation does not imply a physically oscillating force.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\left(\frac{du}{d\theta}\right)^2=\frac{2mE}{L^2}-u^2-\frac{2mV(1/u)}{L^2},\qquad u=\frac1r$$

$u$ has units $m^{-1}$ and $\theta$ is in rad. This route assumes nonzero $L$; purely radial motion is handled separately.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: r,b,p are lengths (m); $u=1/r$ is reciprocal length $(m^{-1})$, not speed; v is speed $(m/s)$; $\theta$ is in radians; L is angular momentum; k in $F=-k/r^{2}$ has units J m. Primes here mean $\theta$ derivatives.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Do not substitute $r$ where the potential now expects $1/u$. Eliminating time loses timing information, not the geometric orbit.

examples.title: The inverse-square orbit equation
examples.setup_md: A particle m feels radial force $F_r=-k/r^2$ with $k>0$ and fixed L nonzero. Define $u=1/r$; primes below mean $\theta$ derivatives.

steps.why: Use $r=1/u$ and $\dot\theta=L u^2/m$.
Differentiate in time and substitute $\dot\theta$ again.
Insert the radial force into the radial equation.
Solve a constant-driven oscillator equation in angle, with constants set by the orbit.
Invert u to recover radius.

examples.answer_md: The orbit shape is a conic with eccentricity e; this equation gives shape, not yet its time schedule.
examples.check_md: $e=0$ gives constant radius. A denominator approaching zero can correspond to infinity on an unbound branch.

practice.question_md: For a free particle, $u=\cos\theta/b$. What Cartesian curve does this represent?
practice.answer_md: $x=b$, a straight line.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 286–287; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

7.4.title: Gravity, Kepler’s laws
7.4.summary: Inverse-square attraction produces conic orbits. Energy selects bound or unbound motion, angular momentum sets the shape scale, and the area law supplies the timing.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Use $k=GMm$ for a fixed central mass and $L=mr^2\dot\theta$ for angular momentum.
$a$ is the semimajor axis; $r_p=a(1-e)$ and $r_a=a(1+e)$, so $p=a(1-e^2)$.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: Inverse-square attraction produces conic orbits. Energy selects bound or unbound motion, angular momentum sets the shape scale, and the area law supplies the timing.

parts.title: Calculation of r(theta)
parts.body_md: Binet’s equation gives $r=p/[1+e\cos(\theta-\theta_0)]$, with $p=L^2/(GMm^2)$. Initial position and velocity determine L, e and orientation.

parts.title: The orbits
parts.body_md: $e^2=1+2EL^2/(m k^2)$. With the potential zero at infinity, $E<0$ gives an ellipse (including the circular $e=0$ case), $E=0$ a parabola and $E>0$ a hyperbola for nondegenerate L. Bound ellipses have $E=-k/(2a)$.

parts.title: Why they are conics
parts.body_md: Multiplying the polar equation by its denominator relates distance to a focus to distance from a fixed directrix. Squaring and completing the square gives the familiar ellipse or hyperbola equations; $e=1$ is the parabolic boundary.

parts.title: Kepler’s three laws
parts.body_md: The orbit is an ellipse with the gravitating center at a focus; equal areas are swept in equal times; and period squared is proportional to semimajor axis cubed. The area law needs only a central force; the conic and period laws use inverse-square attraction.

parts.title: Reduced mass
parts.body_md: If both bodies move appreciably, use their separation r, reduced mass $\mu =m_{1} m_{2}/(m_{1}+m_{2})$, and potential $-Gm_{1}m_{2}/r$. The relative acceleration involves $G(m_{1}+m_{2})$, so the exact period law uses the total mass.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$r=\frac{p}{1+e\cos\theta},\qquad p=\frac{L^2}{m\alpha},\quad V=-\frac\alpha r$$

For a fixed central mass $M$, $\alpha=GMm$ $(J\cdot m)$, $p,r$ (m), $e$ dimensionless. For comparable masses use the reduced mass in the relative problem.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $r,r_{0},r_{p},r_{a},a,b,p,R$ are lengths (m); e is dimensionless eccentricity; E is J; L is angular momentum; $k=GMm$ is J m; $M,m,m_{1},m_{2},\mu$ are kg; T is period (s); $\Omega$ is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The force center is a focus, not generally the geometric center of the ellipse. The two-body period uses $G(M+m)$.

examples.title: Launch faster than circular, but below escape
examples.setup_md: At radius $r_{0}$ around fixed mass M, launch a test particle tangentially at $v_0=\sqrt{3GM/(2r_0)}$. Find its other turning radius.

steps.why: Use the tangential launch to determine angular momentum and the conic parameter.
The speed exceeds circular, so $r_{0}$ is periapsis rather than apoapsis.
Relate conic parameter to the ellipse semimajor axis.
The farthest radius is the semimajor axis times one plus eccentricity.

examples.answer_md: The orbit is an ellipse from $r_{0}$ to 3r0, with eccentricity $1/2$.
examples.check_md: Its specific energy is $-GM/(4r_{0})$, agreeing with $-GM/(2a)$; the launch speed is below escape.

examples.title: A bigger orbit takes disproportionately longer
examples.setup_md: Two small satellites orbit the same dominant mass M on ellipses with semimajor axes a and 4a.

steps.why: Kepler’s period law depends on semimajor axis, not instantaneous radius.
The common gravitational parameter cancels.
Periods are positive, so take the positive square root.

examples.answer_md: Quadrupling semimajor axis multiplies period by eight, regardless of eccentricity in the ideal two-body model.
examples.check_md: The circular-orbit result is the special case $e=0$, not the only orbit to obey the law.

practice.question_md: A bound orbit has nearest radius R and farthest radius 5R. Find a and e.
hints: Add the turning radii to obtain 2a.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 287–296; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

7.4.1.title: Calculation of r(θ )
7.4.1.summary: An orbit is a path around a central mass. Here we find its shape: how the distance from the centre changes as the particle moves around it.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $r$ is the distance to the central mass; $\theta$ tells you the direction from it. A circular orbit has constant $r$. An elliptical orbit gets nearer and farther as $\theta$ changes.
Gravity points towards the centre, so it produces no torque about that centre. Angular momentum $L=mr^2\dot\theta$ stays constant. Moving closer means sweeping through angle faster.

parts.title: What are we trying to find?
parts.body_md: Imagine looking down on a planet’s orbit. Draw an arrow from the Sun to the planet. Its length is $r$ and its angle is $\theta$. Finding $r(\theta)$ means finding that arrow’s length at each angle—it gives the orbit’s shape, without first finding where the planet is at every time.

parts.title: The useful change of variable
parts.body_md:
Set $u=1/r$, the reciprocal of the distance. A larger $u$ means the particle is closer to the centre. This substitution makes the inverse-square gravity equation much simpler:

$$\frac{d^2u}{d\theta^2}+u=\frac{GMm^2}{L^2}. $$

Here $M$ is the fixed central mass, $m$ is the orbiting particle’s mass, and $G$ is the gravitational constant. The derivative is with respect to angle, not time. The equation tells us how distance changes as the direction turns.

parts.title: Read the orbit equation
parts.body_md:
Its solution can be written as

$$r(\theta)=\frac{p}{1+e\cos(\theta-\theta_0)},\qquad p=\frac{L^2}{GMm^2}.$$

$p$ sets the orbit’s size and has units of length. The dimensionless eccentricity $e$ sets its shape: $e=0$ is a circle and $0<e<1$ is an ellipse. The angle $\theta_0$ sets which direction points towards closest approach. These constants come from the starting position and velocity; they are not extra forces.

parts.title: A simple check: the circle
parts.body_md:
Put $e=0$. The angle-dependent term disappears, so $r=p$ everywhere: the distance never changes. For an ellipse, the cosine varies between $1$ and $-1$, giving the closest and farthest distances

$$r_{\min}=\frac{p}{1+e},\qquad r_{\max}=\frac{p}{1-e}. $$

This is why a small eccentricity looks nearly circular, while a larger eccentricity gives a bigger near-to-far difference.

parts.title: Connect it to the starting speed
parts.body_md: At distance $r_0$, circular speed is $v_c=\sqrt{GM/r_0}$ and escape speed is $v_{\rm esc}=\sqrt{2GM/r_0}$. For a purely sideways (tangential) launch between those speeds, the particle starts at the closest point of a bound ellipse. The worked example uses exactly that setup.

examples.title: Launch faster than circular, but below escape
examples.setup_md: At distance $r_0$ from a fixed mass $M$, a small particle of mass $m$ starts moving sideways, perpendicular to the radius, at $v_0=\sqrt{3GM/(2r_0)}$. How far from the centre does it get before moving closer again?

steps.why: The velocity is perpendicular to the radius, so $L=mr_0v_0$. Substituting it into $p=L^2/(GMm^2)$ gives $p=r_0^2v_0^2/(GM)=3r_0/2$.
The speed is greater than circular speed, but less than escape speed. The particle initially moves outward, so $r_0$ is the closest point. Use $r_{\min}=p/(1+e)$, then solve $1+e=p/r_0=3/2$.
At the farthest point the cosine is $-1$. Substitute the size $p$ and shape $e$ we just found into the largest-radius formula.
Dividing by $1/2$ doubles $3r_0/2$. The particle gets three times as far from the centre as it was at launch.

examples.answer_md: The distance varies from $r_0$ to $3r_0$. This is an ellipse with eccentricity $e=1/2$.
examples.check_md: The specific energy at launch is $v_0^2/2-GM/r_0=-GM/(4r_0)<0$, so the orbit is bound. Its semimajor axis is the average of the two extreme radii, $a=(r_0+3r_0)/2=2r_0$, consistent with energy $-GM/(2a)$.

practice.question_md: A particle is launched sideways at exactly circular speed at distance $R$. Find $p$ and $e$, and explain why its distance stays constant.
practice.answer_md: $p=R$ and $e=0$.

visual.description: Source reference on Morin pp. 287–289; use its applicable geometry or equations alongside these worked examples. No prepared interactive scene is claimed.

7.4.2.title: The orbits
7.4.2.summary: The energy sign classifies a gravitational orbit because gravitational potential tends to zero far away.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $V=-k/r$ uses zero energy at infinity; changing the additive zero would change the numerical energy sign convention.
$e=0$ is circular, $0<e<1$ elliptical, $e=1$ parabolic and $e>1$ hyperbolic for nonradial motion.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: The energy sign classifies a gravitational orbit because gravitational potential tends to zero far away.

parts.title: Bound versus unbound
parts.body_md: Negative total energy cannot reach infinity because kinetic energy would have to become negative there. Zero energy reaches infinity with speed tending to zero; positive energy retains a nonzero asymptotic speed.

parts.title: Turning radii and degeneracies
parts.body_md: For a bound nonradial orbit there are two positive radial turning points. For an unbound flyby there is one finite periapsis and an infinite branch. The $L=0$ radial collision/escape case is degenerate and is better handled directly with energy.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$e^2=1+\frac{2EL^2}{m\alpha^2}$$

For $V=-\alpha/r$, fixed-center mass $m$, and nonzero $L$: circle $e=0$, ellipse $0<e<1$, parabola $e=1$, hyperbola $e>1$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $r,r_{0},r_{p},r_{a},a,b,p,R$ are lengths (m); e is dimensionless eccentricity; E is J; L is angular momentum; $k=GMm$ is J m; $M,m,m_{1},m_{2},\mu$ are kg; T is period (s); $\Omega$ is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Negative total energy does not mean negative kinetic energy. It means the binding potential outweighs the positive kinetic term.

examples.title: Classify three launch speeds
examples.setup_md: At radius R, compare launches with speeds $\sqrt{GM/R}$, $\sqrt{2GM/R}$ and $\sqrt{3GM/R}$. Assume a nonzero tangential component.

steps.why: Evaluate kinetic plus gravitational potential per unit mass.
Substitute the three speeds separately.
For the positive-energy case, potential tends to zero at infinity.

examples.answer_md: The cases are bound elliptical (circular if exactly tangential at the first speed), parabolic and hyperbolic.
examples.check_md: Energy determines boundness, but the direction also affects angular momentum and eccentricity within that class.

practice.question_md: An object far from a planet has incoming speed $v_{\infty}$. What is its speed at radius R, ignoring drag?
hints: Conserve energy from infinity to R.
At infinity the potential is zero.
practice.answer_md: $v^2=v_\infty^2+2GM/R$.

7.4.3.title: Proof of conic orbits
7.4.3.summary: The polar orbit formula is not merely shaped like an ellipse: it can be converted directly into the standard conic equation.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$, and $r^2=x^2+y^2$.
$x^2+2cx=(x+c)^2-c^2$ shifts the center of a quadratic curve.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: The polar orbit formula is not merely shaped like an ellipse: it can be converted directly into the standard conic equation.

parts.title: Focus and directrix
parts.body_md: From $r=p/(1+e\cos\theta)$ obtain $r+ex=p$. For $e>0$ on the appropriate branch, r equals e times distance to the line $x=p/e$. The origin is therefore a focus and e is the eccentricity.

parts.title: Ellipse parameters
parts.body_md: For $0\le e<1$, the completed-square equation gives semiaxes $a=p/(1-e^2)$ and $b=p/\sqrt{1-e^2}$. The center is shifted from the force center; the attracting body is at a focus, not generally at the ellipse’s center.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$p=r+ex\ \Longrightarrow\ (1-e^2)x^2+y^2+2pex-p^2=0$$

$p$ is the semilatus rectum (m), $e$ dimensionless, and $x,y$ coordinates relative to the focus (m).

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $r,r_{0},r_{p},r_{a},a,b,p,R$ are lengths (m); e is dimensionless eccentricity; E is J; L is angular momentum; $k=GMm$ is J m; $M,m,m_{1},m_{2},\mu$ are kg; T is period (s); $\Omega$ is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: The origin of these coordinates is a focus. A shift is needed to write the familiar centered ellipse equation.

examples.title: Convert the orbit into an ellipse
examples.setup_md: Take $r=p/(1+e\cos\theta)$ with $0\le e<1$ and orientation $\theta _{0}=0$.

steps.why: Multiply through and use $x=r \cos (\theta )$.
Square the expression for r.
Expand and collect terms.
Complete the square in x.
Divide by the right-hand side and identify the two semiaxes.

examples.answer_md: This is an ellipse centered at $x=-pe/(1-e^2)$, with the original origin at one focus.
examples.check_md: At $e=0$ the shift vanishes and both semiaxes equal p, giving a circle.

practice.question_md: For $p=3R/2$ and $e=1/2$, find the ellipse’s semimajor axis and center coordinate.
hints: The center is at $x=-ae$ for this orientation.
practice.answer_md: $a=2R$ and $x_{center}=-R$.

7.4.4.title: Kepler’s laws
7.4.4.summary: The area law connects the geometric orbit to its period. Integrating one constant area rate around an ellipse gives Kepler’s period law.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An ellipse with semiaxes a,b has area $\pi ab$.
$dA/dt=L/(2m)$ for a particle moving under a central force.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: The area law connects the geometric orbit to its period. Integrating one constant area rate around an ellipse gives Kepler’s period law.

parts.title: Three different claims
parts.body_md: The ellipse law uses inverse-square attraction. The equal-area law follows from zero torque and holds for any central force. The period law combines the inverse-square ellipse geometry with that area rate.

parts.title: Derive the period
parts.body_md: $T=(\pi ab)/(L/(2m))$. For gravity, $b=a\sqrt{1-e^2}$ and $L^2=GMm^2a(1-e^2)$. Substitution cancels m and eccentricity, leaving $T^2=4\pi^2a^3/(GM)$.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{L}{2m},\qquad T^2=\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3$$

For a light body orbiting fixed mass $M$, $a$ is ellipse semimajor axis (m), $T$ period (s), and $A$ swept area $(m^{2})$.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $r,r_{0},r_{p},r_{a},a,b,p,R$ are lengths (m); e is dimensionless eccentricity; E is J; L is angular momentum; $k=GMm$ is J m; $M,m,m_{1},m_{2},\mu$ are kg; T is period (s); $\Omega$ is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Equal areas do not mean equal distances or equal angles. An orbiting body moves faster near periapsis.

examples.title: A bigger orbit takes disproportionately longer
examples.setup_md: Two small satellites orbit the same dominant mass M on ellipses with semimajor axes a and 4a.

steps.why: Kepler’s period law depends on semimajor axis, not instantaneous radius.
The common gravitational parameter cancels.
Periods are positive, so take the positive square root.

examples.answer_md: Quadrupling semimajor axis multiplies period by eight, regardless of eccentricity in the ideal two-body model.
examples.check_md: The circular-orbit result is the special case $e=0$, not the only orbit to obey the law.

practice.question_md: Two ellipses around the same dominant mass have the same semimajor axis but different eccentricity. Compare their periods and their speeds along the paths.
hints: The period formula has no eccentricity.
The local speed still depends on radius through energy.
practice.answer_md: Their periods match, but their local speeds and distributions of time around the path differ.

7.4.5.title: Reduced mass
7.4.5.summary: In a real two-body orbit, neither body must be fixed. Separate their common center-of-mass motion from their relative motion.

prerequisites.refresher_md: $\mathbf R=(m_1\mathbf r_1+m_2\mathbf r_2)/(m_1+m_2)$.
$\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ is the inertia of the relative separation coordinate.

parts.title: Picture and route
parts.body_md: In a real two-body orbit, neither body must be fixed. Separate their common center-of-mass motion from their relative motion.

parts.title: Relative equation
parts.body_md: With $\mathbf r=\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2$, $\mu\ddot{\mathbf r}=-Gm_1m_2\mathbf r/r^3$. Equivalently, $\ddot{\mathbf r}=-G(m_1+m_2)\mathbf r/r^3$. Use reduced mass in energy and angular momentum; use total mass in the gravitational parameter of the acceleration.

parts.title: Individual orbits
parts.body_md: In the CM frame, $\mathbf r_1=(m_2/M)\mathbf r$ and $\mathbf r_2=-(m_1/M)\mathbf r$. The two ellipses have the same period and scaled sizes. The period law uses the relative ellipse’s semimajor axis, the sum of the two individual semimajor axes.

parts.title: Relations, symbols and assumptions
parts.body_md:
$$\mu=\frac{m_1m_2}{m_1+m_2},\qquad T=\tfrac12M\dot R^2+\tfrac12\mu\dot r^2$$

$M=m_1+m_2$ (kg), $\mathbf r=\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2$ (m), and $V=-Gm_1m_2/r$ for gravity.

parts.title: Symbols and units
parts.body_md: $r,r_{0},r_{p},r_{a},a,b,p,R$ are lengths (m); e is dimensionless eccentricity; E is J; L is angular momentum; $k=GMm$ is J m; $M,m,m_{1},m_{2},\mu$ are kg; T is period (s); $\Omega$ is $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: Catch the common mistake
parts.body_md: Replace the mass in the relative kinetic term, not the product $m_1m_2$ in the gravitational potential. Relative semimajor axis is the separation orbit's size.

examples.title: A binary with unequal masses
examples.setup_md: Masses m and 3m move in circular orbits around their common center of mass. Their separation is R.

steps.why: Compute the inertia of their relative motion.
The heavier body remains closer to the CM.
Use total mass and relative radius in the circular relative-motion equation.
Convert angular frequency to a common orbital period.
Each speed uses its own CM radius, not the full separation.

examples.answer_md: Both orbit with the same angular frequency; the lighter mass travels three times farther and faster.
examples.check_md: The two momenta have equal magnitudes in the CM frame. In the limit of one overwhelmingly heavy mass, reduced mass approaches the lighter mass.

practice.question_md: Two equal masses m orbit each other with separation R. What radius does each travel, and what total mass goes in the relative period law?
hints: The CM is midway between equal masses.
The relative equation contains the sum of the masses.
practice.answer_md: Each radius is $R/2$; use $T^2=4\pi^2R^3/(2Gm)$.

8.1.title: Pancake object in x-y plane
8.1.summary: Describe planar rotation, translation and axle changes without mixing their meanings.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

\(\mathbf R=M^{-1}\sum m_i\mathbf r_i\) is the mass-weighted position. Relative coordinates \(\boldsymbol\rho_i=\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R\) satisfy \(\sum m_i\boldsymbol\rho_i=0\). That identity is why translation and spin separate cleanly.

In \(I=\int r_\perp^2\,dm\), \(r_\perp\) is the shortest distance to the chosen axis, not necessarily distance to the origin. \(I\) has units $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}$. A quoted moment without its axis is incomplete.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: A flat moving body can spin while its center moves. Start by naming the origin and the axis. Then separate CM motion from spin; only after that impose rolling or a fixed pivot. Study the four tools below one at a time. For an opening conversation, use the two-bead example and ask which radius counts before revealing the first calculation.

parts.title: 8.1.1 · From a moving bead to a rigid body
parts.body_md: A bead at radius \(r\) moves tangentially, so \(v=r\omega\). Its angular momentum is \(r(mv)=mr^2\omega\). Add all the beads: $$I_z=\int(x^2+y^2)\,dm,\qquad L_z=I_z\omega,\qquad T=\frac12I_z\omega^2.$$ Here \(\omega\) is in $\mathrm{rad}/s$, with radians dimensionless. For a flat body rotating in the \(x,y\) plane, \(\mathbf L\) points along \(\hat z\). The energy formula follows from adding \(dm\,v^2/2\); it is not a separate guess.

parts.title: 8.1.1 · Recognize the method
parts.body_md: Use this form when there is one rigid rotation about a specified fixed axis. Draw the axis first; mark perpendicular distances. Do not use the distance along the rod or the diameter in place of the radius. Ask: which bead contributes more, and why does doubling radius multiply its contribution by four?

parts.title: 8.1.2 · The two pieces
parts.body_md: Imagine carrying the center of a spinning wheel along a path. Each point has \(\mathbf v=\mathbf V+\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho\). For planar motion, $$\mathbf L_O=\mathbf R\times M\mathbf V+I_{\rm CM}\omega\hat z,\qquad T=\frac12MV^2+\frac12I_{\rm CM}\omega^2.$$ \(\mathbf R\) runs from the named origin to the CM. The first term of \(\mathbf L_O\) is the angular momentum that a point mass at the CM would have; the second is spin. Cross terms vanish because the CM-relative mass-weighted position and velocity sum to zero.

parts.title: 8.1.2 · Rolling is a constraint, not another energy
parts.body_md: For a round body rolling on a stationary surface, \(V=R\omega\). The bottom point is instantaneously at rest and the top moves at \(2V\). With \(I=\beta MR^2\), energy gives \(v^2=2gh/(1+\beta)\), and on an incline \(a=g\sin\theta/(1+\beta)\). Static friction must be large enough; if the body slips these formulas do not apply. The safe recipe is to keep CM translation and CM spin separate until inserting no slip.

parts.title: 8.1.3 · Why the extra term is Md²
parts.body_md: Write each perpendicular position as its CM-relative part plus the axis displacement. Expanding the square in the inertia integral gives the original \(I_{\rm CM}\), \(Md^2\), and a cross term. The cross term is zero because \(\int\boldsymbol\rho\,dm=0\). Thus $$I_O=I_{\rm CM}+Md^2.$$ The axes must be parallel. \(d\) is their shortest separation; mass \(M\) is the entire body’s mass.

parts.title: 8.1.3 · Comparing two off-center axes
parts.body_md: If neither axis is through the CM, shift each from the CM separately: \(I_A-I_B=M(d_A^2-d_B^2)\). It is usually wrong to add \(M\) times the square of the distance directly from A to B. A rod has \(I_{\rm CM}=M\ell^2/12\), so an end axle gives \(M\ell^2/12+M(\ell/2)^2=M\ell^2/3\).

parts.title: 8.1.4 · Distances make the theorem
parts.body_md: For a sheet lying in \(z=0\), \(I_x=\int y^2dm\), \(I_y=\int x^2dm\), and \(I_z=\int(x^2+y^2)dm\). Therefore $$I_z=I_x+I_y.$$ All three mutually perpendicular axes must meet at the same point in the sheet. The point need not be the CM. Symmetry may additionally give \(I_x=I_y\), but the theorem alone does not.

parts.title: 8.1.4 · Where it stops working
parts.body_md: A disk has \(I_z=MR^2/2\), so each central diameter has \(MR^2/4\). A three-dimensional ball is not a sheet: \(I_x+I_y\) includes two extra copies of \(\int z^2dm\). Do not apply the sheet theorem to it.

examples.title: Two beads on a light crossbar
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two beads, each mass \(m\), are fixed at distances \(a\) and \(2a\) from a fixed perpendicular axle. The light bar turns counterclockwise at \(\omega\). Find angular momentum and kinetic energy.

steps.why: Add mass times squared axle distance for each bead; the bar has negligible mass.
Square the factor of two before adding.
Every bead has the same angular speed about this fixed axle.
Add the bead kinetic energies through the same moment of inertia.

examples.answer_md: \(\mathbf L=5ma^2\omega\hat z\), \(T=5ma^2\omega^2/2\).
examples.check_md: \(L\) has units $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s$ and \(T\) joules. Reversing the spin reverses \(L_z\), but leaves \(T\) positive.

examples.title: A rolling hoop loses height
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A thin hoop of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\), initially at rest, rolls without slipping down a fixed rough ramp through vertical height \(h\). Assume static friction is sufficient. Find its speed.

steps.why: The lost gravitational energy becomes translation plus spin; static contact does no work on the fixed surface.
For a hoop all mass is at radius R, and no slip relates the two speeds.
Substitute both relations explicitly.
Solve for the positive speed.

examples.answer_md: \(v=\sqrt{gh}\).
examples.check_md: The radius cancels. A nonrotating frictionless slider would reach \(\sqrt{2gh}\), so the hoop is slower because some energy is in spin.

practice.question_md: A thin disk rolls without slipping through height \(h\). Its central moment is \(MR^2/2\). Find its speed and explain why simply using \(T=Mv^2/2\) is incomplete.
hints: The center translates while the disk spins.
practice.answer_md: \(v=\sqrt{4gh/3}\). The missing term is CM spin energy \(Mv^2/4\). Check: this lies between the hoop and frictionless-slider speeds.

steps.why: The two parallel axes are separated by one radius.
The reference axis passes through the center of mass, so the parallel-axis theorem applies.
Add the translational shift term, using the total disk mass.

practice.question_md: For a rod of length \(\ell\), compare perpendicular axes at distances \(\ell/4\) and \(\ell/2\) from its CM. What is \(I_B-I_A\)?

The central moments cancel in the difference.

examples.title: A rectangular sheet rotates about a diagonal
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A uniform sheet of mass \(M\) has sides \(a,b\). Its central in-plane axes are along the sides. Find its normal-axis moment, and the moment about an in-plane line making angle \(\phi\) with the side of length \(a\).

steps.why: Distance from the x axis depends on y, hence the opposite side length appears.
The mass lies in one plane through all three axes.
The xy cross moment is zero by reflection symmetry of the centered rectangle.

examples.check_md: At \(\phi=0\) the result is \(I_x\). A square gives the same in-plane moment for every central direction.

practice.question_md: A thin ring has normal-axis moment \(MR^2\). Find its moment about a central diameter, then about a tangent line in the ring’s plane.
hints: The two central diameters are equivalent by circular symmetry.
Shift the diameter axis parallel by distance \(R\).
practice.answer_md: \(I_{\rm diameter}=MR^2/2\), \(I_{\rm tangent}=3MR^2/2\). The tangent result exceeds the central one by exactly \(MR^2\).

parts.title: Slice a three-dimensional body
parts.body_md: For rotation about \(z\), a particle at \((x,y,z)\) has speed \(\omega\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Its height does not alter that speed. Stack thin slices to obtain $$I_z=\int(x^2+y^2)dm,\quad L_z=I_z\omega,\quad T=\frac12I_z\omega^2.$$ The full vector \(\mathbf L\) may have x and y components even when \(\boldsymbol\omega\) points along z; Chapter 9 explains them. CM energy decomposition and the parallel-axis theorem still hold. The perpendicular-axis theorem generally does not.

parts.title: Find the center before shifting an axis
parts.body_md: Use symmetry to eliminate coordinates, then choose slices that have a simple mass. With volume density \(\rho\), \(dm=\rho\,dV\); with surface density \(\sigma\), \(dm=\sigma\,dA\). CM uses one power of position, inertia two. For a solid hemisphere, disks of area \(\pi(R^2-z^2)\) lead to \(z_{\rm CM}=3R/8\), whereas a thin shell gives \(R/2\).

examples.title: The center of a curved half-shell
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A thin uniform hemispherical shell of radius \(R\) occupies \(0\le z\le R\). Find its CM height above the equatorial plane.

steps.why: A thin spherical band has area $2\pi R dz$; its slant compensates its shrinking circumference.
Integrate the mass bands.
Take the mass-weighted mean height.

examples.answer_md: The CM lies on the symmetry axis at \(z=R/2\).
examples.check_md: A solid hemisphere instead has \(3R/8\); the shell result is farther up because mass is restricted to the surface.

examples.title: Two masses stacked above one another
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two point masses \(m\) lie at \((a,0,h)\) and \((a,0,-h)\), fixed to a light rotor turning about z at speed \(\omega\). Find \(I_z\), \(T\), and explain the role of \(h\).

steps.why: Both perpendicular distances to z are a; vertical height does not enter.
Each mass has speed $a\omega$.
The off-axis angular-momentum components cancel for the symmetric pair.

examples.answer_md: \(I_z=2ma^2\), \(\mathbf L=2ma^2\omega\hat z\), \(T=ma^2\omega^2\).
examples.check_md: Changing h leaves this motion’s energy unchanged, but would change moments about horizontal axes.

practice.question_md: A solid hemisphere has density \(\rho\). Set up the integrals for its mass and first moment about its flat face and find \(z_{\rm CM}\).
hints: At height z, the disk radius squared is \(R^2-z^2\).
practice.answer_md: \(M=2\pi\rho R^3/3\), first moment \(=\pi\rho R^4/4\), so \(z_{\rm CM}=3R/8\). Units reduce from kg m to m after dividing by mass; the result lies between base and tip.

8.3.title: Calculating moments of inertia
8.3.summary: Choose slices that turn a three-dimensional integral into known pieces.

prerequisites.refresher_md: In \(I=\int r_\perp^2\,dm\), \(r_\perp\) is the shortest distance to the chosen axis, not necessarily distance to the origin. \(I\) has units $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}$. A quoted moment without its axis is incomplete.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Start with the annulus: a single ring already has a known moment, so a stack of rings requires only one integral. Then use scaling to see which factors came from mass and which from distance.

parts.title: 8.3.1 · The reusable recipe
parts.body_md: Name the axis; choose a slice with a known moment; express \(dm\) in one variable; integrate; replace density by the stated total mass. A slice may itself need a parallel-axis shift. Uniform line, area and volume densities have units $\mathrm{kg}/m, \mathrm{kg}/m^{2}$ and $\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$ respectively.

parts.title: 8.3.1 · Common bodies, with the axes stated
parts.body_md: For uniform bodies: a ring has \(MR^2\) about its central normal axis and \(MR^2/2\) about a diameter. A thin disk has \(MR^2/2\) about the normal and \(MR^2/4\) about a diameter. A thin rod has \(M\ell^2/12\) about a central transverse axis and \(M\ell^2/3\) about an end. A spherical shell has \(2MR^2/3\), and a solid sphere \(2MR^2/5\), about a central diameter. A rectangular sheet has \(M(a^2+b^2)/12\) about its central normal. These are axis-specific results, not interchangeable body labels.

parts.title: 8.3.1 · How the less obvious shapes are built
parts.body_md: For a spherical shell, symmetry gives three equal central moments and \(I_x+I_y+I_z=2MR^2\), giving \(2MR^2/3\). Integrating concentric shells, \(dI=(2/3)r^2(4\pi\rho r^2dr)\), gives the solid sphere. A very narrow triangular sheet of length \(\ell\) has mass per length proportional to distance from its tip; its tip moment is \(M\ell^2/2\), not a uniform rod’s \(M\ell^2/3\). For an isosceles triangle with common sides \(\ell\) and half apex angle \(\beta\), strips parallel to its base give $$I_{\rm tip}=\frac{M\ell^2}{2}\left(1-\frac23\sin^2\beta\right).$$ Splitting a regular N-gon of circumradius R into such triangles gives $$I=\frac{MR^2}{2}\left(1-\frac23\sin^2\frac\pi N\right).$$ As N grows, it tends to the disk moment.

parts.title: 8.3.2 · Scaling needs a physical normalization
parts.body_md: If all lengths scale by s at fixed density in d dimensions, mass scales by \(s^d\) and inertia by \(s^{d+2}\). A line gives \(s^3\), a sheet \(s^4\), and a solid \(s^5\). At fixed total mass the factor is instead \(s^2\). Compare one large shape with smaller translated copies of itself. Add their moments using the parallel-axis theorem.

parts.title: 8.3.2 · Where the number comes from
parts.body_md: Scaling alone only says that \(I\) is proportional to \(M\ell^2\); it cannot determine the coefficient. The explicit \(Md^2\) shifts supply the missing numerical information. The same method can work for self-similar fractal distributions if their mass-scaling law and centers are known, but a generic shape need not split into convenient similar pieces.

examples.title: Build an annulus from rings
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A uniform annular plate has mass \(M\), inner radius \(a\), outer radius \(b\). Find its moment about its central normal axle.

steps.why: Normalize the surface density and choose concentric rings.
Every point on a ring is distance r from the axle.
Integrate r cubed.
Factor $b^{4}-a^{4}$ and cancel $b^{2}-a^{2}$.

examples.check_md: At $a=0$ this becomes the solid-disk result. As a approaches b at fixed total mass, it becomes the thin-ring result.

examples.title: Recover a rod moment without integrating
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A uniform rod of length \(\ell\), mass \(M\), has unknown central moment \(I\). Use two identical rods end to end to derive I.

steps.why: At unchanged linear density, doubling length doubles mass and quadruples every squared distance.
The long rod is two short rods with their centers each $\ell /2$ from the new central axis.
Equate the two descriptions of the same long rod.
Solve the nonhomogeneous equation; the shift term supplies the dimensional scale.

examples.check_md: Keeping mass fixed instead of density would give length scaling by four, not eight; that would describe a different construction.

practice.question_md: A thin annular plate has radii R and 2R and mass M. Find its normal-axis moment and its central diameter moment.
hints: The annulus is a planar circularly symmetric object.
Two equal diameter moments add to its normal-axis moment.
practice.answer_md: \(I_z=5MR^2/2\), \(I_{\rm diameter}=5MR^2/4\). Check: the first lies between \(MR^2\) and \(4MR^2\), the bounds set by its inner and outer radii.

visual.description: Use the existing rod to inspect an axis and its lever distances; the worked annulus is a separate analytical example.

hints: Mass scales by area; squared distance supplies another factor of nine.
With mass fixed, remove the mass-scaling factor.

8.4.title: Torque
8.4.summary: Choose a legal origin, draw external lever arms, and then use torque to change angular momentum.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

\(\mathbf R=M^{-1}\sum m_i\mathbf r_i\) is the mass-weighted position. Relative coordinates \(\boldsymbol\rho_i=\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R\) satisfy \(\sum m_i\boldsymbol\rho_i=0\). That identity is why translation and spin separate cleanly.

In \(I=\int r_\perp^2\,dm\), \(r_\perp\) is the shortest distance to the chosen axis, not necessarily distance to the origin. \(I\) has units $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}$. A quoted moment without its axis is incomplete.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: For a fixed hinge, the hinge force disappears from the torque equation. For a freely moving body, use the CM and keep translation as a separate equation. First identify the origin; then mark the direction of each cross product.

parts.title: 8.4.1 · The derivative, one term at a time
parts.body_md: For constant particle mass and a fixed inertial origin, $$\frac{d\mathbf L}{dt}=\dot{\mathbf r}\times\mathbf p+\mathbf r\times\dot{\mathbf p}=\mathbf v\times m\mathbf v+\mathbf r\times\mathbf F=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F.$$ The first term is zero because the vectors are parallel. Define \(\boldsymbol\tau=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F\). Torque has units N m; angular momentum has $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s$. Use the perpendicular lever arm \(r\sin\theta\).

parts.title: 8.4.1 · Pick the origin before taking the cross product
parts.body_md: A force through the origin has no torque about that origin. The same force can have torque about another origin. In a planar drawing, \(\tau_z=xF_y-yF_x\), which is often safer than guessing clockwise signs.

parts.title: 8.4.2 · Why internal forces disappear
parts.body_md: For a pair, \(\mathbf F_{21}=-\mathbf F_{12}\) and a central force is parallel to \(\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2\). Its combined torque is \((\mathbf r_1-\mathbf r_2)\times\mathbf F_{12}=0\). Summing particles therefore yields $$\frac{d\mathbf L_O}{dt}=\sum\boldsymbol\tau_{O,\rm ext}.$$ Central internal forces and an inertial fixed origin are the assumptions here. No rigidity is needed for this conservation law; rigidity is needed to replace the angular momentum by a fixed inertia times angular velocity.

parts.title: 8.4.2 · When τ=Iα is legitimate
parts.body_md: For a rigid body in a fixed plane about a fixed axle, \(L_z=I_z\omega\) with constant I, so \(\tau_z=I_z\alpha\). A hinge can exert a large force but zero torque about its own point. Choose it to remove the unknown from the torque equation, then use \(\sum\mathbf F=M\mathbf a_{\rm CM}\) if support forces are requested.

parts.title: 8.4.3 · Specify which angular momentum you mean
parts.body_md: Morin uses positions and velocities relative to a moving, nonrotating origin: $$\mathbf L_O^{\rm rel}=\sum(\mathbf r_i-\mathbf r_O)\times m_i(\mathbf v_i-\mathbf v_O).$$ Differentiating gives $$\frac{d\mathbf L_O^{\rm rel}}{dt}=\boldsymbol\tau_{O,\rm ext}-M(\mathbf R-\mathbf r_O)\times\mathbf a_O.$$ This is not the same definition as using laboratory momenta about a moving point; that alternative has a different correction. State your convention.

parts.title: 8.4.3 · The safe choices and rolling trap
parts.body_md: The correction is zero if the origin is the system CM, if it has zero acceleration, or if its acceleration is parallel to the displacement to the CM. The CM or a fixed point are usually the easiest choices. A momentarily stationary contact point is not automatically a fixed point: zero velocity at one instant does not mean zero acceleration. For a collision, the center of one struck object is not necessarily the CM of the whole chosen system. Choosing it carelessly can invalidate angular-momentum conservation.

examples.title: A central pull gives no torque
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A bead has position \(\mathbf r=a\hat x+b\hat y\) and feels \(\mathbf F=-k\mathbf r\). Find its torque about the force center.

steps.why: Use the same origin for r and torque.
Parallel or antiparallel vectors have zero cross product.
The origin is fixed, so zero torque conserves angular momentum.

examples.answer_md: \(\mathbf L\) is constant even though the particle can accelerate.
examples.check_md: The force can change kinetic energy; zero torque does not imply zero force or constant speed.

examples.title: A horizontal rod is released at a hinge
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A uniform rod of mass \(M\), length \(\ell\), is hinged at its left end and released horizontally. Find its initial angular acceleration and the initial vertical hinge force. Take counterclockwise positive.

steps.why: Gravity acts at the CM and initially turns the rod clockwise; the hinge force has zero hinge torque.
Apply $\tau =I\alpha$ about the fixed hinge.
At release $\omega =0$, so there is no centripetal acceleration yet.
Use linear Newton’s law as well to find the support force.
The hinge still supports part of the weight while the CM accelerates downward.

examples.answer_md: \(\alpha=-3g/(2\ell)\); \(H_y=Mg/4\) upward.
examples.check_md: Angular acceleration has units $s^{-2}$. The CM acceleration is less than g, consistent with a positive upward hinge force.

practice.question_md: A disk with \(I_{\rm CM}=MR^2/2\) rolls down an incline without slipping. Use CM torque and translation to find its acceleration and required static friction.
hints: Add the inertia contribution and solve.
practice.answer_md: \(a=2g\sin\theta/3\), \(f=Mg\sin\theta/3\) uphill. It requires \(f\le\mu_s Mg\cos\theta\), or \(\mu_s\ge\tan\theta/3\). The friction direction follows the needed spin-up torque, not a rule that it always opposes CM motion.

visual.description: Existing hinged falling rod supports the release and torque picture; the rolling-disk practice is separate.

examples.title: An accelerating observer invents a torque term

steps.why: There is no real force on the mass.

steps.math: \frac{d\mathbf L_O^{\rm rel}}{dt}=\boldsymbol\tau_{O,\rm real}-M(\mathbf R-\mathbf r_O)\times\mathbf a_O

Reverse the usual x cross y order to obtain the sign.

practice.question_md: An extended body has CM at \(\mathbf R\). Choose the origin to be the CM even while the body accelerates. What happens to the correction term, and what does the torque equation become?
hints: The difference \(\mathbf R-\mathbf r_O\) is now zero.
This is independent of the value of \(\mathbf a_O\).
practice.answer_md: The correction vanishes: \(d\mathbf L_{\rm CM}/dt=\boldsymbol\tau_{\rm CM,ext}\). Check: translating the entire object changes no CM-relative positions or velocities.

8.5.title: Collisions
8.5.summary: During impact, use the conservation laws allowed by the external impulses and by whether the collision is elastic.

parts.title: Choose the system and the instant
parts.body_md: An impact can create both translation and rotation. For an isolated system, total linear and angular momentum survive both elastic and inelastic collisions. Macroscopic kinetic energy survives only an elastic collision. In a sticking collision, some energy becomes deformation and heat. A support can supply external linear impulse while having zero angular impulse about its own point; then conserve angular momentum there, not total linear momentum.

parts.title: A free object needs its new CM
parts.body_md: If a pellet sticks to a free rod, find the combined CM, add both bodies’ moments about that CM, conserve total \(\mathbf P\) for CM velocity, and conserve total \(\mathbf L\) about a fixed point or the whole-system CM for spin. The original rod center can accelerate during the collision and is not automatically a legal moving origin. Do not omit the orbital \(\mathbf R\times M\mathbf V\) term when using another fixed origin.

parts.title: Count constraints before solving
parts.body_md: A rough elastic contact can exchange rotation; a smooth contact supplies only normal impulse. Identify that direction before writing component equations. After solving, check the sign of outgoing velocity and whether the bodies separate. An algebraic no-change root is not the colliding branch.

examples.title: A pellet sticks to a hinged wheel
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A pellet of mass m, speed v, strikes tangentially and sticks to the rim of a fixed-axle disk of mass M and radius R. The disk starts at rest. Neglect axle torque during impact.

steps.why: The incoming momentum is perpendicular to the radius at impact.
After sticking, both disk and pellet rotate about the same fixed axle.
Angular momentum about the axle is conserved; the axle can supply linear impulse but no axle torque.
Solve for the common angular speed.

examples.answer_md: \(\omega=mv/[R(M/2+m)]\).
examples.check_md: \(T_f/T_i=m/(M/2+m)<1\). Mechanical energy is lost, as expected for sticking; linear momentum of pellet+disk need not be conserved because of the axle.

examples.title: Elastic pellet reflection from a pinned rotor
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A pellet of mass m moving tangentially at speed v hits a rotor at radius b. The rotor has fixed-axis moment I and starts at rest. The collision is elastic. Find signed outgoing pellet speed u and rotor speed $\omega$.

steps.why: The axle contributes no angular impulse about itself.
Elasticity permits conservation of macroscopic kinetic energy.
Eliminate the rotor speed with angular momentum.
Substitute into energy and divide by v−u for the nontrivial collision.
Solve the resulting linear equation, then substitute back.

examples.answer_md: The pellet reverses when \(I>mb^2\); the displayed u includes that sign.
examples.check_md: As $I\to \infty , u\to -v$ and $\omega \to 0$. At $I=mb^{2}$ the pellet stops and its energy transfers to the rotor. The discarded $v=u$ root describes no impulse.

practice.question_md: A pellet of mass m sticks at distance b from a fixed axle of a stationary rotor of moment I. Its incoming perpendicular speed is v. Find $\omega$ and the fraction of initial kinetic energy remaining.
practice.answer_md: \(\omega=mbv/(I+mb^2)\); \(T_f/T_i=mb^2/(I+mb^2)\). It is between zero and one for positive I. At $b=0$ there is no angular momentum transferred about the axle.

8.6.title: Angular impulse
8.6.summary: A short force pulse has linked linear and angular impulses even when its detailed time profile is unknown.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

In \(I=\int r_\perp^2\,dm\), \(r_\perp\) is the shortest distance to the chosen axis, not necessarily distance to the origin. \(I\) has units $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}$. A quoted moment without its axis is incomplete.

parts.title: Integrate the law, do not guess the force
parts.body_md: $$\mathbf J=\int\mathbf F\,dt=\Delta\mathbf P,\qquad\mathbf J_\theta=\int\boldsymbol\tau\,dt=\Delta\mathbf L.$$ J has units N s and angular impulse N m s. If the application vector r is effectively constant during a brief hit, $$\Delta\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times\mathbf J.$$ This relates changes, not arbitrary initial values. Several contacts require a sum of their separate cross products; one net impulse can hide a nonzero couple.

parts.title: Recover point velocities
parts.body_md: After the impulse, compute CM translation and angular velocity separately. Then use \(\mathbf v_P=\mathbf V_{\rm CM}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho_P\). A rod end can initially move backward even while its CM moves forward. A zero-velocity point after an impulse is an instantaneous kinematic fact, not necessarily a support or a safe future torque origin.

examples.title: Choose a strike that leaves one rod end instantaneously still
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A free uniform rod of mass M and length $\ell$ lies along x and starts at rest. A short impulse \(J\hat y\) acts at \(x=b\) from its CM. Find b so that the left end has zero velocity immediately afterward.

steps.why: The total linear impulse fixes the CM speed.
The same impulse has angular impulse bJ about the CM.
The rotational velocity of the left end opposes CM translation.
Set the left-end velocity to zero and solve.

examples.answer_md: Strike at \(\ell/6\) from the CM toward the right end.
examples.check_md: The location does not depend on impulse magnitude. The right-end speed is $2J/M$, while the left end is only instantaneously stationary; it is not a permanent pivot.

examples.title: Opposite impulses create pure spin
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A uniform rod along x receives simultaneous impulses \(+J\hat y\) at its right end and \(-J\hat y\) at its left end. It starts at rest. Find its motion immediately afterward.

steps.why: The impulses cancel as vectors, so the CM stays at rest.
Both torques turn the rod in the same counterclockwise sense.
Divide total angular impulse by the central moment.

examples.answer_md: Pure counterclockwise spin at \(12J/(M\ell)\), with zero CM speed.
examples.check_md: Zero net force impulse does not imply zero torque impulse. The spin energy \(6J^2/M\) is supplied by the two striking agents.

practice.question_md: A free uniform rod receives \(J\hat y\) at its right endpoint. Find the immediate velocities of its right and left ends.
practice.answer_md: Right end: \(4J/M\) in +y. Left end: \(-2J/M\) in y. The mean of the endpoint velocities is $J/M$, consistent with the CM motion; their difference is \(\omega\ell\).

visual.description: Use the supplied Morin source on printed pages 331–333 for the axes and geometry. No new simulation is claimed.

9.1.title: Preliminaries concerning rotations
9.1.summary: Recognize the translation and three-dimensional rotation hidden in a complicated-looking motion.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Start with one marked point on a plate. Find its velocity from a chosen body point before worrying about angular momentum. Then put the motor on the turning platform to see why the angular-velocity arrow need not align with a visible axle.

parts.title: 9.1.1 · Choose a point, then describe the rest
parts.body_md: Chasles’ theorem says that for any point P fixed in a rigid body, $$\mathbf v_Q=\mathbf v_P+\boldsymbol\omega\times(\mathbf r_Q-\mathbf r_P).$$ Rigidity preserves all pairwise distances, so relative motion cannot stretch or shear; its instantaneous velocity field is a rotation. The chosen point need not be the CM for this kinematic statement, although the CM simplifies momentum and energy.

parts.title: 9.1.1 · Instantaneous does not mean permanently fixed
parts.body_md: The instantaneous axis can move or turn. A rolling wheel’s current contact point has zero velocity, but that material point leaves the ground later. In three dimensions there may also be translation along the instantaneous rotation axis; do not assume some point must be at rest in the lab. A deformable object needs additional internal motion and does not obey one rigid angular-velocity field.

parts.title: 9.1.2 · What the vector means
parts.body_md: \(\boldsymbol\omega\) points along the instantaneous rotation axis by the right-hand rule; its magnitude is in $\mathrm{rad}/s$. A point has velocity $$\mathbf v=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r,$$ with speed \(\omega r\sin\theta=\omega r_\perp\). A point on the axis has zero relative velocity. For an ordinary three-dimensional rigid body this velocity field determines a unique angular velocity.

parts.title: 9.1.2 · Add rates, not finite turns
parts.body_md: For nested frames, \(\boldsymbol\omega_{A/C}=\boldsymbol\omega_{A/B}+\boldsymbol\omega_{B/C}\). Express both in the same current basis before adding. Finite rotations about different axes generally do not commute; two successive ninety-degree turns are not represented by simply adding angle vectors. The addition rule concerns infinitesimal rates. For an ideal zero-thickness rod, adding an angular-velocity component along the rod changes no point velocity; this mathematical degeneracy is removed by a finite cross-section.

examples.title: Velocity of a corner on a moving plate
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A rigid plate’s center moves at \(V\hat x\), and its angular velocity is \(\Omega\hat z\). A corner is at \(a\hat x+b\hat y\) relative to the center. Find its instantaneous velocity.

steps.why: Add center motion to rotation relative to the center.

steps.math: \hat z\times\hat x=\hat y,\qquad\hat z\times\hat y=-\hat x
steps.why: Use a right-handed basis before inserting signs.
Collect the two Cartesian components.

examples.answer_md: \(\mathbf v_P=(V-\Omega b)\hat x+\Omega a\hat y\).
examples.check_md: At $a=b=0$ it reduces to the center velocity; for $V=0$ the velocity is perpendicular to the corner’s radius.

examples.title: A motor turns on a rotating platform
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A platform turns at \(\Omega\hat z\). A motor shaft fixed horizontally in the platform points along \(\hat n(t)=\cos(\Omega t)\hat x+\sin(\Omega t)\hat y\). Its rotor spins relative to the platform at rate s. Find the rotor’s lab angular velocity.

steps.why: Instantaneous angular velocities add when expressed as vectors in one basis.
The motor axis itself changes direction in the lab.
The shaft and platform-axis directions are perpendicular.

examples.answer_md: \(\boldsymbol\omega=s\cos\Omega t\,\hat x+s\sin\Omega t\,\hat y+\Omega\hat z\).
examples.check_md: At $s=0$ the rotor simply follows the platform. Constant magnitude does not imply a fixed angular-velocity direction.

practice.question_md: A body has \(\mathbf V_{\rm CM}=V\hat z\), \(\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega\hat z\). Can any point on its axis be stationary in the lab when V is nonzero?
hints: Its relative rotational velocity is zero on the axis.
Elsewhere the rotation velocity is horizontal and cannot cancel a vertical V.
practice.answer_md: No. Every point retains vertical velocity V; the motion is a screw motion. This checks that instantaneous rotation plus translation need not give a stationary lab point.

practice.question_md: At $t=0$ in the motor example, find the velocity relative to the shared origin of a rotor point at \(a\hat y\).
hints: Take each cross product with \(a\hat y\).
\(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), \(\hat z\times\hat y=-\hat x\).
practice.answer_md: \(\mathbf v=-a\Omega\hat x+as\hat z\). Units are $m/s$. Both contributions are perpendicular to the point’s displacement.

9.2.title: The inertia tensor
9.2.summary: Use one matrix to track how geometry redirects angular momentum.

prerequisites.idea: A matrix is a component recipe
prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

\(\mathbf R=M^{-1}\sum m_i\mathbf r_i\) is the mass-weighted position. Relative coordinates \(\boldsymbol\rho_i=\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R\) satisfy \(\sum m_i\boldsymbol\rho_i=0\). That identity is why translation and spin separate cleanly.

For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Begin with the single mass above its rotation plane: draw r and p before doing any matrix work. Its sideways L makes the tensor necessary. Then separate free translation and learn how the matrix changes when the origin moves.

parts.title: 9.2.1 · Build the tensor from mass geometry
parts.body_md: For rotation about an origin, \(\mathbf v=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r\). Inserting this into \(\mathbf L=\int\mathbf r\times\mathbf v\,dm\) gives $$I_{ij}=\int(r^2\delta_{ij}-x_i x_j)\,dm,\qquad\mathbf L=\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega.$$ Diagonal entries are ordinary axis moments; off-diagonal entries are negative products such as \(I_{xy}=-\int xy\,dm\). The matrix is symmetric and depends on mass distribution, origin and axes, not on the spin rate.

parts.title: 9.2.1 · Energy and interpretation
parts.body_md: $$T=\frac12\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf I\boldsymbol\omega=\frac12\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L.$$ Every tensor entry has $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}$ units. A sideways component of L is real: a particle rotating above the origin has a position vector tilted away from its circular-plane radius. \(\mathbf r\times\mathbf p\) then tilts too. Opposite symmetrically placed particles can cancel these sideways components. Use a real orthonormal basis; a skew pair of directions cannot be treated as Cartesian components.

parts.title: 9.2.2 · The general decomposition
parts.body_md: Write \(\mathbf r=\mathbf R+\boldsymbol\rho\) and \(\mathbf v=\mathbf V+\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho\). The CM identity removes cross terms, giving $$\mathbf L_O=\mathbf R\times M\mathbf V+\mathbf I_{\rm CM}\boldsymbol\omega,$$ $$T=\frac12MV^2+\frac12\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf I_{\rm CM}\boldsymbol\omega.$$ Both terms of L must be resolved in the same axes. A translating reference frame whose axes stay parallel to the lab has the same angular-velocity vector.

parts.title: 9.2.2 · Do not attach Iω to arbitrary translation
parts.body_md: \(\mathbf L_O=\mathbf I_O\boldsymbol\omega\) alone describes pure rotation about O. It is not the general formula for a freely flying body. Picking the CM makes spin independent of the object’s translational speed; picking another fixed origin requires the orbital term.

parts.title: 9.2.3 · The tensor shift
parts.body_md: Let \(\mathbf d\) point from a new origin O to the CM, with axes parallel at both points. Then $$\mathbf I_O=\mathbf I_{\rm CM}+M(d^2\mathbf1-\mathbf d\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}).$$ For example \(\Delta I_{xx}=M(d_y^2+d_z^2)\), \(\Delta I_{xy}=-Md_xd_y\). The transpose symbol just makes the outer-product matrix whose ij entry is \(d_i d_j\).

parts.title: 9.2.3 · Connection to the scalar theorem
parts.body_md: For a unit axis \(\hat n\), its moment is \(I_{\hat n}=\hat n^{\mathsf T}\mathbf I\hat n\). The shift adds \(M[d^2-(\hat n\cdot\mathbf d)^2]\), which is \(M\) times the squared perpendicular axis separation. The tensor theorem therefore contains the earlier scalar theorem. If axes rotate as well, transform the tensor basis separately; do not mix rotation with origin displacement.

examples.title: One mass above the rotation plane
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A mass m attached to a light support is instantaneously at \((a,0,h)\). The support rotates about the fixed z axis with \(\omega\hat z\). Find the full angular momentum about the origin.

steps.why: Only the distance a from the z axis contributes to velocity.
Use its actual position relative to the requested origin.
The vertical offset creates a horizontal angular-momentum component.
Only the z component contributes to the scalar dot product with $\omega$.

examples.answer_md: \(\mathbf L=m\omega(-ah,0,a^2)\), which is generally not parallel to \(\boldsymbol\omega\).
examples.check_md: At $h=0$ the familiar planar result returns. The kinetic energy is independent of h, as the actual speed is $a\omega$.

examples.title: Shift a rectangular block tensor to a corner
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A uniform rectangular solid has edges a,b,c. Its central tensor in edge-parallel axes is \(M\operatorname{diag}(b^2+c^2,a^2+c^2,a^2+b^2)/12\). Find the tensor about a corner with parallel axes.

steps.why: This is the vector from the corner to the CM.

steps.math: \mathbf I_O=\mathbf I_{\rm CM}+M\left(d^2\mathbf1-\mathbf d\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\right)
steps.why: Add the tensor of a point mass M located at the CM.
The x-axis shift depends only on the y and z displacements.
The central cross terms vanish, but the corner shift creates negative products.

examples.answer_md: The diagonal entries are \(M(b^2+c^2)/3\), \(M(a^2+c^2)/3\), \(M(a^2+b^2)/3\); the symmetric off-diagonals are the three displayed products.
examples.check_md: For $a=b=c$ the diagonal entries agree by symmetry. Shifting along x alone changes yy and zz but leaves xx unchanged.

practice.question_md: A body has principal CM moments \((I,2I,3I)\), spin components \((\Omega,\Omega,0)\), and no translation. Find L and T.
hints: Multiply each component by its matching moment.
Take the dot product of $\omega$ with L for energy.
practice.answer_md: \(\mathbf L=(I\Omega,2I\Omega,0)\), \(T=3I\Omega^2/2\). L is not parallel to $\omega$ because the two nonzero components were multiplied by unequal moments.

visual.description: Existing cube inertia setup illustrates origin-dependent tensor components; the rectangular-block example uses general dimensions.

examples.title: A spinning sphere flies past an origin
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A uniform sphere of mass M, radius R has CM position \(b\hat x\), CM velocity \(V\hat y\), and spin \(\omega\hat x\). Find angular momentum about the fixed origin and total kinetic energy.

steps.math: \mathbf L_{\rm orbital}=b\hat x\times MV\hat y=MbV\hat z
steps.why: Treat CM translation as a point-mass contribution.
A sphere has the same central moment about every axis.
The two angular-momentum contributions are vectors, not generally parallel scalars.
Translation and spin energies add as positive scalars.

examples.answer_md: The displayed vector L and scalar T are the complete CM decomposition.
examples.check_md: At $b=0$ orbital L disappears while translational energy remains. Thus zero orbital angular momentum does not mean no translation.

practice.question_md: In the sphere example replace \(V\hat y\) by \(V\hat x\). What changes in L and T?
hints: The CM velocity is now parallel to its position.
The cross product of parallel vectors is zero.
The speed and spin rate remain unchanged.
practice.answer_md: Orbital L becomes zero, leaving \(2MR^2\omega\hat x/5\). T is unchanged. The comparison checks that orbital L depends on direction, whereas translational energy depends only on speed.

9.2.3.title: The parallel-axis theorem
9.2.3.summary: Moving the origin shifts all tensor entries in a controlled way; rotating axes is a separate operation.

prerequisites.refresher_md: \(\mathbf R=M^{-1}\sum m_i\mathbf r_i\) is the mass-weighted position. Relative coordinates \(\boldsymbol\rho_i=\mathbf r_i-\mathbf R\) satisfy \(\sum m_i\boldsymbol\rho_i=0\). That identity is why translation and spin separate cleanly.
