prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

parts.title: The tensor shift
parts.body_md: Let \(\mathbf d\) point from a new origin O to the CM, with axes parallel at both points. Then $$\mathbf I_O=\mathbf I_{\rm CM}+M(d^2\mathbf1-\mathbf d\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}).$$ For example \(\Delta I_{xx}=M(d_y^2+d_z^2)\), \(\Delta I_{xy}=-Md_xd_y\). The transpose symbol just makes the outer-product matrix whose ij entry is \(d_i d_j\).

parts.title: Connection to the scalar theorem
parts.body_md: For a unit axis \(\hat n\), its moment is \(I_{\hat n}=\hat n^{\mathsf T}\mathbf I\hat n\). The shift adds \(M[d^2-(\hat n\cdot\mathbf d)^2]\), which is \(M\) times the squared perpendicular axis separation. The tensor theorem therefore contains the earlier scalar theorem. If axes rotate as well, transform the tensor basis separately; do not mix rotation with origin displacement.

examples.title: Shift a rectangular block tensor to a corner
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A uniform rectangular solid has edges a,b,c. Its central tensor in edge-parallel axes is \(M\operatorname{diag}(b^2+c^2,a^2+c^2,a^2+b^2)/12\). Find the tensor about a corner with parallel axes.

steps.why: This is the vector from the corner to the CM.

steps.math: \mathbf I_O=\mathbf I_{\rm CM}+M\left(d^2\mathbf1-\mathbf d\mathbf d^{\mathsf T}\right)
steps.why: Add the tensor of a point mass M located at the CM.
The x-axis shift depends only on the y and z displacements.
The central cross terms vanish, but the corner shift creates negative products.

examples.answer_md: The diagonal entries are \(M(b^2+c^2)/3\), \(M(a^2+c^2)/3\), \(M(a^2+b^2)/3\); the symmetric off-diagonals are the three displayed products.
examples.check_md: For $a=b=c$ the diagonal entries agree by symmetry. Shifting along x alone changes yy and zz but leaves xx unchanged.

practice.question_md: A body’s CM tensor is diagonal. Shift the origin by distance d along x with axes unchanged. Which entries change?
hints: All cross products of different displacement components vanish.
practice.answer_md: \(I_{yy}\) and \(I_{zz}\) each increase by \(Md^2\); \(I_{xx}\) and all off-diagonals stay the same. The x axis is the same geometric line before and after shifting along itself.

visual.description: Use the supplied Morin source on printed pages 382–383 for the axes and geometry. No new simulation is claimed.

9.3.title: Principal axes
9.3.summary: Choose axes that make each angular-momentum component equal to one moment times the matching angular-velocity component.

prerequisites.idea: A matrix is a component recipe
prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

In \(I=\int r_\perp^2\,dm\), \(r_\perp\) is the shortest distance to the chosen axis, not necessarily distance to the origin. \(I\) has units $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}$. A quoted moment without its axis is incomplete.

parts.title: Recognize principal axes physically
parts.body_md: A principal direction obeys \(\mathbf I\hat e_i=I_i\hat e_i\): rotation along it gives L along the same direction. In its orthonormal basis, $$L_i=I_i\omega_i,\qquad T=\frac12\sum_i I_i\omega_i^2.$$ Reflection symmetry often makes cross-product integrals vanish. A real symmetric tensor always has an orthonormal principal basis; for less symmetric shapes solve \(\det(\mathbf I-\lambda\mathbf1)=0\), then \((\mathbf I-\lambda\mathbf1)\mathbf e=0\), and normalize.

parts.title: Repeated moments and changing coordinates
parts.body_md: If two principal moments agree, every direction in their plane is principal. If all three agree, every direction is principal. Rotational symmetry by an angle other than 0 or $\pi$ around an axis forces equality in the transverse plane. Principal axes belong to a specified origin: a centered rectangle’s side axes need not remain principal after shifting to a corner. If columns of Q are principal unit vectors written in old coordinates, $$\boldsymbol\omega_{\rm principal}=Q^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\omega_{\rm old},\quad\mathbf I_{\rm old}=Q\operatorname{diag}(I_1,I_2,I_3)Q^{\mathsf T}.$$ This is a coordinate conversion, not a new physical rotation.

parts.title: The tilted-disk recognition test
parts.body_md: When a disk rolls around a circle or a tilted body spins, first mark its symmetry axis and a diameter axis. A thin disk uses \(MR^2/2\) for its normal and \(MR^2/4\) for a diameter. Break the actual $\omega$ into those directions before multiplying. The body may need a torque to maintain a prescribed rotation about a nonprincipal axis, because its L changes direction.

parts.title: A square viewed from a corner
parts.body_md: For a uniform square sheet of side a with origin at a corner and x,y along its sides, \(I_{xx}=I_{yy}=Ma^2/3\), \(I_{xy}=-Ma^2/4\), and \(I_{zz}=2Ma^2/3\). The in-plane diagonal through the CM is principal with moment \(Ma^2/12\); the perpendicular in-plane diagonal direction through the chosen corner has moment \(7Ma^2/12\). Their sum gives the normal moment. This is the physical version of testing diagonal vectors in a symmetric matrix: moving the origin changes the principal directions and moments.

examples.title: Resolve a tilted disk spin into its own axes
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A thin disk has symmetry axis \(\hat e_3\), with perpendicular central axes \(\hat e_1,\hat e_2\). Its angular velocity is \(\Omega(\sin\theta\hat e_1+\cos\theta\hat e_3)\). Find L and the angle $\beta$ it makes with \(\hat e_3\).

steps.why: A diameter moment differs from the normal-axis moment.
Multiply components in the disk’s principal basis.
Compare perpendicular and axial components to find the direction.

examples.answer_md: \(\mathbf L=MR^2\Omega(\sin\theta\hat e_1/4+\cos\theta\hat e_3/2)\). For \(0<\theta<\pi/2\), $\beta$ is smaller than $\theta$.
examples.check_md: At $\theta =0$ or $\pi /2, \omega$ is along a principal axis and L is parallel to it; at intermediate angles it is not.

examples.title: Find principal directions without a matrix course
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. The tensor is \(I_0\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&2&0\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix}\). Test the directions \((1,1,0)\), \((1,-1,0)\), and \((0,0,1)\).

steps.why: The output points along the input, so this direction is principal with moment $I_{0}$.
The other diagonal direction is also principal, with a different factor.
The z direction is already uncoupled.
Normalize and choose the sign of the second axis to make a right-handed orthonormal basis.

examples.answer_md: Principal moments are \(I_0,3I_0,4I_0\).
examples.check_md: Their sum equals the original matrix trace $8I_{0}$, and the three axes are mutually perpendicular; changing an eigenvector’s sign changes no physical axis.

practice.question_md: Using the tensor in the second example, find L for \(\boldsymbol\omega=\Omega\hat x\) directly, then using principal axes.
hints: The first matrix column gives the direct answer.
With the displayed right-handed axes, \(\hat x=(\hat e_1-\hat e_2)/\sqrt2\).
Multiply the two principal components by $I_{0}$ and $3I_{0}$, then convert back.
practice.answer_md: Both routes give \(\mathbf L=I_0\Omega(2,-1,0)\). Check: \(\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf L=2I_0\Omega^2>0\), and the output is tilted away from x.

visual.description: Existing tilted rod demonstrates the separation between a visible axle, principal directions, and L; the disk calculations are separate.

9.4.title: Two basic types of problems
9.4.summary: Recognize whether the problem asks for a sudden velocity change or a torque that maintains a turning angular momentum.

prerequisites.idea: A matrix is a component recipe
prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: An impulsive-blow problem works forward from a change in L to a new $\omega$. A steady-motion problem works backward from the prescribed motion of L to the required torque. Both begin with the same origin and principal-axis decisions.

parts.title: 9.4.1 · Five steps for an impulsive blow
parts.body_md: Use the CM for a freely floating body, or a fixed pivot for a constrained one. Compute \(\Delta\mathbf L=\mathbf r_{\rm hit}\times\mathbf J\). Find principal moments about that same origin. Use \(\omega_i=L_i/I_i\), including any initial spin. Compute \(\mathbf u_P=\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\rho_P\). Finally add the origin’s velocity; for a free body \(\Delta\mathbf V=\mathbf J/M\).

parts.title: 9.4.1 · Immediate motion is not the whole later motion
parts.body_md: During a sufficiently short impulse, treat the lever arm and orientation as fixed. The body’s later torque-free orientation can be complicated, even though the immediate velocities are easy. If a pivot is present, its impulse changes linear momentum; do not reuse the free-body CM impulse equation without including that support impulse.

parts.title: 9.4.2 · The steady-rotation recipe
parts.body_md: Choose a fixed pivot or the CM; find its principal moments; express the physical $\omega$ in those axes; obtain L; identify how L moves in the lab; calculate the actual torque; equate vectors. When L rigidly precesses at a known rate \(\boldsymbol\Omega\), $$\frac{d\mathbf L}{dt}=\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf L.$$ Only the component of L perpendicular to $\Omega$ contributes. $\Omega$ is the rate of that arrow’s precession; it need not equal the full spin vector $\omega$.

parts.title: 9.4.2 · Do not replace a turning arrow by a scalar derivative
parts.body_md: A constant angular speed does not guarantee zero torque. If L has constant length but traces a cone, its derivative has magnitude \(\Omega L_\perp\). Using \(d|L|/dt=0\) would miss the entire torque. Match the torque direction as well as its magnitude before canceling trigonometric factors.

examples.title: Strike the corner of a free rectangular plate
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A thin rectangular plate of mass M has side lengths 2a along x and 2b along y. A short impulse \(J\hat z\) acts at its corner \((a,b,0)\). It starts at rest. Find its angular velocity and the struck corner’s immediate velocity.

steps.why: Linear impulse moves the CM; angular impulse about the CM sets spin.
Use the central principal moments of the rectangular sheet.
Divide each angular-momentum component by its own moment.
Find the corner’s rotational velocity with a cross product.
Add the CM velocity to the relative rotational velocity.

examples.answer_md: \(\boldsymbol\omega=(3J/(Mb),-3J/(Ma),0)\); the struck corner initially moves at \(7J/M\) along +z.
examples.check_md: The large corner speed does not violate momentum: the mass-weighted rotational velocities average to zero. Units of $\omega$ are $s^{-1}$.

examples.title: A weighted arm sweeps a cone
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A rigid arm pivots at a fixed point and has its CM distance d along its axis. Its transverse pivot moment is I; spin about its own ideal thin axis is negligible. It sweeps a cone of fixed angle $\theta$ from downward vertical at rate $\Omega$. Find $\Omega$.

steps.why: Resolve vertical angular velocity perpendicular to the arm; the component along the thin arm contributes no angular momentum.
Project L onto the radius of its cone in angular-momentum space.
That horizontal component rotates at $\Omega$.
Gravity supplies the matching pivot torque.
Cancel $\sin\theta$ for a nonvertical cone.

examples.answer_md: \(\Omega=\sqrt{Mgd/(I\cos\theta)}\), for \(0<\theta<\pi/2\).
examples.check_md: For a point mass at distance $d, I=Md^{2}$ and the usual conical-pendulum result returns. Exactly $\theta =0$ is a degenerate motion; the formula gives its small-cone limiting frequency.

practice.question_md: A motor forces a body to turn steadily about a fixed direction that is not principal. Must zero angular acceleration imply zero torque?
hints: The body axes can carry L around even if the body components do not change.
The lab derivative includes a cross product.
practice.answer_md: No. For constant body components, \(\boldsymbol\tau=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L\), generally nonzero when L is not parallel to $\omega$. A principal-axis rotation is the zero-torque special case.

visual.description: Use the supplied Morin source on printed pages 388–393 for the axes and geometry. No new simulation is claimed.

9.4.1.title: Motion after an impulsive blow
9.4.1.summary: After a brief hit, convert angular impulse to L, then to ω in principal axes, then to point velocities.

practice.question_md: For a square plate with $a=b$, find the velocity of the opposite corner \((-a,-a,0)\) immediately after the example’s impulse.
hints: The rotational velocity reverses at the opposite corner.
The same CM velocity \(J\hat z/M\) must be added.
practice.answer_md: \(\mathbf v_{\rm opposite}=-5J\hat z/M\). Check: averaging velocities of opposite corners gives $J/M$, the center velocity.

9.4.2.title: Frequency of motion due to a torque
9.4.2.summary: For steady directional change, torque is the rate at which the angular-momentum arrow turns.

practice.question_md: A uniform slender rod of length $\ell$ swings as the conical arm. Insert \(d=\ell/2\) and \(I=M\ell^2/3\) to find its precession rate.
hints: Substitute the pivot moment, not the central moment.
Cancel M and one power of $\ell$.
practice.answer_md: \(\Omega=\sqrt{3g/(2\ell\cos\theta)}\). It has inverse-second units and grows without bound as the ideal cone approaches horizontal.

9.5.title: Euler’s equations
9.5.summary: Euler’s equations keep the easy body-frame inertia while accounting for the fact that the axes themselves rotate.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

prerequisites.idea: A matrix is a component recipe
prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

parts.title: Derive the missing term
parts.body_md: For any vector, $$\left(\frac{d\mathbf A}{dt}\right)_{\rm lab}=\left(\frac{d\mathbf A}{dt}\right)_{\rm body}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A.$$ Use body-fixed principal axes, constant moments, and a fixed pivot or the CM. With \(L_i=I_i\omega_i\), the torque components are $$\tau_1=I_1\dot\omega_1+(I_3-I_2)\omega_2\omega_3,$$ $$\tau_2=I_2\dot\omega_2+(I_1-I_3)\omega_3\omega_1,$$ $$\tau_3=I_3\dot\omega_3+(I_2-I_1)\omega_1\omega_2.$$ Every component on both sides is expressed in the current body basis; a component derivative is not the lab vector derivative.

parts.title: Use the equations without memorizing a wall
parts.body_md: You can always start with \(\boldsymbol\tau=\dot{\mathbf L}_{\rm body}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L\) and take the cross product. If all moments agree, the cross term vanishes. With no torque, both \(\sum I_i\omega_i^2/2\) and \(\sum I_i^2\omega_i^2\) are constant: energy and squared angular momentum provide independent checks. The intermediate-axis sign test is a useful application, while the symmetric top gives a solvable full motion.

examples.title: Torque required to hold two spin components fixed
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A body has principal moments \(I_1=I\), \(I_2=2I\), \(I_3=3I/2\). Its body components are held at \((\Omega,\Omega,0)\). Find the necessary torque.

steps.why: The components are specified constant in the body frame, not necessarily as a fixed lab vector.
Each of these cross terms contains $\omega _{3}$.
The remaining cross term turns L with the body.

examples.answer_md: \(\boldsymbol\tau=I\Omega^2\hat e_3\).
examples.check_md: Its power \(\boldsymbol\tau\cdot\boldsymbol\omega\) is zero, so a nonzero torque can redirect L without changing kinetic energy.

examples.title: Why the intermediate axis is unstable
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A torque-free body has \(I_1<I_2<I_3\) and spins nearly about \(\hat e_2\), with \(\omega_2\approx\Omega\). Linearize in small \(\omega_1,\omega_3\).

steps.why: Keep terms first order in the small components in Euler’s first equation.
Use Euler’s third equation at the same order.
Differentiate the first equation and substitute the third.
Both numerator factors are negative, so the product is positive and perturbations include exponential growth.

examples.answer_md: The intermediate-axis steady spin is unstable; small deviations can grow.
examples.check_md: Repeating the sign test about the smallest or largest moment gives an oscillation equation instead of exponential growth. This is a linear local stability statement, not a full large-flip trajectory.

practice.question_md: For a torque-free body with all moments equal to I, what do Euler’s equations say about its angular velocity?
hints: $L=I\omega$ is parallel to $\omega$, so the lab cross term also vanishes.
practice.answer_md: All body components of $\omega$ are constant, and $\omega$ is also a fixed lab vector. Energy and L stay constant. This is stronger than the general torque-free case, where $\omega$ may wobble.

visual.description: Use the supplied Morin source on printed pages 393–396 for the axes and geometry. No new simulation is claimed.

9.6.title: Free symmetric top
9.6.summary: Describe one torque-free symmetric top from both the body and laboratory viewpoints.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

prerequisites.idea: A matrix is a component recipe
prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Imagine marking an axis on a tossed disk and also drawing its fixed angular momentum in space. Solve what the marks see first; then explain how the marked axis moves around the fixed arrow.

parts.title: 9.6.1 · Solve Euler’s equations with symmetry
parts.body_md:
With \(I_1=I_2=I\), no external torque, and body-fixed principal axes, $$\omega_3=s,\quad 
u= rac{I_3-I}{I}s,\quad\dot\omega_1=-
u\omega_2,\quad\dot\omega_2=
u\omega_1.$$ Therefore \(\omega_1=A\cos(
u t+\delta)\), \(\omega_2=A\sin(
u t+\delta)\). The parameters $s,A,
u$ have inverse-second units. For an oblate rotor \(I_3>I\), $
u$ has the sign of s; for a prolate rotor it has the opposite sign.

parts.title: 9.6.1 · What a body observer sees
parts.body_md: In the same axes \(\mathbf L=(I\omega_1,I\omega_2,I_3s)\). The transverse projections of L and $\omega$ remain parallel, but their axial components have different scale factors. Both arrows trace cones in the body coordinates. This does not mean that L turns in the lab: the lab torque is zero. For \(I_3=I\), $\nu$ vanishes and every direction is principal.

parts.title: 9.6.2 · Use fixed L to avoid solving orientation matrices
parts.body_md: For the symmetric top, $$\mathbf L=I\boldsymbol\omega+(I_3-I)s\hat e_3,\qquad\boldsymbol\omega=\frac{\mathbf L}{I}-\nu\hat e_3.$$ Since \(\dot{\hat e}_3=\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat e_3\), its lab precession rate is \(L/I\), and \(\cos\theta=I_3s/L\) is constant. This rate differs from the body-frame component frequency $\nu$.

parts.title: 9.6.2 · Keep the three arrows separate
parts.body_md: L is fixed in the inertial frame. The symmetry axis is fixed in the body. $\omega$ is generally fixed in neither frame, even though its magnitude is constant for the symmetric top. You cannot conclude \(d\boldsymbol\omega/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\omega=0\), because that rotating-arrow formula alone applies only to a body-fixed vector.

parts.title: Check whether the moments describe a real body
parts.body_md: Positive moments are not completely arbitrary: \(I_1+I_2-I_3=2\int z^2dm\ge0\), with cyclic versions. A symmetric top therefore has \(I_3\le2I\). A thin disk reaches equality; a real prolate rotor can have a much smaller axial moment. Keep this geometric constraint when inventing examples or changing a simulation’s parameters.

examples.title: Watch a free disk from painted axes
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A torque-free symmetric rotor has \(I_1=I_2=I\), \(I_3=2I\), and initial body components \((A,0,s)\). Find the later components.

steps.why: The symmetry-axis component is conserved; the difference in moments sets the body-frame frequency.
Insert the moments into the first two Euler equations.
These functions obey both differential equations and the initial conditions.

examples.answer_md: The transverse spin components rotate at s relative to the painted body axes.
examples.check_md: \(\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2=A^2\), so both energy and \(L^2=I^2A^2+4I^2s^2\) remain constant.

examples.title: Find the laboratory wobble frequency
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Use the rotor above, with \(I_3=2I\), \(\omega_3=s\), transverse amplitude A. Find the angle of its symmetry axis to fixed L and its lab precession rate.

steps.why: Compute the conserved angular-momentum magnitude.
L projected on the symmetry axis is $I_{3}s$.
Separate the part along fixed L from the part along the body axis.
The second term cannot turn its own axis.
Read the rate at which the body axis sweeps around L.

examples.answer_md: Its symmetry axis precesses at \(\sqrt{A^2+4s^2}\), at fixed $\theta$.
examples.check_md: If $A=0$ the cone collapses, so the formally assigned precession rate describes no visible axis motion; the actual body still spins at s.

practice.question_md: Why does a torque-free wobbling rotor not violate \(\boldsymbol\tau=d\mathbf L/dt\)?
hints: The torque law uses the lab derivative.
Body components can change because the axes turn.
Add the transport cross product to the component derivative.
practice.answer_md: The changing body components obey \(\dot{\mathbf L}_{body}=-\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf L\), so the two terms cancel in the lab derivative. Thus L is fixed even though the rotor wobbles.

visual.description: Use the existing free-disk wobble scene to distinguish the lab and body descriptions.

9.6.1.title: View from the body frame
9.6.1.summary: A free symmetric top has a constant axial spin and rotating transverse components in its body frame.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

prerequisites.idea: A matrix is a component recipe
prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

parts.title: Solve Euler’s equations with symmetry
parts.body_md:
With \(I_1=I_2=I\), no external torque, and body-fixed principal axes, $$\omega_3=s,\quad 
u= rac{I_3-I}{I}s,\quad\dot\omega_1=-
u\omega_2,\quad\dot\omega_2=
u\omega_1.$$ Therefore \(\omega_1=A\cos(
u t+\delta)\), \(\omega_2=A\sin(
u t+\delta)\). The parameters $s,A,
u$ have inverse-second units. For an oblate rotor \(I_3>I\), $
u$ has the sign of s; for a prolate rotor it has the opposite sign.

parts.title: What a body observer sees
parts.body_md: In the same axes \(\mathbf L=(I\omega_1,I\omega_2,I_3s)\). The transverse projections of L and $\omega$ remain parallel, but their axial components have different scale factors. Both arrows trace cones in the body coordinates. This does not mean that L turns in the lab: the lab torque is zero. For \(I_3=I\), $\nu$ vanishes and every direction is principal.

parts.title: Check whether the moments describe a real body
parts.body_md: Positive moments are not completely arbitrary: \(I_1+I_2-I_3=2\int z^2dm\ge0\), with cyclic versions. A symmetric top therefore has \(I_3\le2I\). A thin disk reaches equality; a real prolate rotor can have a much smaller axial moment. Keep this geometric constraint when inventing examples or changing a simulation’s parameters.

examples.title: Watch a free disk from painted axes
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A torque-free symmetric rotor has \(I_1=I_2=I\), \(I_3=2I\), and initial body components \((A,0,s)\). Find the later components.

steps.why: The symmetry-axis component is conserved; the difference in moments sets the body-frame frequency.
Insert the moments into the first two Euler equations.
These functions obey both differential equations and the initial conditions.

examples.answer_md: The transverse spin components rotate at s relative to the painted body axes.
examples.check_md: \(\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2=A^2\), so both energy and \(L^2=I^2A^2+4I^2s^2\) remain constant.

practice.question_md: For a prolate symmetric rotor with \(I_3=I/2\), initial \((A,0,s)\), find \(\omega_2(t)\).
hints: Compute $\nu$ before choosing a sine sign.
practice.answer_md: \(\omega_2=-A\sin(st/2)\), with \(\omega_1=A\cos(st/2)\). The negative initial slope checks the precession direction.

visual.description: Existing free-disk scene illustrates torque-free wobble; its moments need not equal this prolate practice rotor.

9.6.2.title: View from a fixed frame
9.6.2.summary: In the lab, angular momentum stays fixed while the body axis and angular velocity generally precess around it.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

parts.title: Use fixed L to avoid solving orientation matrices
parts.body_md: For the symmetric top, $$\mathbf L=I\boldsymbol\omega+(I_3-I)s\hat e_3,\qquad\boldsymbol\omega=\frac{\mathbf L}{I}-\nu\hat e_3.$$ Since \(\dot{\hat e}_3=\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat e_3\), its lab precession rate is \(L/I\), and \(\cos\theta=I_3s/L\) is constant. This rate differs from the body-frame component frequency $\nu$.

parts.title: Keep the three arrows separate
parts.body_md: L is fixed in the inertial frame. The symmetry axis is fixed in the body. $\omega$ is generally fixed in neither frame, even though its magnitude is constant for the symmetric top. You cannot conclude \(d\boldsymbol\omega/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\boldsymbol\omega=0\), because that rotating-arrow formula alone applies only to a body-fixed vector.

parts.title: Check whether the moments describe a real body
parts.body_md: Positive moments are not completely arbitrary: \(I_1+I_2-I_3=2\int z^2dm\ge0\), with cyclic versions. A symmetric top therefore has \(I_3\le2I\). A thin disk reaches equality; a real prolate rotor can have a much smaller axial moment. Keep this geometric constraint when inventing examples or changing a simulation’s parameters.

examples.title: Find the laboratory wobble frequency
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Use the rotor above, with \(I_3=2I\), \(\omega_3=s\), transverse amplitude A. Find the angle of its symmetry axis to fixed L and its lab precession rate.

steps.why: Compute the conserved angular-momentum magnitude.
L projected on the symmetry axis is $I_{3}s$.
Separate the part along fixed L from the part along the body axis.
The second term cannot turn its own axis.
Read the rate at which the body axis sweeps around L.

examples.answer_md: Its symmetry axis precesses at \(\sqrt{A^2+4s^2}\), at fixed $\theta$.
examples.check_md: If $A=0$ the cone collapses, so the formally assigned precession rate describes no visible axis motion; the actual body still spins at s.

practice.question_md: A symmetric rotor has \(I_3=3I/2\), $s>0$, and $A=s$. Find the two precession frequencies and the axis tilt.
hints: Project L onto the body axis.
practice.answer_md: \(\nu=s/2\), \(\Omega_{\rm lab}=\sqrt{13}s/2\), \(\cos\theta=3/\sqrt{13}\). Both rates have inverse-second units and describe different observers.

visual.description: Existing torque-free disk visual supports comparing the fixed L arrow with its moving symmetry axis.

9.7.title: Heavy symmetric top
9.7.summary: A heavy symmetric top combines spin, precession and nutation; each has a different geometric meaning.

prerequisites.idea: A matrix is a component recipe
prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Mark the top axis and upward vertical first. Identify the three angle rates, then use torque or the Lagrangian to predict whether the axis stays at one tilt or bobs. Work through the component example before asking for a steady-precession calculation.

parts.title: 9.7.1 · Build the orientation in three motions
parts.body_md: Use $\theta$ for the angle between the symmetry axis \(\hat e_3\) and upward vertical \(\hat z\). The horizontal line of nodes \(\hat e_1\) is the intersection of the horizontal plane and the plane perpendicular to \(\hat e_3\); $\phi$ is its azimuth. $\psi$ tracks rotation of the material around \(\hat e_3\) relative to that intermediate frame. Let \(\hat e_2\) complete a right-handed basis, so \(\hat z=\sin\theta\hat e_2+\cos\theta\hat e_3\).

parts.title: 9.7.1 · A convention matters more than an angle name
parts.body_md: Morin’s intermediate axes follow $\phi$ and $\theta$ but not $\psi$. They are still principal axes for a symmetric top because every transverse axis has the same moment I. They are not all painted on the body. At $\theta =0$ the line of nodes is undefined; the body orientation remains physical, but these coordinates become singular. A different Euler-angle convention has different component formulas. Angles are dimensionless radians and their rates are in $s^{-1}$.

parts.title: 9.7.2 · The components that belong in the inertia formula
parts.body_md: $$\boldsymbol\omega=\dot\theta\hat e_1+\dot\phi\hat z+\dot\psi\hat e_3,$$ hence $$\omega_1=\dot\theta,\quad\omega_2=\dot\phi\sin\theta,\quad\omega_3=\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta.$$ $\dot\theta$ changes tilt, $\dot\phi$ moves the axis around vertical, and $\dot\psi$ spins material relative to the moving reference plane. The vertical component of $\omega$ is not generally $\dot\phi$.

parts.title: 9.7.2 · Why adding two projections fails
parts.body_md: Vertical and the symmetry axis are usually not perpendicular. You may add the rotation vectors along those directions, but you may not treat their coefficients as orthogonal Cartesian components for \(\omega^2\) or \(T\). Resolve onto \(\hat e_1,\hat e_2,\hat e_3\) first. Axial spin \(\omega_3\) includes part of the precession even when the painted marks seem to spin at $\dot\psi$.

parts.title: 9.7.3 · Use the actual moving basis
parts.body_md: About the fixed pivot let \(I_1=I_2=I\), axial moment $I_{3}$, and CM distance $\ell$. Then $$\mathbf L=I\dot\theta\hat e_1+I\dot\phi\sin\theta\hat e_2+I_3\omega_3\hat e_3,$$ and gravity gives \(\boldsymbol\tau=Mg\ell\sin\theta\hat e_1\). The intermediate frame turns with \(\boldsymbol\Omega_f=\dot\theta\hat e_1+\dot\phi\hat z\), excluding $\dot\psi$. Therefore use \(\dot{\mathbf L}_{lab}=\dot{\mathbf L}_{components}+\boldsymbol\Omega_f\times\mathbf L\), not the full body spin in that cross term.

parts.title: 9.7.3 · Three equations and their physical jobs
parts.body_md: $$\dot\omega_3=0,$$ $$I\ddot\phi\sin\theta+\dot\theta(2I\dot\phi\cos\theta-I_3\omega_3)=0,$$ $$I\ddot\theta=(Mg\ell+I\dot\phi^2\cos\theta-I_3\omega_3\dot\phi)\sin\theta.$$ Gravity has no axial torque, so axial spin stays constant. The second equation couples changing tilt to changing precession; the third balances gravitational tendency to fall against the turning angular momentum. Moments here are about the pivot, not about the CM.

parts.title: 9.7.4 · Energy in the Euler coordinates
parts.body_md: $$\mathcal L=\frac I2(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+\frac{I_3}2(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2-Mg\ell\cos\theta.$$ Potential energy increases with CM height. $\psi$ and $\phi$ are absent as coordinates, hence $$p_\psi=I_3\omega_3,\qquad p_\phi=I\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+I_3\omega_3\cos\theta=L_z$$ are conserved. Euler–Lagrange for $\theta$ reproduces the torque equation.

parts.title: 9.7.4 · Reduction must retain the conserved momenta
parts.body_md: Do not replace \(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta\) by a constant before varying the original Lagrangian: it depends on $\theta$ and $\dot\phi$, so that shortcut discards real derivatives. After obtaining the conservation laws, substitute them into the energy to get $$E=\frac I2\dot\theta^2+\frac{(K-I_3s\cos\theta)^2}{2I\sin^2\theta}+\frac{I_3s^2}2+Mg\ell\cos\theta.$$ The $\theta$-dependent terms form an effective potential; its turning points bound nutation.

parts.title: 9.7.5 · Balance a uniformly turning L
parts.body_md: For \(\dot\theta=0\), \(\dot\phi=\Omega\), \(\omega_3=s\), nonvertical $\theta$ obeys $$I\Omega^2\cos\theta-I_3s\Omega+Mg\ell=0.$$ The perpendicular angular momentum is \(L_\perp=(I_3s-I\Omega\cos\theta)\sin\theta\), so \(\Omega L_\perp=Mg\ell\sin\theta\) gives the same relation. For \(\cos\theta>0\), real roots require \((I_3s)^2\ge4IMg\ell\cos\theta\).

parts.title: 9.7.5 · When the familiar slow formula is valid
parts.body_md: For rapid spin on the slow branch, $$\Omega_{slow}\simeq\frac{Mg\ell}{I_3s},\qquad\Omega_{fast}\simeq\frac{I_3s}{I\cos\theta}.$$ The first approximation neglects the quadratic $\Omega$ term; it is not the general initial-value solution. At $\theta =\pi /2$ the equation is linear and \(\Omega=Mg\ell/(I_3s)\) is exact when $s\ne 0$. Exactly vertical motion needs separate treatment because cancellation of $\sin\theta$ is invalid.

parts.title: 9.7.6 · Why a sideways torque matters
parts.body_md: A fast top’s L is nearly along its axis. Gravity about the pivot acts sideways to that L, so a short interval adds \(d\mathbf L=\boldsymbol\tau\,dt\), turning its direction. Repeated sideways changes make the axis travel around vertical. The simple slow-precession picture assumes the top is already close to the steady motion; it does not explain arbitrary release by itself.

parts.title: 9.7.6 · Dumbbell intuition and its limit
parts.body_md: For an ideal two-mass dumbbell, an impulse can immediately change the instantaneous plane of the velocities. A disk has many points and a physical plane: its orientation cannot change instantaneously. The new $\omega$ and L generally do not align with its old symmetry axis, producing torque-free wobble between small external impulses. This is the local origin of nutation in the heavy top.

parts.title: 9.7.6 · Choose the torque origin honestly
parts.body_md: About the pivot, the support force has zero lever arm and gravity produces torque. About the CM, uniform gravity produces zero torque but the support force generally does. Both descriptions agree when the appropriate moments and translational motion are included. The top falls initially if released with no precession; a suitable sideways push can place it on the steady branch.

parts.title: 9.7.7 · Linearize around fast-spin slow precession
parts.body_md: When axial spin dominates precession and tilt changes are small, the coupled equations give nutation frequency $$\omega_n\simeq I_3s/I$$ and mean precession \(\Omega_s\simeq Mg\ell/(I_3s)\). A general small perturbation has \(\dot\phi=\Omega_s+A\cos(\omega_n t+\gamma)\), \(\dot\theta=-A\sin\theta_0\sin(\omega_n t+\gamma)\). These are approximations, not the full finite-amplitude top solution.

parts.title: 9.7.7 · Read the trace, not just its coordinates
parts.body_md: The angular $\theta$ amplitude is $\sin\theta_{0}$ times the oscillatory $\phi$ amplitude. Actual tip displacements use \(\ell\,d\theta\) and \(\ell\sin\theta_0\,d\phi\), so the small bobbing is circular in the tangent plane. A correctly launched top has no nutation; a top released with zero precession has a special cusp-like trace in this approximation. A larger push can create loops, but finite amplitudes require the full equations or effective potential.

examples.title: Spin plus precession at sixty degrees
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A top has fixed \(\theta=\pi/3\), precession rate $\Omega$, and material spin rate \(\dot\psi=s\) relative to the intermediate frame. Find $\omega$ components.

steps.why: Add the instantaneous angular velocities as vectors.
Resolve vertical into orthogonal principal directions.
Add only components along the same axis.

examples.answer_md: \(\omega_3\) is not merely s; precession adds $\Omega /2$ to it.
examples.check_md: At $\Omega =0$ the formula becomes pure axial spin; the orthogonal squared components give \(\omega^2=s^2+s\Omega+\Omega^2\).

examples.title: The two steady precession rates
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A symmetric top has \(\theta=\pi/3\), \(I_3s=3\sqrt{IMg\ell}\). Find its two constant-tilt precession rates.

steps.why: Insert the tilt and axial angular momentum into the steady-tilt equation.
Solve the quadratic, keeping both roots.

examples.answer_md: Both rates are positive. The minus sign is the slow branch; the plus sign is the fast branch.
examples.check_md: Their product is \(2Mg\ell/I\), which agrees with the constant coefficient divided by the quadratic coefficient.

examples.title: A small extra sideways push
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A fast top initially on slow precession at tilt $\theta _{0}$ receives a small change $\Delta \Omega$ to its precession, with no initial tilt velocity. Let \(\Omega_s=Mg\ell/(I_3s)\), \(\omega_n=I_3s/I\), and assume \(|\Delta\Omega|/\omega_n\ll1\). Find the first-order motion.

steps.why: The perturbation oscillates about slow precession.
Integrate while satisfying the initial azimuth.
The coupled tilt equation supplies the quadrature oscillation.
Integrate from the specified initial tilt.

examples.answer_md: An extra positive precession push makes $\theta$ initially decrease, so the axis initially rises; the motion then nutates.
examples.check_md: At $t=0, \theta =\theta _{0}, \dot\theta=0, \dot\phi=\Omega_s+\Delta\Omega$. The amplitudes are small by assumption, and the period is \(2\pi/|\omega_n|\).

practice.question_md: A rapidly spinning top is released tilted with zero precession. Is the slow-precession formula its exact motion immediately afterward?
hints: Its initial tilt acceleration is nonzero.
The slow formula assumes a matched steady launch.
practice.answer_md: No. Initially \(\ddot\theta=(Mg\ell/I)\sin\theta_0\), so it starts to fall and develops precession with nutation. The slow-precession rate describes an approximate mean for rapid spin, not the complete release transient.

examples.title: A pure change of tilt
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A symmetric top is held at fixed azimuth $\phi$ while its axis tilts at rate q; the body has no rotation relative to the line-of-nodes frame, so \(\dot\psi=0\). Find its angular velocity.

steps.why: State the three coordinate rates separately.
Only the line-of-nodes rotation remains.

examples.answer_md: The top rotates about the horizontal line of nodes at rate q.
examples.check_md: The direction is perpendicular to both vertical and the top axis, as required to change tilt without changing azimuth.

practice.question_md: If the top axis is horizontal, what value of $\theta$ is used here? Is $\theta =0$ downward or upward?
hints: A horizontal axis is perpendicular to vertical.
Keep this convention when writing potential energy.
practice.answer_md: Horizontal means \(\theta=\pi/2\); $\theta =0$ is upward. Thus \(V=Mg\ell\cos\theta\) is largest at the upward orientation for a CM distance $\ell$ above the pivot.

hints: Set the whole sum to zero.
The remaining $\omega$ is transverse, not zero.

examples.title: Release a tilted spinning top without precession
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. At an instant a fixed-pivot symmetric top has tilt \(0<\theta_0<\pi\), \(\dot\theta=\dot\phi=0\), axial spin s, and moments $I,I,I_{3}$. Find its initial tilt acceleration.

steps.why: Use the tilt equation at the release instant.
The two precession terms vanish initially.

examples.answer_md: The tilt initially increases: the axis starts falling, even if s is large.
examples.check_md: At a vertical orientation $\sin\theta$ vanishes. Spin changes the later coupled motion, but cannot cancel the initial gravitational tilt acceleration with zero precession.

practice.question_md: Which moment should a top with central transverse moment \(I_C\) and CM distance $\ell$ use in its pivot equations?
hints: The torque is taken about the fixed pivot.
The transverse axis is parallel to the central transverse axis.
practice.answer_md: \(I=I_C+M\ell^2\). The axial moment is unchanged when shifting along the symmetry axis. Using \(I_C\) alone would overestimate the initial tilt acceleration.

9.7.4.title: Lagrangian method
9.7.4.summary: The Lagrangian packages the same top dynamics into energy and two conserved angular momenta.

prerequisites.refresher_md: If \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial q=0\), the Euler–Lagrange equation says \(d(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\dot q)/dt=0\). A cyclic coordinate can still move.

parts.title: Energy in the Euler coordinates
parts.body_md: $$\mathcal L=\frac I2(\dot\theta^2+\dot\phi^2\sin^2\theta)+\frac{I_3}2(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta)^2-Mg\ell\cos\theta.$$ Potential energy increases with CM height. $\psi$ and $\phi$ are absent as coordinates, hence $$p_\psi=I_3\omega_3,\qquad p_\phi=I\dot\phi\sin^2\theta+I_3\omega_3\cos\theta=L_z$$ are conserved. Euler–Lagrange for $\theta$ reproduces the torque equation.

parts.body_md: Do not replace \(\dot\psi+\dot\phi\cos\theta\) by a constant before varying the original Lagrangian: it depends on $\theta$ and $\dot\phi$, so that shortcut discards real derivatives. After obtaining the conservation laws, substitute them into the energy to get $$E=\frac I2\dot\theta^2+\frac{(K-I_3s\cos\theta)^2}{2I\sin^2\theta}+\frac{I_3s^2}2+Mg\ell\cos\theta.$$ The $\theta$-dependent terms form an effective potential; its turning points bound nutation.

examples.title: Get precession from conserved vertical momentum
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A top has fixed axial spin s and conserved \(L_z=K\). Express precession as a function of its current tilt.

steps.why: Azimuth is cyclic, so its conjugate momentum is conserved.
Solve for precession at nonsingular tilts.

examples.answer_md: Changing tilt generally changes precession even without a vertical torque.
examples.check_md: At $\theta =\pi /2$ the result is $K/I$. Near a pole the Euler coordinates can be singular, so do not interpret a divergent coordinate rate alone as infinite physical speed.

practice.question_md: At an instant when $\theta =\pi /2$, write the conserved energy in terms of $\dot\theta, K$ and s.
hints: The gravity term is zero at the chosen reference height.
practice.answer_md: \(E=I\dot\theta^2/2+K^2/(2I)+I_3s^2/2\) at that instant. Every term has joule units; this value alone does not guarantee that $\theta$ will remain horizontal.

9.7.5.summary: A top keeps a constant tilt only when its initial precession matches a steady branch.

prerequisites.refresher_md: The first row tells you \(L_x=I_{xx}\omega_x+I_{xy}\omega_y+I_{xz}\omega_z\); the other rows work the same way. All components must use the same orthonormal axes. Changing axes changes the numbers, not the physical arrow.

parts.title: Balance a uniformly turning L
parts.body_md: For \(\dot\theta=0\), \(\dot\phi=\Omega\), \(\omega_3=s\), nonvertical $\theta$ obeys $$I\Omega^2\cos\theta-I_3s\Omega+Mg\ell=0.$$ The perpendicular angular momentum is \(L_\perp=(I_3s-I\Omega\cos\theta)\sin\theta\), so \(\Omega L_\perp=Mg\ell\sin\theta\) gives the same relation. For \(\cos\theta>0\), real roots require \((I_3s)^2\ge4IMg\ell\cos\theta\).

parts.title: When the familiar slow formula is valid
parts.body_md: For rapid spin on the slow branch, $$\Omega_{slow}\simeq\frac{Mg\ell}{I_3s},\qquad\Omega_{fast}\simeq\frac{I_3s}{I\cos\theta}.$$ The first approximation neglects the quadratic $\Omega$ term; it is not the general initial-value solution. At $\theta =\pi /2$ the equation is linear and \(\Omega=Mg\ell/(I_3s)\) is exact when $s\ne 0$. Exactly vertical motion needs separate treatment because cancellation of $\sin\theta$ is invalid.

examples.title: The two steady precession rates
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A symmetric top has \(\theta=\pi/3\), \(I_3s=3\sqrt{IMg\ell}\). Find its two constant-tilt precession rates.

steps.why: Insert the tilt and axial angular momentum into the steady-tilt equation.
Solve the quadratic, keeping both roots.

examples.answer_md: Both rates are positive. The minus sign is the slow branch; the plus sign is the fast branch.
examples.check_md: Their product is \(2Mg\ell/I\), which agrees with the constant coefficient divided by the quadratic coefficient.

practice.question_md: At $\theta =\pi /3$, what minimum positive axial angular momentum permits steady precession?
practice.answer_md: \(I_3s\ge\sqrt{2IMg\ell}\). At equality the two roots merge. This is an existence condition for that steady tilt, not a guarantee for arbitrary release conditions.

visual.description: The existing heavy-top scene lets you compare steady precession with nutating initial conditions.

9.7.6.title: An “explanation” of precession
9.7.6.summary: Precession is a continuous change of angular momentum; the top’s shape cannot jump to follow it instantly.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

parts.title: Why a sideways torque matters
parts.body_md: A fast top’s L is nearly along its axis. Gravity about the pivot acts sideways to that L, so a short interval adds \(d\mathbf L=\boldsymbol\tau\,dt\), turning its direction. Repeated sideways changes make the axis travel around vertical. The simple slow-precession picture assumes the top is already close to the steady motion; it does not explain arbitrary release by itself.

parts.title: Dumbbell intuition and its limit
parts.body_md: For an ideal two-mass dumbbell, an impulse can immediately change the instantaneous plane of the velocities. A disk has many points and a physical plane: its orientation cannot change instantaneously. The new $\omega$ and L generally do not align with its old symmetry axis, producing torque-free wobble between small external impulses. This is the local origin of nutation in the heavy top.

parts.title: Choose the torque origin honestly
parts.body_md: About the pivot, the support force has zero lever arm and gravity produces torque. About the CM, uniform gravity produces zero torque but the support force generally does. Both descriptions agree when the appropriate moments and translational motion are included. The top falls initially if released with no precession; a suitable sideways push can place it on the steady branch.

examples.title: An impulse tips L without moving the top instantly
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A fast top initially has angular momentum \(L_0\hat z\). A brief torque impulse adds \(J_L\hat x\), with \(J_L\ll L_0\). Find the immediate direction change of L.

steps.why: Integrate the torque through the short impulse.
Take the ratio of perpendicular to original components.
Use the small-angle approximation.

examples.answer_md: L tilts immediately by approximately \(J_L/L_0\), while the physical top orientation is continuous.
examples.check_md: An angular impulse has the same $\mathrm{kg} m^{2}/s$ units as L. An instantaneous jump of body position would require unbounded point velocity, which this finite impulse does not produce.

practice.question_md: If the transverse angular impulse is reversed, what happens to the immediate L tilt? Does the body instantly tilt too?
hints: Change the sign of $J_{L}$ in the vector sum.
The tilt angle changes sign to first order.
Velocity may change discontinuously; position remains continuous.
practice.answer_md: L tilts in the opposite direction by approximately \(|J_L|/L_0\). The body orientation does not jump. This distinction is why precession and nutation must be obtained from motion, not a sequence of discontinuous body tilts.

9.7.7.title: Nutation
9.7.7.summary: Nutation is the axis bobbing around its average precession, and its amplitude records how the motion was started.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An equation \(\ddot q+\omega_n^2q=0\) gives sine/cosine motion at angular frequency $\omega$ₙ. The coefficient of cosine depends on initial displacement; sine depends on initial velocity.

parts.title: Linearize around fast-spin slow precession
parts.body_md: When axial spin dominates precession and tilt changes are small, the coupled equations give nutation frequency $$\omega_n\simeq I_3s/I$$ and mean precession \(\Omega_s\simeq Mg\ell/(I_3s)\). A general small perturbation has \(\dot\phi=\Omega_s+A\cos(\omega_n t+\gamma)\), \(\dot\theta=-A\sin\theta_0\sin(\omega_n t+\gamma)\). These are approximations, not the full finite-amplitude top solution.

parts.title: Read the trace, not just its coordinates
parts.body_md: The angular $\theta$ amplitude is $\sin\theta_{0}$ times the oscillatory $\phi$ amplitude. Actual tip displacements use \(\ell\,d\theta\) and \(\ell\sin\theta_0\,d\phi\), so the small bobbing is circular in the tangent plane. A correctly launched top has no nutation; a top released with zero precession has a special cusp-like trace in this approximation. A larger push can create loops, but finite amplitudes require the full equations or effective potential.

examples.title: A small extra sideways push
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A fast top initially on slow precession at tilt $\theta _{0}$ receives a small change $\Delta \Omega$ to its precession, with no initial tilt velocity. Let \(\Omega_s=Mg\ell/(I_3s)\), \(\omega_n=I_3s/I\), and assume \(|\Delta\Omega|/\omega_n\ll1\). Find the first-order motion.

steps.why: The perturbation oscillates about slow precession.
Integrate while satisfying the initial azimuth.
The coupled tilt equation supplies the quadrature oscillation.
Integrate from the specified initial tilt.

examples.answer_md: An extra positive precession push makes $\theta$ initially decrease, so the axis initially rises; the motion then nutates.
examples.check_md: At $t=0, \theta =\theta _{0}, \dot\theta=0, \dot\phi=\Omega_s+\Delta\Omega$. The amplitudes are small by assumption, and the period is \(2\pi/|\omega_n|\).

practice.question_md: In the small-kick example, what is the largest change of tilt from its initial value for $\Delta \Omega >0$ and $s>0$?
hints: This is twice the oscillation amplitude about the shifted mean.
practice.answer_md: The maximum rise is a decrease \(2\Delta\Omega\sin\theta_0/\omega_n\) in $\theta$. The mean shifts by half that amount. The result is valid only while that change remains small.

10.1.title: Relating the coordinates
10.1.summary: Changing coordinates changes measured velocities and accelerations because the axes themselves move.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

parts.title: Position and one derivative
parts.body_md: Let the moving origin have lab position R(t), and let its axes rotate at $\Omega (t)$. For a particle \(\mathbf r_{lab}=\mathbf R+\mathbf r\). For any vector A, $$D_{lab}\mathbf A=D_{rel}\mathbf A+\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf A.$$ Therefore \(\mathbf v_{lab}=\dot{\mathbf R}+\mathbf v_{rel}+\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r\). Components must all be expressed in one basis before adding.

parts.title: The second derivative
parts.body_md: Apply the same rule to both the relative velocity and the rotating-position term: $$\mathbf a_{lab}=\ddot{\mathbf R}+\mathbf a_{rel}+2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v_{rel}+\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)+\dot{\boldsymbol\Omega}\times\mathbf r.$$ The origin term comes from translation; the double cross product from rotation; the factor two from two product-rule contributions; the last term from changing rotation rate or direction. R and r are in metres, velocities $m/s, \Omega s^{-1}$, and every displayed term has $m/s^{2}$ units.

examples.title: A bead fixed on a rotating disk
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A bead is fixed at rotating coordinates \(r=a\hat x\). The disk rotates steadily at \(\Omega\hat z\) about a stationary origin. Find its laboratory velocity and acceleration.

steps.why: Its coordinates on the disk are constant.
Its basis vectors still turn in the laboratory.
Differentiate again to obtain the inward acceleration.

examples.answer_md: The bead is at rest in the rotating coordinates but accelerates inward in the lab.
examples.check_md: The acceleration magnitude $\Omega ^{2}a$ equals $v^{2}/a$; fixed rotating coordinates do not imply zero lab acceleration.

examples.title: A bead slides outward along a spinning radial slot
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A slot rotates at constant \(\Omega\hat z\). At an instant the bead has \(r=a\hat x\), relative velocity \(u\hat x\), and relative acceleration zero. Find its lab acceleration.

steps.why: The origin is fixed and $\Omega$ is constant.
Evaluate the tangential cross term and inward double cross product.

examples.answer_md: \(-\Omega^2a\hat x+2\Omega u\hat y\).
examples.check_md: The tangential term has two equal contributions: radial motion changes rotational speed, and the radial velocity direction itself turns.

practice.question_md: A particle is fixed at \(a\hat x\) on a disk whose angular speed is $\Omega$ and angular acceleration \(\alpha\hat z\). What acceleration does the lab see?
hints: The relative velocity and acceleration vanish.
The double cross product is inward.
practice.answer_md: \(\mathbf a_{lab}=-\Omega^2a\hat x+\alpha a\hat y\). At $\Omega =0$ only the tangential start-up acceleration remains.

visual.description: Use the supplied Morin source on printed pages 458–460 for the axes and geometry. No new simulation is claimed.

10.2.title: The fictitious forces
10.2.summary: Choose one frame, then add only the inertial-force terms that its motion and the particle’s motion require.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

An arrow painted on a body has \(d\mathbf A/dt=\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A\). If its components also change relative to that body, add that component derivative. A vector can have constant length while its direction changes.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Picture an accelerating train, a steady carousel, a moving walker, and a speeding-up carousel. These isolate translation, centrifugal, Coriolis and azimuthal terms before combining them.

parts.title: The complete rotating-frame force equation
parts.body_md: Let A be the origin’s inertial acceleration, $\Omega$ the frame angular velocity, and r,v,a the particle’s position, velocity and acceleration measured within the moving frame. Then $$m\mathbf a=\mathbf F_{real}-m\mathbf A-m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v-m\dot{\boldsymbol\Omega}\times\mathbf r.$$ A and $\Omega$ describe the frame; r and v describe this particle inside it. Put every vector in one common basis. Real forces still come from interactions such as contact, tension and gravity. The added terms reorganize the coordinate acceleration and do not need new interacting objects.

parts.title: 10.2.1 · The train-floor picture
parts.body_md: If the frame origin accelerates at \(\mathbf A=\ddot{\mathbf R}\), use $$m\mathbf a_{rel}=\mathbf F_{real}-m\mathbf A.$$ The term \(-m\mathbf A\) points opposite the frame acceleration and has newton units. A loose object does not need a new physical agent pulling it backward; the floor accelerates relative to it. The term is spatially uniform for a nonrotating frame.

parts.title: 10.2.1 · Effective gravity and weight
parts.body_md: In gravity, \(\mathbf g_{eff}=\mathbf g-\mathbf A\). A scale measures the contact force needed to keep you with the frame. Upward elevator acceleration increases that force; downward acceleration decreases it. In free fall, \(\mathbf A=\mathbf g\), a small freely falling lab has no uniform apparent gravity. Differences in gravity across its size can still remain.

parts.title: 10.2.2 · Away from the axis, not necessarily the origin
parts.body_md: $$\mathbf F_{cent}=-m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)=m\Omega^2\mathbf r_\perp.$$ The perpendicular displacement is measured from the rotation axis. An object stationary in the rotating frame has zero Coriolis force. Its real inward force balances centrifugal force there; in the lab only the real force supplies its inward acceleration. Do not include centrifugal force and lab centripetal acceleration in the same equation.

parts.title: 10.2.2 · Effective gravity on a rotating planet
parts.body_md: Ignoring oblateness for a first model, \(\mathbf g_{eff}=\mathbf g+\Omega^2\mathbf r_\perp\). At the equator its magnitude is \(g-\Omega^2R\); at the poles the rotational correction vanishes. At latitude $\lambda$, the outward radial component is \(\Omega^2R\cos^2\lambda\), with an additional equatorward component. Plumb lines follow effective gravity, not exactly the radius. Real planetary shape and mass distribution also change gravity; do not attribute every latitude difference to rotation alone.

parts.title: 10.2.3 · Use relative velocity and a signed cross product
parts.body_md: $$\mathbf F_{cor}=-2m\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v_{rel}.$$ It is perpendicular to relative velocity, so \(\mathbf F_{cor}\cdot\mathbf v_{rel}=0\). It vanishes for motion parallel to the axis or rest in the rotating frame. On a counterclockwise platform it pushes horizontal motion to its right. A person walking tangentially with the rotation requires extra inward real force: expanding \(m(\Omega r+u)^2/r\) separates the centrifugal, Coriolis, and relative circular-motion pieces.

parts.title: 10.2.3 · Earth: fall and Foucault motion
parts.body_md: Use local east, north, up axes. At latitude $\lambda$, \(\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega\cos\lambda\hat n+\Omega\sin\lambda\hat z\). Downward motion therefore deflects east. For a long, small-amplitude Foucault pendulum, only the vertical $\Omega$ component drives leading horizontal plane precession: $$\Omega_F=-\Omega\sin\lambda$$ with counterclockwise positive when viewed from above. The plane rotates clockwise in the north, counterclockwise in the south, with period \(2\pi/(\Omega|\sin\lambda|)\). It does not precess at the equator in this approximation; its lab plane is nearly fixed at a pole.

parts.title: 10.2.4 · The Euler or azimuthal term
parts.body_md: $$\mathbf F_{az}=-m\dot{\boldsymbol\Omega}\times\mathbf r.$$ For a fixed rotation-axis direction it is tangential and opposes the frame’s angular acceleration. The general vector formula also applies when the axis direction changes. Units are $\mathrm{kg}\cdot s^{-2}\cdot m = N$. Unlike Coriolis force it does not require relative velocity; unlike centrifugal force it requires $\Omega$ to change.

parts.title: 10.2.4 · An ice skater’s two tangential terms
parts.body_md: Model the hands as masses at radius r, moving inward at speed $u=-\dot r$, with no external axial torque. In the skater’s frame the hands stay on fixed radial lines, so Coriolis and azimuthal tangential forces cancel: $$2m\Omega u=mr\dot\Omega.$$ Thus \(\dot\Omega=-2\Omega\dot r/r\), which integrates to \(r^2\Omega=constant\). This is the same result as lab angular-momentum conservation. Pulling inward generally increases kinetic energy; muscular work supplies it.

examples.title: A plumb line in an accelerating carriage
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A carriage accelerates horizontally at \(A\hat x\). A mass hangs motionless relative to it on a light string. Find the string tilt and tension.

steps.why: The carriage frame adds the translational inertial acceleration opposite its own acceleration.
Tension balances both components for zero carriage-frame acceleration.
Resolve tension along the string, with $\theta$ measured backward from downward vertical for the bob.

examples.answer_md: The bob hangs backward by \(\arctan(A/g)\); tension is \(m\sqrt{g^2+A^2}\).
examples.check_md: At $A=0$ the string is vertical and $T=mg$. The lab sees the same tension providing horizontal acceleration A.

examples.title: How far out can a rider stand?
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A horizontal carousel rotates steadily at $\Omega$. A rider is at rest on it with coefficient of static friction $\mu$. Find the largest radius that does not require slipping.

steps.why: In the rotating frame, inward friction balances outward centrifugal force.
Vertical forces balance; static friction has a maximum, not a fixed value.
Combine the force requirement with the friction limit.

examples.answer_md: \(r_{max}=\mu g/\Omega^2\).
examples.check_md: The lab description gives the same inward friction from centripetal acceleration. Doubling $\Omega$ quarters the permitted radius.

examples.title: A dropped ball’s eastward drift
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. At latitude $\lambda$, release a ball from height h at rest relative to the ground. Use constant effective g, ignore drag and curvature, and retain first order in Earth’s rotation $\Omega$.

steps.why: Use the zeroth-order vertical fall for the small correction.
Evaluate $-2\Omega \times v$ using the horizontal northward component $\Omega \cos \lambda$.
Integrate from zero eastward speed.
Integrate once more from the release point.
Insert the unperturbed landing time.

examples.answer_md: The leading deflection is eastward in either hemisphere.
examples.check_md: It vanishes at the poles and scales as $h^{3/2}$. Corrections from the acquired horizontal speed enter at higher order in $\Omega$.

practice.question_md: A bead is fixed on a steadily rotating platform whose center also accelerates at A. Which inertial forces remain?
hints: Origin acceleration and rotation still remain.
practice.answer_md: Translation \(-m\mathbf A\) and centrifugal \(-m\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)\) remain; Coriolis and azimuthal terms vanish. Real forces must balance the remaining terms for the bead to stay fixed.

10.2.1.summary: A translating accelerating frame adds the same inertial acceleration to every free mass.

practice.answer_md: \(N=m(g-a)\). At $a=g$ the reading becomes zero. For faster downward motion with $a>g,$ a person cannot remain on the floor without an additional restraint.

steps.math: \mathbf F_{cor}=-2m\Omega\hat z\times u\hat x=-2m\Omega u\hat y
steps.why: The right-hand rule followed by the minus sign gives the backward tangential force.
Staying on the radial line requires zero tangential relative acceleration.
The lab torque changes the angular momentum consistently.

examples.answer_md: The Coriolis force is backward tangential; real contact force must act forward tangential.
examples.check_md: Reversing radial velocity reverses both signs; standing still removes this force.

examples.title: A dropped ball’s eastward drift

practice.question_md: At latitude 30° north, what is the ideal Foucault plane’s precession period in units of the planet’s rotation period?

10.2.4.summary: Changing a frame’s angular velocity creates an azimuthal inertial force even on an object at rest in that frame.

examples.title: A platform starts speeding up
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A mass is held fixed at \(r\hat x\) on a disk with angular acceleration \(\alpha\hat z\). Find the tangential force needed.

steps.math: \mathbf F_{az}=-m\alpha\hat z\times r\hat x=-m\alpha r\hat y
steps.why: Changing frame rotation produces a backward azimuthal inertial force.
Real friction must cancel it for zero relative acceleration.

examples.answer_md: The required real tangential force is \(m\alpha r\).
examples.check_md: The lab torque $rF=mr^{2}\alpha$ matches the time derivative of angular momentum at fixed radius.

practice.question_md: In the ideal skater model, the radius halves. By what factors do $\Omega$ and rotational energy change?
hints: Substitute both changes rather than assuming energy conservation.
practice.answer_md: $\Omega$ becomes four times larger and T becomes four times larger. The positive energy change comes from the inward work against the centrifugal tendency.

10.3.title: Tides
10.3.summary: Tides measure differences in gravity across a body after its common free-fall acceleration is removed.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For small \(\epsilon\), \((1+\epsilon)^n\simeq1+n\epsilon\). Keep terms linear in the declared small parameter and state what you dropped. An approximation is useful only in its stated limit.

For perpendicular vectors, the magnitude is \(AB\); in general it is \(AB\sin\theta\). Curl the right hand from the first vector toward the second. In an \(x,y\) drawing, \(\hat x\times\hat y=\hat z\), out of the page. Reversing the order changes the sign.

parts.title: Stretch along the source line, squeeze across it
parts.body_md: In a freely falling, nonrotating frame, the leading relative acceleration near a source M at distance R is $$\mathbf a_{tidal}=\frac{GM}{R^3}\left[3\hat n(\hat n\cdot\mathbf r)-\mathbf r\right].$$ Here \(\hat n\) lies along the source line, r is displacement from the reference origin, and \(|r|\ll R\). With x along that line, the components are \(GM(2x,-y,-z)/R^3\). The longitudinal factor two comes from changing inverse-square strength; transverse compression comes from converging force directions.

parts.title: Potential and two bulges
parts.body_md: The tidal potential per unit mass is $$\Phi_{tidal}=\frac{GM}{2R^3}(r^2-3(\hat n\cdot\mathbf r)^2).$$ Its negative gradient gives the acceleration. Water can redistribute toward the two source-line directions; the far-side bulge results because the solid Earth accelerates toward the source more than that far-side water. A simple equilibrium picture gives two main bulges, while real coastlines, ocean dynamics, source inclination and lag alter actual tides.

parts.title: Compare sources with M/R³, not M/R²
parts.body_md: The Sun’s ordinary pull on Earth is stronger than the Moon’s, but its tidal coefficient is smaller because tides involve another inverse distance. Aligned solar and lunar contributions reinforce (spring tides); perpendicular configurations partly offset (neap tides). For a spherical source of density $\rho$ and small apparent angular radius $\alpha$, \(M/R^3\propto\rho\alpha^3\), explaining why apparent size and density can help compare tidal strength.

parts.title: Separate orbit translation from Earth’s spin
parts.body_md: A frame translating with Earth but not rotating removes the nearly uniform orbital acceleration without adding a position-dependent orbital centrifugal term. Earth’s own rotation contributes its persistent equatorial bulge. That axisymmetric effect differs from the changing tidal pattern relative to the ground. Tidal gradients cannot be removed throughout a finite region merely by choosing free fall.

examples.title: Two freely falling masses separated radially
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A source M lies distance R from a reference falling mass. A test mass is x closer to the source, with $|x|\ll R$. Find its relative acceleration.

steps.why: Subtract the reference mass’s acceleration; both individual attractions point toward the source.
Expand to first order in separation.
The uniform attraction cancels, leaving a stretching term.

examples.answer_md: Positive x accelerates farther forward; negative x accelerates farther backward relative to the reference.
examples.check_md: It vanishes with separation and has acceleration units. The source attracts both masses; the far-side relative outward motion is not repulsive gravity.

examples.title: A diagonal separation in a tidal field
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A source lies along x. Two nearby freely falling particles have separation \(\boldsymbol\delta=d\hat x+d\hat y\), small compared with source distance R. Find their relative acceleration and instantaneous separation-length acceleration when initially comoving.

steps.why: The radial direction stretches while the transverse direction compresses.
Normalize the initial separation vector.
At zero relative velocity, the second derivative of separation length is this projection.

examples.answer_md: The separation initially grows at second derivative \(GMd/(\sqrt2R^3)\), while its direction also changes.
examples.check_md: A purely transverse separation gives a negative length acceleration; a purely radial one gives twice the coefficient with a positive sign.

practice.question_md: A second source has eight times the mass and twice the distance of the first. Compare their tidal coefficients and ordinary gravitational accelerations.
practice.answer_md: The tidal coefficients are equal: $8/2^{3}=1$. The second ordinary acceleration is twice as large: $8/2^{2}=2$. This checks why a stronger pull need not mean a stronger tide.

11.1.title: Motivation
11.1.summary: Relativity begins with a conflict between successful mechanics, electromagnetic waves and experiments seeking a preferred medium.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.
For small \(\epsilon\), \((1+\epsilon)^n\simeq1+n\epsilon\). Keep terms linear in the declared small parameter and state what you dropped. An approximation is useful only in its stated limit.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: First see exactly what ordinary velocity addition predicts for light. Then use the perpendicular-arm experiment to test the preferred-medium version of that prediction.

parts.title: 11.1.1 · Why Galilean transformations looked inevitable
parts.body_md: With $S^{\prime}$ moving at +v relative to S, Galilean coordinates use \(x=x'+vt'\), \(t=t'\), and unchanged transverse coordinates. Constant velocity differences cancel on taking two time derivatives, so Newtonian acceleration is unchanged. These transformations work extremely well for ordinary speeds and distances.

parts.title: 11.1.1 · The electromagnetic mismatch
parts.body_md: Maxwell’s vacuum equations imply a wave speed \(c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}\). Applying Galilean transformations to those equations does not preserve their form. A proposed ether supplied a preferred rest frame for that speed, like air for sound. Special relativity instead preserves equivalent inertial laws and replaces absolute time. The new rules must reduce to ordinary kinematics where their corrections are negligible.

parts.title: 11.1.2 · Split, reflect, recombine
parts.body_md: A beam splitter sends coherent light down perpendicular arms. Returning waves interfere; a change in relative travel time shifts the interference fringes. The naive ether picture predicts different round-trip times parallel and transverse to the supposed wind. Rotating the apparatus swaps those roles, doubling the equal-arm change.

parts.title: 11.1.2 · What was tested and what follows
parts.body_md: For equal arms L and wavelength $\lambda$, the predicted rotation fringe shift at small $v/c$ is $$\Delta N\simeq\frac{2Lv^2}{\lambda c^2}.$$ The null result challenges the naive ether plus Galilean model. Unequal fixed arm lengths do not invalidate the method because the measurement is a change under rotation, not an absolute path equality. For lengths $L_{1},L_{2}$ replace 2L by $L_{1}+L_{2}$. Ether dragging proposals also confronted stellar aberration: the telescope direction depends on Earth’s velocity. A single null experiment alone is not a logical derivation of every relativity postulate; the theory unifies the evidence.

examples.title: The ordinary train transformation
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A cart moves at v relative to the ground. Two flashes in its coordinates are separated by distance d and time T. Apply Galilean coordinates and ask what they would predict for a right-moving light pulse.

steps.why: Galilean kinematics shares one time and carries the cart displacement along.
Divide displacement by the shared time.
If this rule were applied to light, different inertial frames would measure different light speeds.

examples.answer_md: The prediction c+v conflicts with an invariant vacuum light speed.
examples.check_md: For a slow thrown ball this addition is an accurate approximation; the conflict concerns treating it as exact for all velocities.

examples.title: The predicted round-trip asymmetry
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. In a hypothetical stationary wave medium, two equal arms of length L move at speed v: one parallel and one perpendicular to motion. Assume Galilean lengths and wave speed c in the medium. Find the leading travel-time difference.

steps.why: The forward mirror recedes and the return mirror approaches.
The wave must have horizontal component v to reach the moving transverse mirror.
Expand both expressions through second order in $v/c$.

examples.answer_md: The naive ether model predicts an orientation-dependent round-trip delay \(Lv^2/c^3\).
examples.check_md: It vanishes at $v=0$ and is second order, which explains why a sensitive interference comparison is useful.

practice.question_md: Why did a null interference shift not mean the apparatus detected no light or no interference?
hints: The measurement was the change on rotation.
A fixed interference pattern can still be present.
The expected orientation-dependent difference was absent.
practice.answer_md: Light and interference remained; the predicted rotation-dependent shift was absent. The experimental statement concerns travel-time anisotropy, not absence of a wave.

11.1.2.summary: Michelson–Morley compared light travel times by interference and found no predicted ether-wind rotation signal.
