11.2.title: The postulates
11.2.summary: All inertial frames share the same physical laws and the same vacuum light speed.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

parts.title: Two separate assumptions
parts.body_md: The relativity principle says no inertial frame is preferred: the same laws describe experiments in each. The light postulate says every inertial observer measures the same vacuum light speed c, independent of source motion. Equivalence of frames alone does not force a baseball or sound pulse to have invariant speed; the second assumption adds real physical information.

parts.title: What observers actually measure
parts.body_md: A frame can be represented by a grid of rulers and locally synchronized clocks. Each event receives a coordinate without relying on when a distant eye sees it. Synchronization can use equal-distance light signals. The postulates apply to vacuum light; a material medium can define a rest frame for waves in it. Accelerating frames require more care, but acceleration does not prevent using momentarily comoving inertial frames locally.

parts.title: Avoid a common overstatement
parts.body_md: Invariant light speed limits local material velocities and causal signals, not every rate formed from coordinate distances. Same-frame closing speeds can exceed c. Relativity permits masses in flat spacetime; what special relativity omits is gravitational spacetime curvature, not matter itself.

examples.title: A flash catches a moving receiver
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. In the ground frame a receiver starts distance L ahead and moves at $v<c$. A light flash emitted at $x=0$ at $t=0$ travels toward it. Find the meeting time without changing frames.

steps.why: Both positions use the ground frame and the same coordinate time.
A meeting is one event with equal positions.
Solve the same-frame closing-gap equation.

examples.answer_md: The ground meeting time is $L/(c-v)$.
examples.check_md: This does not say the receiver measures light speed c−v. A changing gap between two ground-frame positions is different from transforming into the receiver’s frame.

examples.title: Two opposite flashes separate
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two light pulses leave the same event in opposite directions in an inertial frame. Find the rate at which their separation grows in that frame.

steps.why: Each pulse individually moves at c.
The separation compares two positions at the same frame time.
Differentiate that separation.

examples.answer_md: The gap grows at 2c in this frame without any object moving at 2c.
examples.check_md: Neither pulse has a rest frame, so this is not the speed measured by a photon observer.

practice.question_md: A moving lamp sends vacuum light forward. Does a ground observer add the lamp’s speed to c?
hints: The source motion does not change light’s local speed.
Frequency and direction can still change between frames.
practice.answer_md: No. The ground measures speed c. Source motion can alter observed frequency and propagation angle, which are separate quantities.

11.3.title: The fundamental effects
11.3.summary: The three effects are different event comparisons: separated simultaneous events, repeated ticks on one clock, and simultaneous endpoints.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Write the two events first. Ask whether they share a location, share a time, or mark opposite ends of a stationary object. That decision tells you which simple effect applies.

parts.title: 11.3.1 · The moving-receiver picture
parts.body_md: A source midway between two train receivers emits opposite flashes. In the train they arrive together. In the ground, light still moves at c while the rear receiver approaches its pulse and the front receiver retreats. Their meeting events therefore happen at different ground times. This is a statement about events after correcting signal travel to an observer.

parts.title: 11.3.1 · Rear clock ahead
parts.body_md: If the train’s own synchronized clocks have proper separation L, at a single ground time the rear clock reads \(vL/c^2\) ahead of the front. Both clocks tick at the same slow rate in the ground frame; one has a fixed offset. For events simultaneous in the train, the ground separation instead is \(\Delta t=\gamma v\Delta x'/c^2\). These formulas describe different choices of event pair; do not swap L and a contracted length casually.

parts.title: 11.3.2 · Derive it with a transverse light clock
parts.body_md: A light clock of mirror height h has rest round-trip interval \(T_0=2h/c\). When it moves horizontally at v, the light takes a diagonal path with vertical speed \(\sqrt{c^2-v^2}\), so $$T=2h/\sqrt{c^2-v^2}=\gamma T_0.$$ The two clock ticks occur at one place in the clock’s rest frame. That condition is essential.

parts.title: 11.3.2 · Reciprocity and its boundary
parts.body_md: Each inertial observer can measure the other’s moving clocks as slow because the comparisons use different simultaneity conventions and event pairs. The equations $T=\gamma T^{\prime}$ and $T^{\prime}=\gamma T$ are not both applicable to the same arbitrary event pair. For a variable-speed clock, \(d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-v(t)^2/c^2}\); integrate along its path.

parts.title: 11.3.2 · Lifetime and twins
parts.body_md: A particle with proper lifetime $\tau _{0}$ travels lab distance \(v\gamma\tau_0\) before that specified decay time; real decay lifetimes are statistical. In an out-and-back twin trip, the traveler changes inertial frames, so the reciprocal one-frame argument cannot be used throughout. Reunion compares accumulated proper times at the same event, removing synchronization ambiguity.

parts.title: 11.3.3 · Why simultaneity changes the answer
parts.body_md: Proper length $L_{0}$ is the object’s rest-frame length. For motion parallel to it, $$L=L_0/\gamma.$$ Transverse dimensions do not contract. The two endpoint events used in the moving-frame measurement are not simultaneous in the rest frame, but the rest endpoints stay fixed, so their spatial separation still gives $L_{0}$. Reversing which object is at rest changes the event pair and removes the apparent reciprocal contradiction.

parts.title: 11.3.3 · Measurements, passing times and clock grids
parts.body_md: If a contracted rod passes one fixed lab marker, its lab passage time is $L/v$. If two trains pass, use each length and their closing-gap speed in one chosen frame; only use relativistic velocity addition when changing the measuring frame. A lattice of synchronized clocks makes these distinctions operational: measure positions at equal readings in that frame. Optical photographs require separate light propagation.

parts.title: 11.3.3 · The particle’s view of a long journey
parts.body_md: A fast short-lived particle sees the source–destination separation contracted. The lab sees its clock dilated. Neither explanation is more physical; they assign different lengths and times to the same events. Keep the particle speed, distance and lifetime in one frame in each equation.

examples.title: Simultaneous train flashes are not simultaneous on the ground
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A train moves at $v=3c/5$. In the train, a rear and front flash occur simultaneously, separated by proper distance L. Find the ground time difference, front minus rear.

steps.why: Identify the pair of events and their easy frame.
Use the time transformation for a train moving in +x.
The front flash occurs later in the ground frame.

examples.answer_md: The ground event-time difference is \(3L/(4c)\).
examples.check_md: This is a coordinate-time difference, not an extra light-travel delay to a camera. At $L=0$ the difference vanishes.

examples.title: A moving clock between two ticks
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A clock moves uniformly at $4c/5$ and ticks with proper interval $T_{0}$. Find the time and distance between ticks in the lab.

steps.why: Evaluate the dimensionless dilation factor.
Both ticks occur at the same place in the clock’s rest frame.
The clock travels between the ticks in the lab.

examples.answer_md: The lab interval is \(5T_0/3\), with displacement \(4cT_0/3\).
examples.check_md: \(c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2=c^2T_0^2\), a direct invariant check.

examples.title: A tilted rod in motion
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A rod has rest-frame endpoint differences \(L_0\cos\theta_0\) along x and \(L_0\sin\theta_0\) along y. It moves along x at speed v. Find its lab length and angle.

steps.why: Only the dimension parallel to motion contracts, using simultaneous lab endpoints.
Combine the lab components with the ordinary spatial Pythagorean theorem.
Divide the transverse endpoint separation by the parallel one.

examples.answer_md: The rod is shorter and more transverse in the lab unless it was already transverse.
examples.check_md: For $\theta _{0}=0, L=L_{0}/\gamma$; for $\theta _{0}=\pi /2, L=L_{0}$. These are coordinate lengths, not a photograph including unequal light-arrival times.

examples.title: Two unequal trains overtake in one ground frame
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A fast train has proper length 2L and ground speed $3c/5$. A slower train ahead has proper length $L$ and ground speed $5c/13$. Find the ground time from fast front passing slow rear to fast rear passing slow front.

steps.why: Contract each train using its own speed relative to the ground.
The fast train must gain the sum of the two ground lengths.
Both velocities use the same ground frame, so ordinary subtraction gives the closing-gap rate.
Divide the required relative displacement by the same-frame closing rate.
The second event occurs at the advancing slow front, not at the fast front.

examples.answer_md: The ground event differences are \((c\Delta t_G,\Delta x_G)=(82L/7,38L/7)\).
examples.check_md: The endpoint conditions matter: the fast front itself travels farther than the separation between the two defined events.

practice.question_md: Two events occur at different places and different times in both frames. Is simple time dilation automatically valid?
hints: Time dilation requires a same-place frame for the clock events.
Check the event locations, not just the existence of a speed.
The full Lorentz transformation contains a spatial term.
practice.answer_md: No. Use \(\Delta t=\gamma(\Delta t'+v\Delta x'/c^2)\). Dropping the spatial term without a same-place condition loses relativity of simultaneity.

11.3.3.title: Length contraction
11.3.3.summary: A moving object’s length is measured from simultaneous endpoint positions in the measuring frame.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Why simultaneity changes the answer
parts.body_md: Proper length $L_{0}$ is the object’s rest-frame length. For motion parallel to it, $$L=L_0/\gamma.$$ Transverse dimensions do not contract. The two endpoint events used in the moving-frame measurement are not simultaneous in the rest frame, but the rest endpoints stay fixed, so their spatial separation still gives $L_{0}$. Reversing which object is at rest changes the event pair and removes the apparent reciprocal contradiction.

parts.title: Measurements, passing times and clock grids
parts.body_md: If a contracted rod passes one fixed lab marker, its lab passage time is $L/v$. If two trains pass, use each length and their closing-gap speed in one chosen frame; only use relativistic velocity addition when changing the measuring frame. A lattice of synchronized clocks makes these distinctions operational: measure positions at equal readings in that frame. Optical photographs require separate light propagation.

parts.title: The particle’s view of a long journey
parts.body_md: A fast short-lived particle sees the source–destination separation contracted. The lab sees its clock dilated. Neither explanation is more physical; they assign different lengths and times to the same events. Keep the particle speed, distance and lifetime in one frame in each equation.

examples.title: A tilted rod in motion
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A rod has rest-frame endpoint differences \(L_0\cos\theta_0\) along x and \(L_0\sin\theta_0\) along y. It moves along x at speed v. Find its lab length and angle.

steps.why: Only the dimension parallel to motion contracts, using simultaneous lab endpoints.
Combine the lab components with the ordinary spatial Pythagorean theorem.
Divide the transverse endpoint separation by the parallel one.

examples.answer_md: The rod is shorter and more transverse in the lab unless it was already transverse.
examples.check_md: For $\theta _{0}=0, L=L_{0}/\gamma$; for $\theta _{0}=\pi /2, L=L_{0}$. These are coordinate lengths, not a photograph including unequal light-arrival times.

examples.title: Two unequal trains overtake in one ground frame
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A fast train has proper length 2L and ground speed $3c/5$. A slower train ahead has proper length $L$ and ground speed $5c/13$. Find the ground time from fast front passing slow rear to fast rear passing slow front.

steps.why: Contract each train using its own speed relative to the ground.
The fast train must gain the sum of the two ground lengths.
Both velocities use the same ground frame, so ordinary subtraction gives the closing-gap rate.
Divide the required relative displacement by the same-frame closing rate.
The second event occurs at the advancing slow front, not at the fast front.

examples.answer_md: The ground event differences are \((c\Delta t_G,\Delta x_G)=(82L/7,38L/7)\).
examples.check_md: The endpoint conditions matter: the fast front itself travels farther than the separation between the two defined events.

practice.question_md: A rod of proper length $L_{0}$ moves at $4c/5$ past one fixed lab marker. How much lab time passes between its ends crossing the marker?
hints: The marker is fixed; use the rod’s lab speed.
practice.answer_md: \(\Delta t=(3L_0/5)/(4c/5)=3L_0/(4c)\). Both events occur at the marker, so this is also the marker clock’s proper time.

11.4.title: The Lorentz transformations
11.4.summary: Use one transformation with explicit event conditions instead of guessing which quantity gains a gamma factor.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Start with a message traveling between train ends, where simple clock dilation alone is invalid. Then recover length contraction by imposing simultaneous endpoint measurements.

parts.title: 11.4.1 · Derivation structure and sign convention
parts.body_md: Let $S^{\prime}$ move at +v along x relative to S, with parallel axes and coincident origins at $t=t^{\prime}=0$. Homogeneity and preservation of inertial straight motion motivate a linear transformation. Symmetry, clock dilation, length contraction and the simultaneity offset fix its coefficients: $$\Delta x=\gamma(\Delta x'+v\Delta t'),\qquad\Delta t=\gamma(\Delta t'+v\Delta x'/c^2).$$ Transverse differences are unchanged. The inverse replaces v by −v.

parts.title: 11.4.1 · A reliable application routine
parts.body_md: Name two events, choose their easy frame, write both differences, then substitute. To check the sign, set $\Delta x^{\prime}=0$: a fixed train point must move right in the ground. Transform differences unless a common origin event has been specified. Every x term has metres and every t term seconds. In the low-speed limit $\gamma \to 1$, but a very large spatial separation can still make \(v\Delta x'/c^2\) relevant.

parts.title: 11.4.1 · Composition
parts.body_md: Two collinear Lorentz transformations give another transformation of the same form, with the relativistic combined speed. This closure means intermediate coordinate choices cannot change the final event coordinates. Boosting back with −v must recover the starting differences.

parts.title: 11.4.2 · Three substitutions, three meanings
parts.body_md: For events simultaneous in $S^{\prime}, \Delta t^{\prime}=0$ gives \(\Delta t=\gamma v\Delta x'/c^2\). For two ticks at one position in $S^{\prime}, \Delta x^{\prime}=0$ gives \(\Delta t=\gamma\Delta t'\). For simultaneous S measurements of a rod at rest in $S^{\prime}, \Delta t=0$ gives \(\Delta x'=\gamma\Delta x\). The algebra is simple; identifying which difference vanishes is the real physical task.

parts.title: 11.4.2 · Do not suppress the conditions
parts.body_md: Reciprocal formulas do not contradict each other because changing the zero condition changes the events being compared. A pair of separated events generally needs both terms in each Lorentz equation. Keep the conditions next to equations while learning; it prevents applying a memorized $\gamma$ to the wrong quantity.

examples.title: Transform a timed message between train ends
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A train moves at $3c/5$. In the train, a message travels from rear to front over distance L at speed $c/2$. Find ground displacement and elapsed time.

steps.why: Define emission and reception in the easy frame.
Transform the displacement.
Transform time including the spatial term.

examples.answer_md: Ground displacement is $11L/4$ and time $13L/(4c)$.
examples.check_md: The resulting speed is $11c/13<c$, and the invariant interval is $3L^{2}$ in both frames.

examples.title: Recover contraction from the endpoint condition
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A rod is at rest in $S^{\prime}$ with length $L_{0}$. $S^{\prime}$ moves at v relative to S. Derive the length measured in S using the inverse transformation.

steps.why: A length measurement in S uses simultaneous endpoint events in S.
The simultaneity condition removes the velocity-time term.
The rod’s endpoints are stationary in $S^{\prime}$, so their spatial difference is always $L_{0}$.

examples.answer_md: Length contraction follows from the specific endpoint condition.
examples.check_md: Setting $\Delta t^{\prime}=0$ instead would describe a different event pair, not an S-frame length measurement.

practice.question_md: Why are event-coordinate differences safer than transforming a single coordinate without stating origins?
hints: The location of coordinate zero is arbitrary.
A translation adds offsets to single-event coordinates.
practice.answer_md: Differences remove arbitrary origin offsets. Single-event formulas are valid too when the origins and their zero-time coincidence are explicitly fixed.

The time term in the spatial equation does not.

11.5.title: Velocity addition
11.5.summary: Transform an object’s velocity by transforming both its displacement and its elapsed time.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Use the forward probe to see the speed bound, then the sideways photon to see why a direction can change as well.

parts.title: 11.5.1 · Divide the two Lorentz equations
parts.body_md: For a particle with speed $u^{\prime}$ in $S^{\prime}$ and $S^{\prime}$ moving at v relative to S, $$u=\frac{u'+v}{1+u'v/c^2},\qquad u'=\frac{u-v}{1-uv/c^2}.$$ All speeds are signed along one line. The factor $\gamma$ cancels because both displacement and elapsed time change. An input $u^{\prime}=c$ remains c; subluminal inputs produce a subluminal output.

parts.title: 11.5.1 · Choose the question before the formula
parts.body_md: If one lab sees two objects approach at speeds a and b, their lab separation closes at a+b. If you ask how fast one moves in the other’s rest frame, use \((a+b)/(1+ab/c^2)\). There is no massive observer at c. For passing trains, determine the contracted lengths and speeds in the chosen observer’s frame before computing a passage time.

parts.title: 11.5.2 · Transform time as well as displacement
parts.body_md: For an x-directed boost, $$u_x=\frac{u'_x+v}{1+vu'_x/c^2},\quad u_y=\frac{u'_y}{\gamma(1+vu'_x/c^2)},\quad u_z=\frac{u'_z}{\gamma(1+vu'_x/c^2)}.$$ The common denominator comes from the transformed time. For $u'_x=0$ the transverse components shrink by $\gamma$, but the particle also gains the lab x component v.

parts.title: 11.5.2 · Angle aberration
parts.body_md: Apply the component formulas to a photon with \(u'_x=c\cos\theta'\), \(u'_y=c\sin\theta'\). Then \(\cos\theta=(\cos\theta'+\beta)/(1+\beta\cos\theta')\). Direction changes while speed remains c. For a massive particle, do not use a photon’s c in the component definitions.

examples.title: Two stages each move at three-fifths c
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A ship moves at $3c/5$ relative to a station and launches a probe forward at $3c/5$ relative to itself. Find the probe’s station speed.

steps.why: Divide the transformed worldline displacement by transformed time.
Insert the two signed speeds.

examples.answer_md: The station speed is $15c/17$, less than c.
examples.check_md: Galilean addition would give $6c/5$. The denominator supplies the correction and tends to one for slow speeds.

examples.title: A sideways photon on a moving ship
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. In a ship moving at $v=3c/5$ along x, a photon is emitted purely along $+y^{\prime}$. Find its lab velocity components and direction.

steps.why: The emission is transverse in the ship frame.
Use the longitudinal and transverse transformations.
Check the invariant light speed and compute its lab angle.

examples.answer_md: The photon is diagonal in the lab, with components $(3c/5,4c/5)$.
examples.check_md: Transverse distance is unchanged, but elapsed coordinate time changes; therefore transverse velocity is not invariant.

examples.title: Recalculate the same overtake from the slow train
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Use the same unequal-train setup: fast proper length 2L at $3c/5$, slow proper length $L$ at $5c/13$ in the ground. Find the elapsed time in the slow train frame.

steps.why: Transform the fast train’s speed into the slow train frame.
Contract only the train moving in this new frame.
The slow train is now at rest with length $L$.
The first event is at its rear and the second at its front.

examples.answer_md: The slow-frame event differences are \((c\Delta t_S,\Delta x_S)=(73L/7,L)\).
examples.check_md: The interval is \((73L/7)^2-L^2=5280L^2/49\), equal to \((82L/7)^2-(38L/7)^2\) in the ground frame. Simple time dilation between these two frames would be invalid because the events are separated spatially in both.

practice.question_md: If a photon has speed c in one inertial frame, can a transverse boost make its total speed smaller than c?
hints: Transverse and longitudinal components change together.
The example’s components form a c-sized vector.
Lorentz transformations preserve a null worldline.
practice.answer_md: No. Its direction and frequency can change, but the transformed components still have magnitude c.

visual.description: Existing velocity-addition graph illustrates collinear speed composition; transverse calculations use the explicit component formulas.

11.6.title: The invariant interval
11.6.summary: The invariant interval classifies which event pairs can be joined by a clock, a light signal, or neither.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: The quantity every inertial frame agrees on
parts.body_md: With the +--- convention, $$s^2=c^2\Delta t^2-|\Delta\mathbf r|^2.$$ Substituting the Lorentz transformation cancels cross terms and leaves the same value. Coordinates change; this quadratic combination does not. Its units are metres squared and it may be negative.

parts.title: Three geometries
parts.body_md: For $s^{2}>0$ (timelike), there is a same-place frame and an inertial clock can connect the events; its proper interval is \(\sqrt{s^2}/c\). For $s^{2}<0$ (spacelike), a simultaneous frame exists and the proper spatial separation is \(\sqrt{-s^2}\). For $s^{2}=0$ (null), a light signal connects the events, but there is no light rest frame. A finite massive clock path always has positive elapsed proper time.

parts.title: Causality and paths
parts.body_md: Proper, time-oriented Lorentz transformations preserve the order of timelike or null-separated events. Spacelike ordering can reverse because no subluminal cause can connect them. For an accelerated clock, sum \(d\tau=\sqrt{dt^2-d\mathbf r^2/c^2}\) along its actual path; the endpoint interval alone gives the straight inertial path’s proper time, not every possible journey.

parts.title: Passing trains: check a result without redoing the collision geometry
parts.body_md: For the unequal-train worked example in 11.3.3 and 11.5.1, the ground event differences are \((c\Delta t,\Delta x)=(82L/7,38L/7)\), while the slow train assigns \((73L/7,L)\). Both give \(s^2=5280L^2/49\). An inertial clock passing through both events moves at \(19c/41\) relative to the ground and records \(\sqrt{5280}L/(7c)\). This is the same-place frame needed for a simple proper-time comparison.

examples.title: Find the clock that can visit both events
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two events have \(\Delta t=5T\), \(\Delta x=3cT\), with no transverse separation. Find the inertial clock that visits both and its elapsed time.

steps.why: Classify the event separation as timelike.
This frame makes both events occur at one location.
The same-place clock measures the proper time.

examples.answer_md: A clock moving at $3c/5$ can visit both and records 4T.
examples.check_md: Its $\gamma =5/4$ gives lab time $\gamma \cdot 4T=5T$.

examples.title: Find a frame where separated events are simultaneous
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two events have \(\Delta x=5cT\), \(\Delta t=3T\). Find the frame making them simultaneous and their proper spatial separation.

steps.why: The separation is spacelike.
Set the transformed time difference to zero.
The simultaneous-frame distance is the proper separation.

examples.answer_md: They are simultaneous in a frame moving at $3c/5$ and separated by 4cT there.
examples.check_md: No material signal can link these events because the required original-frame speed would be $5c/3$.

practice.question_md: For events with $\Delta x=2$ cT and $\Delta t=2T$, can a subluminal frame make them occur at one place?
hints: The required $v=\Delta x/\Delta t$ equals c.
A physical inertial frame must have $|v|<c$.
practice.answer_md: No. They are null-separated, and the required frame would move at c. Every inertial frame still assigns them a lightlike separation.

11.7.summary: A spacetime diagram makes worldlines and different definitions of simultaneity visible.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Draw light first
parts.body_md: Put x horizontally and ct vertically with equal units. Light rays have slopes $\pm 1$. A massive inertial object has a straight worldline inside the light cone; rest gives a vertical line. Accelerated motion is a curved worldline. For an $S^{\prime}$ frame moving at $\beta c$, its time axis obeys $x=\beta ct$ and its space axis $ct=\beta x$.

parts.title: Read coordinates with the correct grid
parts.body_md: The time axis is “here” for the moving observer; lines parallel to its space axis are that observer’s “now.” To read a coordinate, draw a line parallel to the other primed axis, not a perpendicular Euclidean projection. Calibrate unit marks by invariant hyperbolas: a time unit maps to $(ct,x)=(\gamma ,\gamma \beta ),$ a space unit to $(\gamma \beta ,\gamma )$. Their paper length is \(\sqrt{(1+\beta^2)/(1-\beta^2)}\), so an ordinary ruler on the page is not a proper-time ruler.

parts.title: Lengths are cuts across two worldlines
parts.body_md: The endpoints of a moving rod trace parallel worldlines. A lab-simultaneous cut and a primed-simultaneous cut select different pairs of events. That is the diagrammatic content of length contraction. The light cone also shows immediately why spacelike events can change time order but timelike causal events cannot.

examples.title: Draw a moving frame’s here and now axes
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. On an x-horizontal, ct-vertical diagram, $S^{\prime}$ moves at $3c/5$. Write the lines for its time and space axes and locate one unit mark on each.

steps.why: The time axis is the worldline of the moving origin.
The space axis joins events simultaneous at the moving origin’s zero time.
Transform one time unit, measured in the same length units.
Transform one space unit rather than copying paper lengths.

examples.answer_md: The two axes tilt toward the light line, and their unit marks are not at unit Euclidean paper distance.
examples.check_md: The time mark has invariant norm +1; the space mark has norm −1.

examples.title: Read the meeting of a flash and a ship
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A ship starts at $x=L$ when $t=0$ and moves at $c/2$. A flash starts from the origin then. Find the intersection on a Minkowski diagram.

steps.why: The ship worldline is timelike; the flash is a 45-degree null line.
The crossing is one physical meeting event.
Read the coordinates of that intersection.

examples.answer_md: The flash reaches the ship at $t=2L/c, x=2L$.
examples.check_md: The light path remains on $x=ct$. Drawing the ship as a vertical line would silently switch to another frame without transforming the flash.

practice.question_md: In a diagram for $v=3c/5$, is the line $ct=3x/5$ a possible massive object’s worldline?
hints: It is the primed space axis.
A line of simultaneous events is not a trajectory.
practice.answer_md: No. It represents a set of simultaneous $S^{\prime}$ events, not one object moving between them. Treating it as a path would demand superluminal speed.

visual.description: The existing Minkowski train visual supplies worldlines and frame-dependent simultaneity cuts.

11.8.title: The Doppler effect
11.8.summary: Observed frequency depends on both the source clock and the changing signal route.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Draw successive emission and arrival events. For a transverse question, label which frame makes the ray perpendicular and when “closest” is being evaluated.

parts.title: 11.8.1 · Emission time is not reception time
parts.body_md: For a source receding along the line of sight at $\beta c$, $$f_{recv}=\frac{f_0}{\gamma(1+\beta)}=f_0\sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}.$$ For approach reverse the sign of $\beta$. Time dilation slows emission in the receiver frame; increasing path length further separates arrivals. Unlike ordinary coordinate-time questions, Doppler questions explicitly ask when signals hit the receiver.

parts.title: 11.8.1 · Reciprocity and low-speed behavior
parts.body_md: The longitudinal vacuum result depends only on relative motion, not on which object is assigned a medium’s rest frame. Approaching source and approaching receiver give the same factor for the same relative speed. At small $\beta$, recession gives \(f\simeq f_0(1-\beta)\). In sound there is a material rest frame and moving-source/moving-receiver formulas differ.

parts.title: 11.8.2 · General angle formula
parts.body_md: Let $\theta$ be the angle in the receiver frame between the source velocity and the photon’s propagation direction toward that receiver. Then $$f_{recv}=\frac{f_0}{\gamma(1-\beta\cos\theta)}.$$ At $\theta =\pi /2$, the received frequency is $f_{0}/\gamma$. This is the light emitted when the source is at closest approach, received later.

parts.title: 11.8.2 · The other closest-approach question
parts.body_md: If the source is at closest approach at the instant of reception, the incoming photon was emitted earlier while the source approached. In the source rest frame that ray is transverse, giving \(f_{recv}=\gamma f_0\). Equivalently, a receiver circling a stationary source has the latter factor, while a source circling a central receiver has the former. State the geometry instead of relying on the phrase “transverse Doppler.” Ideal clock rates depend on instantaneous speed; signal-path geometry remains a separate step.

examples.title: A receding beacon
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A beacon emits flashes at proper frequency $f_{0}$ and recedes directly from a receiver at $3c/5$. Find the received frequency.

steps.why: The receiver-frame emission interval is time dilated.
The next flash has farther to travel because the source recedes.
Invert the arrival interval.

examples.answer_md: The received frequency is half the proper emission frequency.
examples.check_md: Approach at the same speed gives the reciprocal factor 2, and $\beta =0$ gives $f_{0}$.

examples.title: Two meanings of transverse
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A source passes a stationary receiver at $3c/5$. Compare the received frequency when the source is geometrically at closest approach now and when the receiver sees the light emitted at closest approach.

steps.why: Both questions use the same relative speed.
At the reception instant of geometric closest approach, the arriving ray was emitted earlier; this is transverse in the source frame.
Light emitted at closest approach has transverse direction in the receiver frame; neighboring emission paths have equal length to first order.

examples.answer_md: The first is a blueshift, the second a redshift. They refer to different received photons.
examples.check_md: The distinction disappears at $v=0$. Both follow from the general directional Doppler formula with different ray angles.

practice.question_md: Can ordinary time dilation alone predict every received flash rate?
hints: Time dilation relates emission intervals in coordinate time.
Reception intervals include changing path length.
The longitudinal example includes both factors.
practice.answer_md: No. Multiply the coordinate emission interval by the appropriate path-length factor before taking its reciprocal. Only special geometries remove that factor.

11.9.title: Rapidity
11.9.summary: Rapidity turns repeated collinear boosts into addition and connects that addition to the acceleration an astronaut feels.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Convert one familiar speed to rapidity, add a second boost, then reinterpret the sum as accumulated onboard acceleration.

parts.title: 11.9.1 · Define it and transform with it
parts.body_md: $$\beta=\tanh\eta,\quad\gamma=\cosh\eta,\quad\gamma\beta=\sinh\eta,\quad\eta=\frac12\ln\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}.$$ Thus \(ct=ct'\cosh\eta+x'\sinh\eta\) and \(x=x'\cosh\eta+ct'\sinh\eta\). This hyperbolic rotation preserves \(c^2t^2-x^2\). Rapidity is dimensionless and unbounded even though $|\beta |<1$.

parts.title: 11.9.1 · Composition and diagram angles
parts.body_md: The $\tanh$ addition identity reproduces velocity addition, so collinear rapidities simply add. The visible Euclidean tilt $\theta$ of axes on a Minkowski diagram obeys \(\tan\theta=\beta=\tanh\eta\); $\theta$ is not rapidity. Noncollinear boosts require additional directional bookkeeping and cannot be treated as ordinary scalar rapidity addition.

parts.title: 11.9.2 · What an onboard accelerometer measures
parts.body_md: Proper acceleration a is the acceleration measured in the momentarily comoving inertial frame; an ideal supported mass m feels force $ma$ there. For collinear motion, $$d\eta=\frac{a\,d\tau}{c},\qquad v=c\tanh\left(\eta_0+\frac1c\int a\,d\tau\right).$$ The time in the integral is the ship’s proper time. With constant a and initial rest, $v=c \tanh (a\tau /c)$, so sustained finite acceleration approaches but never reaches c.

parts.title: 11.9.2 · Do not mix acceleration definitions
parts.body_md: The lab acceleration is \(dv/dt=a/\gamma^3\) for collinear motion. Although v grows more slowly in lab time, the astronaut can keep feeling the same force. Rapidity adds because adjacent integrals of proper acceleration add; it is the natural accumulated measure of successive boosts.

examples.title: Compose equal boosts using logarithms
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two collinear boosts each have speed $3c/5$. Find their combined rapidity and velocity.

steps.why: Convert each velocity to an additive rapidity.
Collinear rapidities add.
Convert back using the exponential form of $\tanh$.

examples.answer_md: The combined velocity is $15c/17$.
examples.check_md: This matches direct relativistic velocity addition; reversing a boost changes the rapidity sign.

examples.title: Reach a chosen speed with constant felt acceleration
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A ship starts at rest and maintains constant proper acceleration a along x. How much ship time is needed to reach $3c/5$?

steps.why: Proper acceleration changes rapidity per unit proper time.
Integrate from rest with constant a.
Insert the target speed.

examples.answer_md: The ship records \((c/a)\ln2\).
examples.check_md: At small target speed, $\operatorname{artanh} (v/c)\approx v/c$ and the result reduces to $v/a$.

practice.question_md: Can finite proper acceleration acting for finite proper time produce infinite rapidity?
hints: Rapidity change is an integral of $a/c$.
A bounded acceleration over a finite interval has a finite integral.
Infinite rapidity would be needed to reach c.
practice.answer_md: No. Under those conditions the rapidity is finite and $|v|<c$. This conclusion does not require pretending the lab acceleration stays constant.

11.9.1.title: Definition
11.9.1.summary: Rapidity is the additive parameter hidden inside collinear relativistic velocity addition.

hints: Inverse transformations have opposite boost parameter.
Rapidity adds linearly for collinear boosts.

11.10.title: Relativity without c
11.10.summary: Relativity and symmetry largely fix the transformation structure; experiment determines whether its invariant speed is finite and equals light speed.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: What assumptions do the work
parts.body_md: With homogeneous spacetime, isotropy, linear inertial transformations, reciprocity and closure under composition, one obtains $$x=\Gamma(x'+vt'),\quad t=\Gamma(t'+Kvx'),\quad\Gamma=\frac1{\sqrt{1-Kv^2}}.$$ Composing two boosts forces K to be universal, rather than a different number for each boost. K has inverse-speed-squared units. This is more precise than claiming a bare verbal relativity principle needs no auxiliary regularity or symmetry assumptions.

parts.title: The possible structures
parts.body_md: $K=0$ gives Galilean transformations. $K>0$ gives Lorentz-type transformations with invariant speed \(V=1/\sqrt K\). In our world measurement identifies $V=c$. A formal negative K gives ordinary rotation-like transformations in the space–time plane; preserving a consistent forward-time sector fails under unrestricted composition, so the usual causal, time-oriented inertial structure rejects that branch. The degenerate zero limiting-speed case permits no nonzero boosts.

parts.title: What the light postulate adds
parts.body_md: The essential new empirical statement is a finite invariant speed, not a privileged numerical value in metres per second. Units can change that number. Light provides a physical realization of the invariant speed. This chapter’s kinematics therefore reflects spacetime structure, rather than an arbitrary correction only for optical experiments.

examples.title: A universe with an unspecified limiting speed
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Suppose inertial transformations have universal constant $K>0$ with units $s^{2}/m^{2}$, but nothing identifies it with light yet. Two collinear speeds both equal \(1/(2\sqrt K)\). Find their composition.

steps.why: Use the composition law implied by the generalized transformations.
Substitute the two equal inputs.

examples.answer_md: The result is below the invariant speed \(V=1/\sqrt K\).
examples.check_md: No property of electromagnetic light was needed for this algebra; experiments identify V with c in our world.

examples.title: Recover the Galilean limit
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Use \(x=\Gamma(x'+vt')\), \(t=\Gamma(t'+Kvx')\), with \(\Gamma=(1-Kv^2)^{-1/2}\). Take $K\to 0$ at fixed v and finite event coordinates.

steps.why: The universal limiting speed tends to infinity.
The generalized boost reduces to Galilean coordinates.

examples.answer_md: Absolute shared time is the infinite-limiting-speed special case.
examples.check_md: The limit keeps v and the event separation finite; singular scalings of distances would require a separate limiting argument.

practice.question_md: In the generalized law, if one input velocity equals $V=1/\sqrt{K}$ with $K>0$, what does any allowed collinear boost return?
practice.answer_md: \(u=(V+v)/(1+v/V)=V\). The invariant-speed property follows directly, independent of what physical signal realizes it.

12.1.title: Energy and momentum
12.1.summary: Energy and momentum form a compatible conserved pair; kinetic energy and separate mass sums are not generally conserved.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.
For small \(\epsilon\), \((1+\epsilon)^n\simeq1+n\epsilon\). Keep terms linear in the declared small parameter and state what you dropped. An approximation is useful only in its stated limit.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: First determine speed from momentum, then calculate total energy, and finally let two moving bodies stick to see where their kinetic energy goes.

parts.title: 12.1.1 · Why mv cannot be exact
parts.body_md: A glancing collision viewed in two relatively moving frames has differently transformed transverse velocities. If identical particles exchange equal opposite transverse impulses, momentum $m u$ st compensate the time-dilation factor in those velocities. This motivates $$\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v.$$ Rotational symmetry makes p parallel to v; experiments and the four-vector framework support its conservation across interactions.

parts.title: 12.1.1 · Interpret the variables
parts.body_md: m is invariant mass in kg, v is velocity in the chosen inertial frame, $\gamma$ uses that particle’s total speed, and p is in $\mathrm{kg} m/s$. A component \(p_y=\gamma m v_y\) uses the full-speed $\gamma$, not one computed from vy alone. At small $v, p\approx mv$. As v approaches c at fixed positive m, p diverges; arbitrarily large momentum need not imply superluminal speed.

parts.title: 12.1.2 · The central relations
parts.body_md: $$E=\gamma mc^2,\quad K=(\gamma-1)mc^2,\quad E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4,\quad\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E.$$ For $v\ll c$, \(E=mc^2+mv^2/2+3mv^4/(8c^2)+\cdots\), recovering Newtonian kinetic energy as the first correction. Here mass means invariant mass; energy and momentum depend on frame.

parts.title: 12.1.2 · Massless particles and systems
parts.body_md: A photon has \(m=0\), \(E=pc\), speed c and energy $h\nu$. Do not insert $m=0$ and $\gamma =\infty$ into $\gamma mc^{2}$ as an ordinary product. A collection of photons can have nonzero total invariant mass if their momenta do not all point together. For an isolated system, \(M^2c^4=E_{tot}^2-c^2|\mathbf P_{tot}|^2\), including internal energy and all components of the system.

parts.title: 12.1.2 · A free-particle action supplies the same definitions
parts.body_md: The invariant action \(S=-mc^2\int d\tau\) corresponds to \(\mathcal L=-mc^2\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\). Then \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf v=\gamma m\mathbf v\), and \(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf p-\mathcal L=\gamma mc^2\). Rotational symmetry similarly gives \(\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times\mathbf p\). Adding a prescribed potential in one frame can produce correct force equations there, but a fully relativistic interaction must transform consistently; an arbitrary scalar V(x)dt is not automatically invariant.

parts.title: 12.1.2 · Using c=1 carefully
parts.body_md: Natural units make c dimensionless one by tying time and length units together. E,p and m then share a numerical unit, but their SI dimensions have not become interchangeable. Restore factors by dimensions before comparing with measurements.

examples.title: Recover speed from momentum
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle of mass m has momentum magnitude $3mc/4$. Find its speed.

steps.why: Use relativistic momentum, not $p=mv$.
Square both positive magnitudes.
Solve and choose the direction specified by the momentum.

examples.answer_md: The speed is $3c/5$.
examples.check_md: Its $\gamma =5/4$ gives $\gamma mv=(5/4)m(3c/5)=3mc/4$.

examples.title: Rest, kinetic and total energy
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle of mass m moves at $4c/5$. Find E, kinetic energy K and p, then check the invariant.

steps.why: Total energy includes the rest term.
Subtract rest energy to get the excess energy of motion.
Use the same $\gamma$ as the energy.
Check the mass shell.

examples.check_md: All energy terms have joule units. Replacing total E by K in the invariant would fail.

examples.title: Head-on sticking increases invariant mass
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two identical masses m approach at opposite speeds $3c/5$ and stick with no radiation escaping. Find the final mass.

steps.why: Equal opposite momenta make the final object stationary in this frame.
Sum the total energies before the collision.
The final rest energy includes the converted kinetic energy.

examples.answer_md: The composite mass is $5m/2$, larger than 2m.
examples.check_md: The increase $m/2$ corresponds to the original total kinetic energy $mc^{2}/2$. Total energy is conserved; constituent rest-mass sums need not be.

practice.question_md: Can a zero-total-momentum system contain moving particles?
hints: Internal motion contributes to invariant mass.
practice.answer_md: Yes. Opposite particle momenta can cancel while their kinetic energies remain. The system mass is its total energy divided by $c^{2}$ in that zero-momentum frame.

12.1.1.title: Momentum
12.1.1.summary: Relativistic momentum is the conserved quantity γmv, with the same direction as velocity but a growing magnitude near c.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Why mv cannot be exact
parts.body_md: A glancing collision viewed in two relatively moving frames has differently transformed transverse velocities. If identical particles exchange equal opposite transverse impulses, momentum $m u$ st compensate the time-dilation factor in those velocities. This motivates $$\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v.$$ Rotational symmetry makes p parallel to v; experiments and the four-vector framework support its conservation across interactions.

parts.title: Interpret the variables
parts.body_md: m is invariant mass in kg, v is velocity in the chosen inertial frame, $\gamma$ uses that particle’s total speed, and p is in $\mathrm{kg} m/s$. A component \(p_y=\gamma m v_y\) uses the full-speed $\gamma$, not one computed from vy alone. At small $v, p\approx mv$. As v approaches c at fixed positive m, p diverges; arbitrarily large momentum need not imply superluminal speed.

examples.title: Recover speed from momentum
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle of mass m has momentum magnitude $3mc/4$. Find its speed.

steps.why: Use relativistic momentum, not $p=mv$.
Square both positive magnitudes.
Solve and choose the direction specified by the momentum.

examples.answer_md: The speed is $3c/5$.
examples.check_md: Its $\gamma =5/4$ gives $\gamma mv=(5/4)m(3c/5)=3mc/4$.

practice.question_md: A particle moves with components $(3c/5,0,0)$. What is its x momentum, and is $\gamma$ computed from only an arbitrary chosen component?
hints: For general motion use the sum of squared components.
practice.answer_md: \(p_x=3mc/4\). Here the total speed happens to equal |vx|; in multidimensional motion every momentum component uses the $\gamma$ of the full velocity.

visual.description: Use the supplied Morin source on printed pages 584–586 for the axes and geometry. No new simulation is claimed.

12.1.2.title: Energy
12.1.2.summary: Total energy includes rest energy, kinetic energy and, for a composite object, its internal energy.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.
For small \(\epsilon\), \((1+\epsilon)^n\simeq1+n\epsilon\). Keep terms linear in the declared small parameter and state what you dropped. An approximation is useful only in its stated limit.

parts.title: The central relations
parts.body_md: $$E=\gamma mc^2,\quad K=(\gamma-1)mc^2,\quad E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4,\quad\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E.$$ For $v\ll c$, \(E=mc^2+mv^2/2+3mv^4/(8c^2)+\cdots\), recovering Newtonian kinetic energy as the first correction. Here mass means invariant mass; energy and momentum depend on frame.

parts.title: Massless particles and systems
parts.body_md: A photon has \(m=0\), \(E=pc\), speed c and energy $h\nu$. Do not insert $m=0$ and $\gamma =\infty$ into $\gamma mc^{2}$ as an ordinary product. A collection of photons can have nonzero total invariant mass if their momenta do not all point together. For an isolated system, \(M^2c^4=E_{tot}^2-c^2|\mathbf P_{tot}|^2\), including internal energy and all components of the system.

parts.title: A free-particle action supplies the same definitions
parts.body_md: The invariant action \(S=-mc^2\int d\tau\) corresponds to \(\mathcal L=-mc^2\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\). Then \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf v=\gamma m\mathbf v\), and \(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf p-\mathcal L=\gamma mc^2\). Rotational symmetry similarly gives \(\mathbf L=\mathbf r\times\mathbf p\). Adding a prescribed potential in one frame can produce correct force equations there, but a fully relativistic interaction must transform consistently; an arbitrary scalar V(x)dt is not automatically invariant.

parts.title: Using c=1 carefully
parts.body_md: Natural units make c dimensionless one by tying time and length units together. E,p and m then share a numerical unit, but their SI dimensions have not become interchangeable. Restore factors by dimensions before comparing with measurements.

examples.title: Rest, kinetic and total energy
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle of mass m moves at $4c/5$. Find E, kinetic energy K and p, then check the invariant.

steps.why: Total energy includes the rest term.
Subtract rest energy to get the excess energy of motion.
Use the same $\gamma$ as the energy.
Check the mass shell.

examples.check_md: All energy terms have joule units. Replacing total E by K in the invariant would fail.

examples.title: Head-on sticking increases invariant mass
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two identical masses m approach at opposite speeds $3c/5$ and stick with no radiation escaping. Find the final mass.

steps.why: Equal opposite momenta make the final object stationary in this frame.
Sum the total energies before the collision.
The final rest energy includes the converted kinetic energy.

examples.answer_md: The composite mass is $5m/2$, larger than 2m.
examples.check_md: The increase $m/2$ corresponds to the original total kinetic energy $mc^{2}/2$. Total energy is conserved; constituent rest-mass sums need not be.

practice.question_md: A stationary sealed container absorbs energy Q with zero net added momentum. How much does its total invariant mass increase?
hints: It remains at rest in the chosen frame.
The new rest energy increases by Q.
practice.answer_md: \(\Delta M=Q/c^2\). This includes thermal or stored field energy, provided Q is the net retained energy and the complete system boundary is used.

12.2.title: Transformations of E and p
12.2.summary: Energy and longitudinal momentum mix under a boost, while transverse momentum stays unchanged.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For mass m, total energy E and momentum magnitude p, \(E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4\). For a massive particle \(E=\gamma mc^2\), \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\). Therefore \(\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E\). Total energy includes rest energy; kinetic energy is \(E-mc^2\).

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Boost the pair together
parts.body_md: For $S^{\prime}$ moving at +v along x relative to S, $$E=\gamma(E'+vp'_x),\qquad p_x=\gamma(p'_x+vE'/c^2),\qquad p_y=p'_y,\quad p_z=p'_z.$$ The inverse changes v’s sign. The same linear equations transform total energy and momentum of a complete isolated system. \(E^2-c^2\mathbf p^2\) is invariant.

parts.title: Why conservation survives a change of observer
parts.body_md: The before-minus-after differences transform by that same linear map. If all four differences vanish in one frame, they vanish in every inertial frame. Conserving momentum in every frame therefore cannot be separated from conserving energy. For totals, \(\mathbf V_{CM}=c^2\mathbf P/E\) gives the velocity of the zero-momentum frame when the total four-momentum is timelike.

examples.title: Boost a rest particle
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. In $S^{\prime}$ a mass m is at rest. $S^{\prime}$ moves at $3c/5$ relative to S. Find its energy and momentum in S.

steps.why: Start with the rest-frame four-momentum.
Use the energy transformation.
Use the momentum transformation.

examples.answer_md: E and p agree with the direct $\gamma$ formulas.
examples.check_md: The invariant difference remains $m^{2}c^{4}$; inverse boosting returns zero momentum.

examples.title: Invariant mass of unequal opposite photons
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two photons have energies $3\epsilon$ and $\epsilon$ and travel along +x and −x. Find the system invariant mass and center-of-momentum velocity.

steps.why: Energies add; opposite momenta partially cancel.
Apply the total-system invariant.
Solve the mass and use the boost that removes total momentum.

examples.answer_md: The pair has nonzero invariant mass and a CM frame moving at $c/2$.
examples.check_md: If the photon energies were equal, the CM velocity would vanish. A single photon or perfectly parallel photons have no massive-system rest frame.

practice.question_md: A right-moving photon has energy $\epsilon$ in $S^{\prime}$. Boost with $v=3c/5$ in the same direction. What energy does S assign?
practice.answer_md: $E=2\epsilon$ and $px=2\epsilon /c$. This agrees with the longitudinal blueshift factor and retains $E=pc$.

visual.description: Use the supplied Morin source on printed pages 594–596 for the axes and geometry. No new simulation is claimed.

12.3.title: Collisions and decays
12.3.summary: Collisions and decays are bookkeeping problems for conserved total four-momentum plus each particle’s mass shell.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For mass m, total energy E and momentum magnitude p, \(E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4\). For a massive particle \(E=\gamma mc^2\), \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\). Therefore \(\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E\). Total energy includes rest energy; kinetic energy is \(E-mc^2\).

parts.title: An efficient solution sequence
parts.body_md: Draw all directions in one frame. Write each \(P=(E/c,p_x,p_y,p_z)\). Impose \(\sum P_{before}=\sum P_{after}\), and use \(P_i^2=m_i^2c^2\). Choose a CM frame when symmetry makes it easier. Squaring a relation such as $P-P_{1}=P_{2}$ can eliminate a product whose components you do not need. Check positive energies, subluminal massive speeds and any threshold after algebra; squaring can introduce extraneous roots.

parts.title: Elastic versus inelastic
parts.body_md: Elastic means the particle species and internal rest energies remain unchanged; total energy is conserved in both elastic and inelastic isolated reactions. For equal-mass symmetric billiard scattering from a resting target, outgoing energies are \((E+mc^2)/2\) and $$\cos^2\theta=\frac{E+mc^2}{E+3mc^2}.$$ The two particles approach a ninety-degree mutual angle in the Newtonian limit, while highly energetic lab products are forward-directed.

parts.title: An angle can impose an existence condition
parts.body_md: For a parent of mass M and lab energy E decaying into two equal masses m, a product emitted exactly transverse to parent momentum has \(E_\perp=M^2c^4/(2E)\), from \((P-P_\perp)^2=m^2c^2\). That energy must be at least $mc^{2}$. At a sufficiently large boost an exactly transverse massive product is impossible even though the rest-frame decay is allowed.

examples.title: Two unequal products from a resting parent
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle of mass M at rest decays into masses $m_{1},m_{2}$, with $M\ge m_{1}+m_{2}$. Find the first product’s energy.

steps.why: Use four-momentum conservation and square to remove the second product’s unknown momentum.
In the parent rest frame the Minkowski inner product is $P\cdot P_{1}=ME_{1}$.
Solve the linear energy equation.
Opposite momentum magnitudes follow from the initial zero momentum.

examples.answer_md: The second energy is $Mc^{2}-E_{1}$, with equal opposite product momenta.
examples.check_md: At threshold $M=m_{1}+m_{2}, E_{1}=m_{1}c^{2}$ and both products are at rest. For equal masses each gets $Mc^{2}/2$.

examples.title: Minimum energy for a heavier final state
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A projectile mass m with total energy E hits an identical stationary target. The final state must have total rest mass 3m. Find the kinematic threshold projectile energy, assuming the reaction is otherwise allowed.

steps.why: Only the projectile carries initial momentum.
Compute the available invariant CM energy.
At threshold the products have no relative kinetic energy in the CM frame.
Solve for total projectile energy.

examples.answer_md: The threshold kinetic energy is \(K_{thr}=5mc^2/2\).
examples.check_md: Extra projectile energy is needed beyond the new rest mass because the final system carries lab momentum. This is a kinematic condition, not proof a particular interaction occurs.

practice.question_md: A rest parent of mass 4m decays into two equal masses m. What are each product’s energy, momentum magnitude and speed?
practice.answer_md: Each has $E=2mc^{2}, p=\sqrt{3mc}$ and $v=\sqrt{3c}/2$ in opposite directions. The energies sum to $4mc^{2}$ and momenta cancel.

12.4.title: Particle-physics units
12.4.summary: Particle units keep the numbers manageable while preserving the distinction among energy, momentum and mass.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For mass m, total energy E and momentum magnitude p, \(E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4\). For a massive particle \(E=\gamma mc^2\), \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\). Therefore \(\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E\). Total energy includes rest energy; kinetic energy is \(E-mc^2\).

parts.title: Electron-volts and prefixes
parts.body_md: One electron-volt is the energy magnitude associated with an elementary charge passing through a one-volt potential difference: \(1\ \mathrm{eV}=1.602176634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm J\). keV, MeV, GeV and TeV multiply by $10^{3},10^{6},10^{9}$ and $10^{12}$. A small SI energy can be substantial for one particle.

parts.title: Restore the dimensions
parts.body_md: Quote energy in MeV, momentum in $\mathrm{MeV}/c$, mass in $\mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}$. In $c=1$ work, people often abbreviate all three using MeV; write the units explicitly while learning. \(1\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2\simeq1.783\times10^{-30}\) kg. For orientation the electron rest energy is about 0.511 MeV and proton about 938 MeV; use supplied values in a problem rather than memorizing a table.

examples.title: Read an energy-unit mass correctly
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A hypothetical particle has mass $12 \mathrm{MeV}/c^{2}$ and total energy 20 MeV. Find $pc, \beta$ and kinetic energy.

steps.why: Use the energy relation with $mc^{2}=12 \mathrm{MeV}$.
The c factors cancel in this dimensionless ratio.
Subtract the rest energy, not a mass in kilograms.

examples.answer_md: $p=16 \mathrm{MeV}/c$, speed $4c/5$, kinetic energy 8 MeV.
examples.check_md: The triple 12,16,20 obeys the mass-shell relation exactly.

examples.title: Convert a small mass equivalent to SI
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A sealed object gains 2 MeV of rest energy. Estimate its mass increase using \(1\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2\simeq1.783\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{kg}\).

steps.why: Restore the $c^{2}$ required by dimensions.
Multiply by the supplied conversion.

examples.answer_md: The mass increase is about \(3.57\times10^{-30}\) kg.
examples.check_md: Using $1 \mathrm{eV}=1.602176634\times 10^{-19} J$ and $c\approx 3\times 10^{8} m/s$ gives the same scale.

practice.question_md: A photon has energy 7 MeV. What are its momentum and invariant mass?
hints: Divide by c to get momentum units.
practice.answer_md: $p=7 \mathrm{MeV}/c$ and $m=0$. Energy is nonzero even though invariant mass is zero.

visual.description: Use the supplied Morin source on printed pages 600–601 for the axes and geometry. No new simulation is claimed.

12.5.title: Force
12.5.summary: Force changes relativistic momentum, so its relation to acceleration depends on speed and direction.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For mass m, total energy E and momentum magnitude p, \(E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4\). For a massive particle \(E=\gamma mc^2\), \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\). Therefore \(\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E\). Total energy includes rest energy; kinetic energy is \(E-mc^2\).

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Use a constant straight force to understand the speed limit, then tilt the force and finally change observers to separate the three issues.

parts.title: 12.5.1 · One-dimensional response and work
parts.body_md: For constant mass, $$F=\frac{dp}{dt}=m\gamma^3a,\qquad\frac{dE}{dt}=Fv,\qquad dE=F\,dx.$$ The derivative \(\dot\gamma=\gamma^3va/c^2\) supplies the extra $\gamma$ factors. A constant force does not give constant lab acceleration. Work still equals the change in total energy; with fixed mass it also equals the change in kinetic energy.

parts.title: 12.5.1 · Scope of the formula
parts.body_md: m must be fixed for this simple particle formula. A rocket is an open system whose outgoing momentum $m u$ st be accounted for separately. Force, velocity and time here belong to the same inertial frame. At low speed $\gamma \approx 1$ and the usual $ma$ law reappears.

parts.title: 12.5.2 · Vector form before components
parts.body_md: $$\mathbf F=m\gamma\mathbf a+\frac{m\gamma^3}{c^2}(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a)\mathbf v.$$ Resolving relative to the instantaneous velocity gives \(F_\parallel=m\gamma^3a_\parallel\), \(F_\perp=m\gamma a_\perp\). A parallel acceleration changes $\gamma$ at first order; a transverse one initially turns velocity without changing its magnitude.

parts.title: 12.5.2 · Power and circular motion
parts.body_md: The work rate remains \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=dE/dt\). A purely perpendicular force does no instantaneous work and can maintain a constant-speed circle, requiring \(F=\gamma mv^2/R\). The differing component factors do not mean the particle has two invariant masses; one scalar m plus the velocity-dependent momentum describes both.

parts.title: 12.5.3 · Rest-frame rule with its condition
parts.body_md: If $S^{\prime}$ is the particle’s instantaneous rest frame and S sees it moving at v along x, $$F_x=F'_x,\qquad F_y=F'_y/\gamma,\qquad F_z=F'_z/\gamma.$$ Correspondingly \(a_x=a'_x/\gamma^3\), \(a_y=a'_y/\gamma^2\). These are instantaneous event relations, not a claim that the accelerated particle remains at rest in one inertial frame.

parts.title: 12.5.3 · Why blindly swapping primes fails
parts.body_md: The rest-frame condition chooses which worldline time intervals satisfy $dt=\gamma dt^{\prime}$. Swapping labels without swapping that physical condition answers a different problem. For general frames, use four-force or the full velocity-dependent formula. Along one common boost line, comparing two observers through the rest frame is often simplest. A rod’s orientation and an applied force’s orientation need not transform together.

examples.title: Constant force from rest
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A constant lab force F acts along x on a fixed mass m initially at rest. Find speed as a function of lab time.

steps.why: Integrate $F=dp/dt$ with zero initial momentum.
Use the mass shell rather than solving $\gamma$ algebra repeatedly.
Convert momentum to speed.

examples.answer_md: The speed approaches c while momentum continues to grow linearly.
examples.check_md: For $Ft\ll mc, v\approx Ft/m$. At every finite time the denominator keeps $v<c$.

examples.title: A diagonal force need not give diagonal acceleration
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle moves along +x at $3c/5$. At one instant its force has equal components $F_{0}$ in x and y. Find its acceleration components.

steps.why: Resolve parallel and transverse to the instantaneous velocity.
Insert $\gamma =5/4$.
The acceleration is more transverse than the force.

examples.answer_md: Force and acceleration are not parallel in this case.
examples.check_md: At $v=0$ both $\gamma$ factors become one and their directions coincide.

examples.title: A rod and a force transform differently
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A bead is initially at rest on a rod at 45° to $x^{\prime}$. A spring force $F^{\prime}$ points along the rod. The rod’s frame moves at $3c/5$ along x. Find the lab rod angle and force angle immediately after release.

steps.why: The rod’s x dimension contracts while its y dimension stays unchanged.
Use the instantaneous-rest-frame force transformation.
Force components transform differently from the rod’s dimensions.
The resulting acceleration still follows the moving rod.

examples.answer_md: The rod and acceleration have tangent $5/4$; the force angle has tangent $4/5$.
examples.check_md: No extra constraint force is needed merely to rotate F into a. Force and acceleration need not align.

practice.question_md: Does a nonzero force necessarily change total energy?
hints: A perpendicular force can turn momentum.
Energy depends on speed, not direction.
practice.answer_md: No. A force perpendicular to velocity has zero instantaneous power. Constant-speed circular motion provides a concrete example.

12.6.title: Rocket motion
12.6.summary: A rocket changes mass while transferring energy and momentum into exhaust, so track the complete system.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For mass m, total energy E and momentum magnitude p, \(E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4\). For a massive particle \(E=\gamma mc^2\), \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\). Therefore \(\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E\). Total energy includes rest energy; kinetic energy is \(E-mc^2\).
\(\eta=\operatorname{artanh}(v/c)\), and collinear boosts add $\eta$. For photons, energy and momentum magnitudes satisfy $E=pc$.

parts.title: Ideal photon exhaust
parts.body_md: For a rocket emitting purely backward photons, conservation of the sum E+cp gives $$\gamma m(1+\beta)=M,\qquad \frac mM=\sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}}=e^{-\eta}.$$ Equivalently \(dm/m=-d\beta/(1-\beta^2)\). M is initial mass at rest, m is the remaining invariant mass, and exhaust is fully collimated. This is a highly ideal conversion model, not the performance of an ordinary chemical rocket.

parts.title: The local and lab descriptions
parts.body_md: In the instantaneous rocket rest frame, an infinitesimal energy \(-c^2dm\) is emitted backward to first order, giving momentum \(c\,dm\). Lab photon energies are Doppler shifted; do not assign the same emitted energy to both frames. Combining rocket and exhaust conservation avoids treating changing mass as if the remaining rocket were a closed fixed-mass particle.

parts.title: Limits and energy accounting
parts.body_md: The final result depends on mass ratio, not burn duration or individual photon frequency. Rocket lab energy is \(E=Mc^2/(1+\beta)\). In the ideal limiting sequence $m\to 0, \beta \to 1$ and the rocket retains energy approaching $Mc^{2}/2$ while the exhaust carries the other half. No finite positive final mass reaches c. Ordinary material exhaust requires its own energy–momentum model; do not reuse the photon relation unchanged.

examples.title: A photon rocket spends half its mass
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. An ideal rocket starts at rest with mass M and emits all exhaust photons backward along one line. Its final mass is $M/2$. Find its final speed.

steps.why: Each backward photon has $E_\gamma+c p_\gamma=0$, so the rocket retains the initial total of this combination.
Insert the rocket’s energy and momentum.
Rearrange the invariant combination.
Solve for the speed.

examples.answer_md: The ideal final speed is $3c/5$.
examples.check_md: Final rocket energy is $(5/4)(M/2)c^2=5Mc^2/8$; exhaust carries $3Mc^2/8$ and opposite momentum.

examples.title: Add a second identical mass-ratio burn
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. The same photon rocket halves its remaining mass again, using backward exhaust in its own instantaneous frame. Find final speed relative to the original rest frame.

steps.why: The photon-rocket mass relation is an additive rapidity relation.
Two half-mass burns add ln2 each.
Convert total rapidity to speed.

examples.answer_md: The final speed is $15c/17$, not $6c/5$.
examples.check_md: Relativistically adding two $3c/5$ boosts gives the same result.

practice.question_md: What fraction of initial mass remains when an ideal photon rocket reaches $4c/5$?
hints: The ratio inside the root is $1/9$.
practice.answer_md: $m/M=1/3$. The remaining energy is $\gamma mc^{2}=(5/3)(M/3)c^{2}=5Mc^{2}/9$, leaving $4Mc^2/9$ in exhaust; the momenta cancel in the original rest frame.

12.7.title: Relativistic strings
12.7.summary: A constant-tension relativistic string stores energy proportional to length, and that energy contributes inertia.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For mass m, total energy E and momentum magnitude p, \(E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4\). For a massive particle \(E=\gamma mc^2\), \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\). Therefore \(\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E\). Total energy includes rest energy; kinetic energy is \(E-mc^2\).

parts.title: What “massless” means in this model
parts.body_md: The ideal string has zero energy at zero length, but stretching it to length $\ell$ stores \(U=T\ell\). Its rest-frame mass equivalent is $T\ell /c^{2}$; a stretched string is not energyless. The endpoint force has constant magnitude T independent of extension, unlike a Hooke spring. In one-dimensional problems the useful laws are \(dp/dt=\pm T\) and \(dE/dx=\pm T\).

parts.title: Wall and two-endpoint problems
parts.body_md: For an outgoing endpoint attached to a wall, \(\ell_{max}=(\gamma-1)mc^2/T\) and \(t_{stop}=\gamma mv/T\). For two initially resting masses m at $x=0$ and M at $x=\ell$, equal opposite impulses give equal |p|. Energy gained by each over its traveled distance yields $$x_{meet}=\ell\frac{M+T\ell/(2c^2)}{M+m+T\ell/c^2}.$$ This is the initial center of energy including the uniform string energy.

parts.title: Limits explain the result
parts.body_md: For $T\ell \ll mc^{2},Mc^{2}$, the meeting point tends to $M\ell /(M+m)$, the Newtonian result. For stored string energy much larger than both endpoint rest energies, both endpoints rapidly approach c and meet near the midpoint. The source’s quark-confinement analogy motivates the ideal model; it does not make this a universal law for ordinary cords.

examples.title: A constant-tension string stops an outgoing mass
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A mass m starts beside a fixed wall at speed $3c/5$, stretching an ideal relativistic string with constant tension T. Find maximum extension and stopping time.

steps.why: Compute the energy available to store in the string.
The constant tension removes energy T per unit distance.
The same force removes momentum T per unit time.

examples.answer_md: Maximum extension is $mc^{2}/(4T)$, reached after $3mc/(4T)$.
examples.check_md: The average outgoing speed is $\ell /t=c/3$, between initial $3c/5$ and final zero.

examples.title: Where unequal endpoint masses meet
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Masses m and 2m are released from rest at opposite ends of a length $\ell$ constant-tension string. Its stored energy is $T\ell =mc^{2}$. Find the meeting location x measured from the initial position of m.

steps.why: Work done by the tension becomes each endpoint’s total-energy increase.
Equal opposite impulses imply equal momentum magnitudes; apply the mass shells.
Solve the linear equation after canceling the matching quadratic x terms.

examples.answer_md: They meet $5\ell /8$ from m’s initial position.
examples.check_md: The initial string mass is $T\ell /c^{2}=m$ at its midpoint; the whole system’s initial center of energy is also $5\ell/8$.

practice.question_md: For equal endpoint masses m, where do they meet for any positive $T\ell$ in this model?
hints: The numerator is half the denominator.
Symmetry gives the same answer before calculation.
practice.answer_md: $x=\ell /2$. The expression respects exact left-right symmetry whether endpoint or string energy dominates.
