13.1.title: Definition of 4-vectors
13.1.summary: A four-vector is defined by how its components change between frames, not by how many entries it has.

prerequisites.refresher_md: Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

parts.title: The definition with dimensions intact
parts.body_md: Write components in order (time,x,y,z), indexed0,1,2,3. A four-vector transforms like \((c\,dt,dx,dy,dz)\) under Lorentz boosts and spatial rotations. For an x boost, $$A^0=\gamma(A^{\prime 0}+\beta A^{\prime 1}),\quad A^1=\gamma(A^{\prime 1}+\beta A^{\prime 0}),\quad A^2=A^{\prime 2},\quad A^3=A^{\prime 3}.$$ All four components in this convention have the same units. The “time component” of momentum, for example, is $E/c$, not a time measurement.

parts.title: A practical proof or disproof
parts.body_md: Transform a candidate in two ways: first by the proposed four-vector rule, then by transforming the ingredients in its definition. Agreement for every allowed transformation establishes the candidate; one counterexample disproves it. Multiplying every component by one invariant scalar works. Altering one component independently generally does not. A pure four-position also needs a fixed origin; displacements avoid translation offsets.

examples.title: Transform a spacetime displacement
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A displacement has \(X'=(5\ell,3\ell,0,0)\), ordered as (ct,x,y,z). Boost to a frame in which $S^{\prime}$ moves at $3c/5$.

steps.why: Use the boost speed, not a speed inferred from the vector’s components.
Transform the time component.
Transform the longitudinal component.

examples.check_md: Its squared norm is $16\ell ^{2}$ both before and after the boost.

examples.title: Test a tempting non-vector
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Consider \(B=(c\,dt,2dx,dy,dz)\). In a frame with $dx^{\prime}=dy^{\prime}=dz^{\prime}=0$ and $cdt^{\prime}=\ell$, compare its actual transformed components with a four-vector prediction.

steps.why: Transform the underlying displacement.
Apply B’s definition after transforming.
A genuine four-vector starting at $(\ell ,0,0,0)$ would have this boost.

examples.answer_md: The results disagree when $\beta \ne 0$, so B is not a four-vector.
examples.check_md: Agreement in one special frame or one boost direction is insufficient; the transformation rule must hold generally.

practice.question_md: If A is a four-vector and m is invariant mass, is mA a four-vector? What if the multiplying factor is the frame-dependent $\gamma$ of some particle?
hints: The same scalar must multiply in every frame.
m does, so it commutes with the transformation.
A frame-dependent multiplier changes the proposed rule.
practice.answer_md: mA is a four-vector. Multiplying by a frame-dependent $\gamma$ does not generally preserve four-vector transformation; further structure would be needed.

13.2.title: Examples of 4-vectors
13.2.summary: Dividing by proper time and multiplying by invariant mass build useful four-vectors without guessing.

prerequisites.idea: A four-component object with a rule
prerequisites.refresher_md: A four-vector is not just any list of four numbers. Under an x-directed boost with $\beta =v/c$ it must obey \(A^0=\gamma(A^{\prime 0}+\beta A^{\prime 1})\), \(A^1=\gamma(A^{\prime 1}+\beta A^{\prime 0})\), with transverse components unchanged. Its spatial part also transforms as an ordinary vector under spatial rotations.
Use the +--- convention: \(A\cdot B=A^0B^0-A^1B^1-A^2B^2-A^3B^3\). This scalar is invariant. The minus signs are essential; a zero norm need not mean a zero vector.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Velocity and momentum
parts.body_md: Along a massive particle’s worldline, $$U=\frac{dX}{d\tau}=\gamma(c,\mathbf v),\qquad P=mU=(E/c,\mathbf p).$$ Proper time is invariant, so the division preserves the transformation rule. A photon has no rest proper-time parameter, so its momentum is used directly rather than defining a photon four-velocity by this formula.

parts.title: Acceleration
parts.body_md: $$A=\frac{dU}{d\tau}=\left(\gamma^4\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a}{c},\ \gamma^2\mathbf a+\gamma^4\frac{(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a)\mathbf v}{c^2}\right).$$ In the instantaneous rest frame, $A=(0,a_{0})$. Its norm is $-a_{0}^{2}$. When v lies along x, the spatial components simplify to \((\gamma^4a_x,\gamma^2a_y,\gamma^2a_z)\). Ordinary acceleration and the spatial part of A are different objects.

parts.title: Force
parts.body_md: $$K=\frac{dP}{d\tau}=\gamma\left(\frac1c\frac{dE}{dt},\mathbf f\right).$$ For fixed mass, $K=mA$ and \(dE/dt=\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf v\). In the instantaneous rest frame $K=(0,f_{0})$. If mass changes, \(K=mA+(dm/d\tau)U\); the fixed-mass simplification no longer applies. Derivatives with respect to invariant $\tau$ preserve four-vector character; dividing by coordinate time generally does not.

examples.title: Four-velocity of a moving clock
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A clock moves at $3c/5$ along x. Find its four-velocity U and check its norm.

steps.why: Divide displacement by invariant proper time.
Insert the speed and $\gamma$.
Check the invariant velocity norm.

examples.answer_md: The spatial component of U is $3c/4$, while ordinary velocity is $3c/5$.
examples.check_md: Ordinary velocity is $cU^{1}/U^{0}$. The spatial components of U can exceed c without describing a physical speed above c.

examples.title: Four-acceleration for straight motion
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. At an instant a particle moves at $3c/5$ along x with lab acceleration a along x. Find its four-acceleration.

steps.why: Differentiate U with respect to proper time, including $\gamma$’s change.
Insert $\beta =3/5$ and $\gamma =5/4$.
Subtract the squares; the proper acceleration magnitude is $\gamma ^{3}a$.

examples.answer_md: The four-acceleration has a nonzero time component in the lab even though its rest-frame time component is zero.
examples.check_md: $U\cdot A=0$, as required by differentiating the constant $U\cdot U=c^{2}$.

practice.question_md: A fixed-mass particle is instantaneously at rest and feels force $f_{0}$ along y. Write U,A,K.
practice.answer_md: \(U=(c,0,0,0)\), \(A=(0,0,f_0/m,0)\), \(K=(0,0,f_0,0)\). Units are speed, acceleration and force respectively.

13.3.title: Properties of 4-vectors
13.3.summary: Linear combinations remain four-vectors and their Minkowski inner products are observer-independent.

prerequisites.idea: A four-component object with a rule
prerequisites.refresher_md: A four-vector is not just any list of four numbers. Under an x-directed boost with $\beta =v/c$ it must obey \(A^0=\gamma(A^{\prime 0}+\beta A^{\prime 1})\), \(A^1=\gamma(A^{\prime 1}+\beta A^{\prime 0})\), with transverse components unchanged. Its spatial part also transforms as an ordinary vector under spatial rotations.
Use the +--- convention: \(A\cdot B=A^0B^0-A^1B^1-A^2B^2-A^3B^3\). This scalar is invariant. The minus signs are essential; a zero norm need not mean a zero vector.

parts.title: Linearity with scalar coefficients
parts.body_md: If A,B are four-vectors and a,b are invariant scalars, aA+bB is a four-vector. The Lorentz map distributes over the combination. This justifies total four-momentum and finite differences before differentiation. Frame-dependent coefficients require a separate transformation analysis.

parts.title: Why the minus signs work
parts.body_md: Under a boost the time and longitudinal components mix with the same-sign $\beta$ terms. In \(A^0B^0-A^1B^1\), their cross terms cancel and \(\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1\) leaves the original product. Transverse spatial dot products are rotation-invariant too. A vector’s squared norm may be positive, negative or zero; Euclidean length intuition does not apply unchanged.

parts.title: A zero-component theorem
parts.body_md: If one specified component of a four-vector is zero in every inertial frame and every spatial orientation, the whole four-vector must be zero. A nonzero spatial component can be rotated into the tested direction; a boost mixes it with time. The phrase “in every frame” is essential: a spatial force can have zero time component in its instantaneous rest frame while being nonzero.

parts.title: Useful orthogonality
parts.body_md: Since $U^{2}=c^{2}$, differentiation gives $U\cdot A=0$. For fixed mass, $U\cdot K=0$ too. In the particle rest frame this says the four-acceleration and four-force have zero time components. In another frame they generally acquire time components, while the invariant orthogonality remains.

examples.title: Use an invariant product to find relative speed
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two particles move at $\pm 3c/5$ along x in the lab. Find their relative Lorentz factor without explicitly boosting velocities.

steps.why: Write their four-velocities in one frame.
The spatial minus sign turns the opposite-velocity product positive.
In particle1’s rest frame $U_{1}=(c,0)$, so the product equals $\gamma_{\mathrm{rel}}c^2$.
Recover the relative speed.

examples.answer_md: The relative speed is $15c/17$.
examples.check_md: This agrees with collinear velocity addition and is less than c despite a lab closing speed $6c/5$.

examples.title: Two nonzero null vectors can sum to a timelike vector
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Let \(A=(q,q,0,0)\), \(B=(q,-q,0,0)\), $q>0$. Find their norms, inner product and sum norm.

steps.why: Each vector is null but nonzero.
The spatial directions are opposite, so their Minkowski inner product is nonzero.
The cross term makes the sum timelike.

examples.answer_md: The sum is(2q,0,0,0), with positive norm $4q^2$.
examples.check_md: This is the geometric reason opposite photons can form a system with nonzero invariant mass.

practice.question_md: Does $A^{2}=0$ imply all components of A vanish?
hints: A time component can cancel a spatial one.
practice.answer_md: No. A nonzero null vector has zero norm. This is different from the stronger condition that one component vanishes in every frame.

13.4.title: Energy, momentum
13.4.summary: Four-momentum combines a useful invariant mass with simple observer transformations.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For mass m, total energy E and momentum magnitude p, \(E^2-p^2c^2=m^2c^4\). For a massive particle \(E=\gamma mc^2\), \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\). Therefore \(\mathbf v=c^2\mathbf p/E\). Total energy includes rest energy; kinetic energy is \(E-mc^2\).

prerequisites.idea: A four-component object with a rule
prerequisites.refresher_md: A four-vector is not just any list of four numbers. Under an x-directed boost with $\beta =v/c$ it must obey \(A^0=\gamma(A^{\prime 0}+\beta A^{\prime 1})\), \(A^1=\gamma(A^{\prime 1}+\beta A^{\prime 0})\), with transverse components unchanged. Its spatial part also transforms as an ordinary vector under spatial rotations.
Use the +--- convention: \(A\cdot B=A^0B^0-A^1B^1-A^2B^2-A^3B^3\). This scalar is invariant. The minus signs are essential; a zero norm need not mean a zero vector.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Calculate a photon pair’s total norm, then boost a momentum perpendicular to one of its components. These show why vector bookkeeping saves algebra.

parts.title: 13.4.1 · One particle and a collection
parts.body_md: For one particle, \(P^2=m^2c^2\), found immediately in its rest frame and therefore true in all frames. For a collection, $$M^2c^4=(\sum_iE_i)^2-c^2|\sum_i\mathbf p_i|^2.$$ Sum first, then square. M is not generally the sum of constituent masses; relative motion and interactions can contribute to the system rest energy.

parts.title: 13.4.1 · Use a subset only with its own bookkeeping
parts.body_md: The total momentum of any specified subset also has an invariant norm, but it need not be conserved if that subset exchanges energy or momentum with its surroundings. In a zero-total-momentum frame, $Mc^{2}$ is simply total energy. A null total momentum, as for parallel photons, has no subluminal CM frame.

parts.title: 13.4.2 · Read the transformation from the definition
parts.body_md: Insert \(P=(E/c,p_x,p_y,p_z)\) into the generic boost rule to obtain \(E=\gamma(E'+vp'_x)\), \(p_x=\gamma(p'_x+vE'/c^2)\), with py,pz unchanged. A boost along another direction mixes its matching momentum component with $E/c$. This route avoids repeating velocity-addition algebra for every particle.

parts.title: 13.4.2 · Conservation components belong together
parts.body_md: Let $\Delta P=P_{\mathrm{after}}-P_{\mathrm{before}}$. If energy is conserved in every inertial frame, $\Delta P^{0}=0$ in every frame. The zero-component theorem then forces all of $\Delta P$ to vanish. Conversely, conservation of a momentum component in every frame and orientation forces energy conservation too. Conservation of only one component in one special frame is not enough.

examples.title: Two photons at a right angle
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two photons each have energy $\epsilon$ and travel along perpendicular x and y directions. Find their system invariant mass.

steps.why: Add all components before squaring.
Subtract the total spatial momentum squared.
Take the positive system mass.

examples.answer_md: The pair’s invariant mass is $\sqrt{2}\epsilon/c^2$.
examples.check_md: Each individual photon mass is zero; summing individual mass squares would miss the cross terms.

examples.title: Transform a momentum with a transverse component
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle has \(P'=(5q,3q,0,0)\) with components in momentum units. Boost along y at $3c/5$. Find the transformed four-momentum.

steps.why: The boost mixes time and y, not x.
The new y momentum arises from the boost.
Components transverse to the boost are unchanged.

practice.question_md: Why is the squared total momentum not the sum of the individual squared momenta?
hints: It includes relative energy and direction.
practice.answer_md: The cross term generally does not vanish. It is precisely why a pair’s invariant mass can differ from the sum of separate particle masses.

13.5.title: Force and acceleration
13.5.summary: Four-force and four-acceleration make frame changes straightforward while keeping ordinary force and acceleration distinct.

prerequisites.idea: A four-component object with a rule
prerequisites.refresher_md: A four-vector is not just any list of four numbers. Under an x-directed boost with $\beta =v/c$ it must obey \(A^0=\gamma(A^{\prime 0}+\beta A^{\prime 1})\), \(A^1=\gamma(A^{\prime 1}+\beta A^{\prime 0})\), with transverse components unchanged. Its spatial part also transforms as an ordinary vector under spatial rotations.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Boost a sideways force, then inspect a circular acceleration. Both are transverse examples, but extracting the ordinary three-vector produces different powers of $\gamma$.

parts.title: 13.5.1 · Rest frame to lab
parts.body_md: For fixed mass and a particle instantaneously at rest in $S^{\prime}$, \(K'=(0,\mathbf f')\). Boost along its lab velocity v: $$K^0=\gamma\beta f'_x,\quad K^1=\gamma f'_x,\quad K^2=f'_y,\quad K^3=f'_z.$$ Compare with \(K=\gamma(\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf v/c,\mathbf f)\). It follows that \(f_x=f'_x\) and \(f_{y,z}=f'_{y,z}/\gamma\). The time component supplies the work–energy equation.

parts.title: 13.5.1 · For two arbitrary inertial frames
parts.body_md: If the particle has velocity $u^{\prime}$ in $S^{\prime}$, define \(D=1+vu'_x/c^2\) and $\gamma_v$ from the boost speed. Then $$f_x=\frac{f'_x+(v/c^2)(\mathbf f'\cdot\mathbf u')}{D},\qquad f_{y,z}=\frac{f'_{y,z}}{\gamma_vD}.$$ This follows from transforming K and using \(\gamma_u=\gamma_v\gamma_{u'}D\). The rest-frame rule is the $u^{\prime}=0$ special case, not a universal prime-swapping rule.

parts.title: 13.5.2 · Transform A, then interpret it
parts.body_md: In the instantaneous rest frame, \(A'=(0,a'_x,a'_y,a'_z)\). Boosting along x gives \((\gamma\beta a'_x,\gamma a'_x,a'_y,a'_z)\). In the lab, the same vector is \((\gamma^4va_x/c,\gamma^4a_x,\gamma^2a_y,\gamma^2a_z)\). Equating components yields $$a_x=a'_x/\gamma^3,\qquad a_{y,z}=a'_{y,z}/\gamma^2.$$ These $\gamma$ factors differ from ordinary force transformations.

parts.title: 13.5.2 · Invariant acceleration magnitude
parts.body_md: For arbitrary directions, $$a_0^2=-A^2=\gamma^6a_\parallel^2+\gamma^4a_\perp^2.$$ This is what an ideal accelerometer measures in the instantaneous rest frame. It is zero for inertial motion, even if the coordinate description in an accelerating frame looks curved. Circular motion has nonzero proper acceleration despite constant speed and energy.

examples.title: Boost a purely sideways rest force
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. In a particle’s instantaneous rest frame, \(K'=(0,0,F_0,0)\). The lab sees the particle at $3c/5$ along x. Find K and ordinary lab force.

steps.why: The four-force is purely transverse to this boost, so its listed components do not change.
Ordinary force is not directly the spatial four-force component.
Divide by the particle’s lab $\gamma$.

examples.answer_md: The four-force components are unchanged, yet the ordinary transverse force is reduced.
examples.check_md: The lab power is zero because the force is perpendicular to the current velocity.

examples.title: Proper acceleration on a fast circular path
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle moves at $4c/5$ on a lab circle of radius R. At an instant its velocity is along x and its inward acceleration along y. Find lab and proper acceleration magnitudes.

steps.why: The geometric circular-acceleration formula remains valid in lab coordinates.
Velocity and acceleration are perpendicular, so the time component vanishes.
The transverse four-acceleration equals its instantaneous-rest-frame spatial value.

examples.answer_md: Lab acceleration is $16c^{2}/(25R)$, proper acceleration $16c^2/(9R)$.
examples.check_md: Its norm is $-a_{0}^{2}$. The required lab force is $\gamma m v^2/R$, while the rest-frame force is $m a_0$.

practice.question_md: Why can $K=mA$ hold while the ordinary equation $f=ma$ fails?
hints: The spatial part of $K$ is $\gamma f$.
The spatial part of A is not simply $\gamma a$ in general.
Extracting components introduces different velocity factors.
practice.answer_md: $K=mA$ is a covariant fixed-mass equation. Its ordinary components give $f_{\parallel}=m\gamma ^{3}a_{\parallel}$ and $f_{\perp}=m\gamma a_{\perp}$, reducing to $f=ma$ only at low speed.

13.5.1.title: Transformation of forces
13.5.1.summary: Four-force transforms linearly; ordinary three-force is recovered by dividing its spatial components by the particle’s gamma.

prerequisites.idea: A four-component object with a rule
prerequisites.refresher_md: A four-vector is not just any list of four numbers. Under an x-directed boost with $\beta =v/c$ it must obey \(A^0=\gamma(A^{\prime 0}+\beta A^{\prime 1})\), \(A^1=\gamma(A^{\prime 1}+\beta A^{\prime 0})\), with transverse components unchanged. Its spatial part also transforms as an ordinary vector under spatial rotations.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Rest frame to lab
parts.body_md: For fixed mass and a particle instantaneously at rest in $S^{\prime}$, \(K'=(0,\mathbf f')\). Boost along its lab velocity v: $$K^0=\gamma\beta f'_x,\quad K^1=\gamma f'_x,\quad K^2=f'_y,\quad K^3=f'_z.$$ Compare with \(K=\gamma(\mathbf f\cdot\mathbf v/c,\mathbf f)\). It follows that \(f_x=f'_x\) and \(f_{y,z}=f'_{y,z}/\gamma\). The time component supplies the work–energy equation.

practice.question_md: A rest-frame force has only x component $F_{0}$. What lab power is delivered when the particle moves at v along x?
hints: Check the transformed time component $K^{0}=\gamma vF_{0}/c$.
practice.answer_md: Power is $F_{0}v$. Multiplying it by $\gamma /c$ yields the same four-force time component as the direct boost.

13.6.title: The form of physical laws
13.6.summary: Covariant equations preserve their meaning across observers; covariance is necessary structure, not proof that an equation describes nature.

prerequisites.idea: A four-component object with a rule
prerequisites.refresher_md: A four-vector is not just any list of four numbers. Under an x-directed boost with $\beta =v/c$ it must obey \(A^0=\gamma(A^{\prime 0}+\beta A^{\prime 1})\), \(A^1=\gamma(A^{\prime 1}+\beta A^{\prime 0})\), with transverse components unchanged. Its spatial part also transforms as an ordinary vector under spatial rotations.
Use the +--- convention: \(A\cdot B=A^0B^0-A^1B^1-A^2B^2-A^3B^3\). This scalar is invariant. The minus signs are essential; a zero norm need not mean a zero vector.

parts.title: Transform both sides
parts.body_md: If $A=B$ is a true four-vector equation in one frame, applying the same Lorentz map gives $A^{\prime}=B^{\prime}$ in another. Scalar equalities formed from invariant products also survive. Tensor equations generalize this to fields such as electromagnetism and gravity. Ordinary component equations may be perfectly valid when they are understood as components of a covariant statement.

parts.title: What covariance does and does not guarantee
parts.body_md: For fixed mass, $K=mA$ is covariant and agrees with observed mechanics. But a made-up four-vector equality can be covariant in form and physically false; experimental content still matters. Nor must every law literally contain only four-vectors: invariant scalars and higher-rank tensors are equally legitimate. The goal is consistent transformation, not a notation requirement.

parts.title: Recover the familiar law where appropriate
parts.body_md: In the instantaneous rest frame, $K=(0,f), A=(0,a)$, so $K=mA$ reduces to $f=ma$. In another frame, the same law yields the direction-dependent $\gamma$ factors. A law should not need a different physical rule merely because we changed coordinates.

examples.title: A law survives a boost when both sides transform together
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. At rest a constant-mass particle has \(A'=(0,a,0,0)\), \(K'=(0,ma,0,0)\). Boost at $3c/5$ along x and check $K=mA$.

steps.why: Transform the four-acceleration.
Transform the four-force with the same linear map.
Multiplication by invariant m commutes with the transformation.

examples.answer_md: The same four-vector equation holds in the new frame.
examples.check_md: Its ordinary acceleration is $a/\gamma ^{3}$ and force $ma$, so interpreting the spatial entries directly as three-vectors would be incorrect.

examples.title: Why a coordinate-biased rule fails even in ordinary space
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Someone proposes \(\mathbf f=m(2a_x,a_y,a_z)\) as a universal law with no physical preferred axis. Test it for eastward acceleration a.

steps.why: The proposed x coefficient doubles the force.
Relabeling axes changes the predicted physical force.

examples.answer_md: The proposal depends on arbitrary coordinate labels and cannot be that universal isotropic law.
examples.check_md: A real anisotropic medium could introduce a tensor and physical directions, but then those coefficients must transform too; arbitrary coordinate labels are not physical structure.

practice.question_md: Is $P^{2}=m^{2}c^{2}$ a frame-independent statement, even though P’s components change?
practice.answer_md: Yes. Every inertial observer computes the same scalar equality from different energy and momentum components.

14.1.title: The Equivalence Principle
14.1.summary: A sufficiently small free-fall lab removes uniform gravity locally; tidal gradients distinguish an extended gravitational field.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

parts.title: Three connected ways to picture equivalence
parts.body_md: A supported lab in gravity behaves locally like an accelerating rocket in empty space. A freely falling small lab behaves locally like an inertial lab. Universal free fall is reflected in the equality, up to a shared unit convention, of gravitational and inertial mass: \(a=(m_g/m_i)g\) must be composition-independent. These are related aspects of equivalence; universal free fall alone is a weaker statement than the full equivalence principle for every local nongravitational experiment.

parts.title: Why the word local matters
parts.body_md: Gravity from a planet varies with position and direction. Neighboring freely falling particles can separate or converge because of tides. One can remove a uniform gravitational acceleration at one event by free-fall coordinates, but not generally remove curvature across a finite laboratory. An accelerating frame in flat spacetime can imitate local supported gravity without creating spacetime curvature.

parts.title: Who feels a force?
parts.body_md: An ideal accelerometer carried by a freely falling person reads zero; a person standing on the ground reads the support acceleration. This does not deny gravity’s observable effects. It changes the organization of the explanation: free particles follow spacetime’s natural paths, while support forces deflect them from those paths.

examples.title: Two scales that agree locally
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A mass m rests on a scale in a small rocket far from gravity with upward proper acceleration g. Compare the scale reading with an identical mass supported in a small stationary lab in gravity g.

steps.why: In the instantaneous rest frame, the scale supplies the mass’s upward acceleration.
In the supported lab, the scale balances the local gravitational tendency.
The local mechanical readings agree.

examples.answer_md: Both scales read $mg$.
examples.check_md: A freely falling scale and mass together instead read zero locally. The distinction is support acceleration, not whether gravity has been declared present in a coordinate description.

examples.title: A finite lab can detect a gravity gradient
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A freely falling reference point is distance R from a spherical source M. A second test particle starts a small distance h radially outward, initially comoving. Find its initial relative acceleration.

steps.why: Take outward as positive and write both inward accelerations.
Expand to first order in $h/R$.
The detectable tidal difference shrinks with the laboratory size.

examples.answer_md: The particles separate radially with initial relative acceleration $2GMh/R^3$.
examples.check_md: This does not violate local equivalence; a gradient measurement compares distinct locations over a finite region.

practice.question_md: Two released materials fall with accelerations g and $(1+\epsilon )g$ in the same tiny region. What would that imply if $\epsilon$ were real and composition-dependent?
hints: In an empty inertial lab freely released objects have no such composition-dependent drift.
Universal free fall is being tested.
practice.answer_md: It would violate the universality of free fall and hence this necessary aspect of equivalence. Ordinary drag or electromagnetic forces must be excluded before interpreting such a difference as gravitational.

14.2.title: Time dilation
14.2.summary: Stationary clocks at higher gravitational potential run faster, and light climbing to them is redshifted.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For small \(\epsilon\), \((1+\epsilon)^n\simeq1+n\epsilon\). Keep terms linear in the declared small parameter and state what you dropped. An approximation is useful only in its stated limit.

An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

parts.title: An accelerating rocket explains the sign
parts.body_md: Imagine light sent from the front of a small upward-accelerating rocket to its rear. During flight $h/c$, the rear receiver gains speed roughly $gh/c$ toward the incoming light, producing a fractional blueshift $gh/c^{2}$. Equivalence gives the corresponding downward-light blueshift in gravity. Reversing the path gives an upward redshift.

parts.title: Clock and photon formulas
parts.body_md: For a static weak potential difference, $$\frac{d\tau_{high}}{d\tau_{low}}\simeq1+\frac{\Phi_{high}-\Phi_{low}}{c^2},$$ $$\frac{f_{received\ at\ high}}{f_{emitted\ at\ low}}\simeq1-\frac{\Phi_{high}-\Phi_{low}}{c^2}.$$ Frequencies here are measured by the local source and receiver clocks. A higher clock’s faster rate and upward light’s redshift are consistent: a fixed train of cycles is counted against differently paced local clocks.

parts.title: Assumptions and clock transport
parts.body_md: Use \(\Delta\Phi\simeq gh\) only over a height where g is nearly constant. The formulas are first order in potential difference divided by $c^2$. To compare clocks brought together later, include motion during their transport as well as their stationary-height intervals. A coordinate-light-speed statement is not a change of locally measured vacuum c.

examples.title: Clock gain between two stationary heights
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two ideal clocks remain at heights0 and h for a reference time T in a weak nearly uniform field g. Ignore transport intervals. Find the upper clock’s extra elapsed time.

steps.why: Potential difference, rather than an arbitrary potential zero, controls the relative rate.
The higher clock runs faster to first order.
Integrate the constant relative rate difference.

examples.answer_md: The upper clock gains $ghT/c^{2}$.
examples.check_md: $gh/c^{2}$ is dimensionless and small in this approximation. The gain vanishes with height or duration.

examples.title: Motion cancels a height advantage
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A clock moves horizontally at constant speed v at height h. A reference clock remains at rest at height0. Find the speed giving equal rates in the weak-field, slow-speed approximation.

steps.why: Include gravitational gain and kinematic loss in the same reference time.
Equal rates require the two first-order corrections to cancel.
Take the positive speed magnitude.

examples.answer_md: The matching speed is $\sqrt{2gh}$, provided $gh\ll c^{2}$ and $v\ll c$.
examples.check_md: This is an instantaneous-rate comparison; takeoff, landing and transport histories must be included for a complete reunited-clock comparison.

practice.question_md: A stationary source at the top sends light down a height h to a stationary lower receiver. What is the leading fractional frequency change?
hints: The receiver is at lower potential.
Reverse the sign of the upward-redshift expression.
Use a local clock for each frequency.
practice.answer_md: \((f_r-f_s)/f_s\simeq+gh/c^2\), a blueshift. The same potential difference makes the upper stationary clock run faster.

14.3.title: Uniformly accelerating frame
14.3.summary: A uniformly accelerating reference frame is assembled from hyperbolic worldlines with different felt accelerations.

prerequisites.refresher_md: An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

Write \(\beta=v/c\), \(\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\). $\gamma$ is dimensionless and at least one for $|v|<c$. At $v=3c/5, \gamma =5/4$; at $v=4c/5, \gamma =5/3$. Inertial frames here have constant relative velocity.

parts.title: Physical picture and route
parts.body_md: Find the path of one accelerating point first. Then add a second point while insisting their comoving distance stay fixed; that requirement creates the acceleration and clock-rate gradients.

parts.title: 14.3.1 · The hyperbolic worldline
parts.body_md: Constant proper acceleration g from rest gives $$v=\frac{gt}{\sqrt{1+(gt/c)^2}},\quad x=\frac{c^2}{g}\left[\sqrt{1+(gt/c)^2}-1\right].$$ Equivalently, in particle proper time, $$ct=\frac{c^2}{g}\sinh(g\tau/c),\qquad x=\frac{c^2}{g}[\cosh(g\tau/c)-1].$$ Thus \((x+c^2/g)^2-c^2t^2=(c^2/g)^2\). The constant proper acceleration has units $m/s^{2}$; $g\tau /c$ is dimensionless.

parts.title: 14.3.1 · Simultaneity lines and the hyperbola center
parts.body_md: The event $P=(ct=0,x=-c^{2}/g)$ is the hyperbola center. Each instantaneous rest-frame simultaneity line through the particle also passes through P. The spacelike proper distance along that line is $c^{2}/g$. P is one spacetime event, not an ordinary stationary object that the particle can keep observing at unchanged distance. The hyperbola’s null asymptotes determine causal horizons when acceleration is maintained indefinitely.

parts.title: 14.3.1 · What is and is not gravitational here
parts.body_md: This is exactly special-relativistic motion in flat spacetime. An accelerated coordinate chart can have a horizon without spacetime curvature or a physical black hole. A finite period of acceleration does not produce the same eternal causal restriction as indefinite acceleration.

parts.title: 14.3.2 · Build a rigid frame from different hyperbolas
parts.body_md: A Born-rigid accelerating frame keeps distances fixed in its momentarily comoving slices. Points labelled by proper distance $\rho >0$ from a common hyperbola center have proper acceleration \(a(\rho)=c^2/\rho\). Relative to a reference point with acceleration g and coordinate $\xi$ ahead of it, $$a(\xi)=\frac{g}{1+g\xi/c^2}.$$ Equal proper accelerations at all points instead make comoving distances grow, the key issue in the accelerating-spaceships/string problem.

parts.title: 14.3.2 · Clock rates inside the cabin
parts.body_md: With reference proper time T and $\xi$ fixed for each cabin point, the flat-spacetime metric is $$ds^2=(1+g\xi/c^2)^2c^2dT^2-d\xi^2-dy^2-dz^2.$$ Therefore a stationary cabin clock has \(d\tau=(1+g\xi/c^2)dT\), and the higher/front clock runs faster. This exact Rindler-chart result recovers the weak-field clock difference for a small cabin, while the proper acceleration varies along it.

parts.title: 14.3.2 · The chart boundary is not a material wall
parts.body_md: The chart requires \(1+g\xi/c^2>0\). At its null boundary $\xi =-c^{2}/g$, the family of static observers would require unbounded acceleration. A freely moving observer can cross a horizon in finite proper time, while the accelerated chart assigns an unbounded coordinate time. Flat spacetime remains regular; the chart’s failure is not a curvature singularity. A globally uniform proper gravity field cannot be mimicked over finite height by a rigid family all sharing one g.

examples.title: Position after a specified lab time under constant proper acceleration
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A particle starts from rest at $x=0$ and has constant proper acceleration g along x. Evaluate its speed and position when lab time is $c/g$.

steps.why: Constant felt acceleration does not mean constant lab acceleration.
Insert the specified lab time.
Integrate the lab velocity with $x(0)=0$.
Evaluate the position.

examples.answer_md: At that time $v=c/\sqrt{2}$ and $x=(\sqrt{2}-1)c^{2}/g$.
examples.check_md: For short times, expanding the square root gives $x\approx gt^{2}/2$ and $v\approx gt$.

examples.title: Front and rear of a rigid accelerating cabin
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. The rear of a cabin has constant proper acceleration g. The front is a proper distance h ahead along the acceleration direction. What acceleration must the front maintain for fixed comoving separation?

steps.why: Both hyperbolas share one center; $\rho$ is their proper distance from that center on a simultaneity slice.
Proper acceleration is inversely proportional to $\rho$.
Substitute the front distance.

examples.answer_md: The front must accelerate less than the rear.
examples.check_md: For a very short cabin $h\to 0$ the accelerations nearly agree; assigning the same acceleration to both ends would not keep their comoving separation fixed.

practice.question_md: Does a Rindler horizon prove that spacetime is curved?
hints: The construction used only inertial Minkowski spacetime.
The horizon depends on indefinite accelerated observer motion.
A coordinate chart can have a boundary in flat spacetime.
practice.answer_md: No. The Rindler horizon is an observer-dependent causal boundary in flat spacetime. Actual gravitational curvature requires additional structure such as nonremovable tidal effects.

parts.title: Clock rates inside the cabin
parts.body_md: With reference proper time T and $\xi$ fixed for each cabin point, the flat-spacetime metric is $$ds^2=(1+g\xi/c^2)^2c^2dT^2-d\xi^2-dy^2-dz^2.$$ Therefore a stationary cabin clock has \(d\tau=(1+g\xi/c^2)dT\), and the higher/front clock runs faster. This exact Rindler-chart result recovers the weak-field clock difference for a small cabin, while the proper acceleration varies along it.

parts.title: The chart boundary is not a material wall
parts.body_md: The chart requires \(1+g\xi/c^2>0\). At its null boundary $\xi =-c^{2}/g$, the family of static observers would require unbounded acceleration. A freely moving observer can cross a horizon in finite proper time, while the accelerated chart assigns an unbounded coordinate time. Flat spacetime remains regular; the chart’s failure is not a curvature singularity. A globally uniform proper gravity field cannot be mimicked over finite height by a rigid family all sharing one g.

examples.title: Front and rear of a rigid accelerating cabin
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. The rear of a cabin has constant proper acceleration g. The front is a proper distance h ahead along the acceleration direction. What acceleration must the front maintain for fixed comoving separation?

steps.why: Both hyperbolas share one center; $\rho$ is their proper distance from that center on a simultaneity slice.
Proper acceleration is inversely proportional to $\rho$.
Substitute the front distance.

examples.answer_md: The front must accelerate less than the rear.
examples.check_md: For a very short cabin $h\to 0$ the accelerations nearly agree; assigning the same acceleration to both ends would not keep their comoving separation fixed.

practice.question_md: The front is at $h=c^{2}/g$ ahead of a rear with acceleration g. Compare its acceleration and clock rate with the rear.
practice.answer_md: The front acceleration is $g/2$ and its stationary clock advances twice as much proper time per common Rindler time interval. This is an ideal extended Rindler frame, not the small-height approximation.

14.4.title: Maximal-proper-time principle
14.4.summary: A freely falling massive particle follows a stationary-proper-time path; in the simple situations here it locally maximizes elapsed time.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For a slowly moving clock in a static weak gravitational potential $\Phi$, relative to a coordinate clock at $\Phi =0$, \(d\tau/dt\simeq1+\Phi/c^2-v^2/(2c^2)\). Keep only first order in $|\Phi |/c^{2}$ and $v^{2}/c^{2}$. For a small vertical height y in nearly uniform gravity, $\Phi =gy$.

For fixed endpoint events, \(\delta\int L(q,\dot q,t)dt=0\) gives \(d(\partial L/\partial\dot q)/dt=\partial L/\partial q\). “Stationary” means zero first-order change, not automatically a global minimum or maximum.

parts.title: A path principle for clocks
parts.body_md: For a massive free particle, extremize \(S=-mc^2\int d\tau\). In flat spacetime the straight timelike path between fixed events maximizes proper time. In curved spacetime a timelike geodesic is locally maximizing over sufficiently short intervals; long paths can have conjugate points and need not be global maxima. The precise general statement is stationarity, which avoids overextending the chapter’s convenient “maximal” language.

parts.title: Competing height and speed effects
parts.body_md: In a static weak field and at low speed, $$d\tau\simeq\left(1+\frac{\Phi}{c^2}-\frac{v^2}{2c^2}\right)dt.$$ A path gains clock time by reaching higher potential but loses time by moving faster. With fixed endpoint times, maximizing this approximation is equivalent to making \(\int(mv^2/2-m\Phi)dt\) stationary. Thus Newtonian gravity emerges from the clock-path principle.

parts.title: Domain of the approximation
parts.body_md: Drop products and squares of $\Phi /c^{2}$ and $v^{2}/c^{2}$ consistently. This formula is not an exact metric for arbitrary strong gravity. A supported object is not following the free path; a normal force changes its worldline. Light follows null paths with $d\tau =0$ and cannot be treated as a massive clock maximizing a positive proper-time integral.

examples.title: A detour reduces elapsed proper time in flat spacetime
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. Two events occur at the same lab position, separated by time T. One clock stays there. Another travels at constant speed v for each half of an ideal out-and-back path, turning around instantaneously. Compare elapsed times.

steps.why: The stationary inertial clock coincides with lab coordinate time.
The speed magnitude is constant except for the ideal instantaneous turn.
The straight inertial path accumulates more proper time.

examples.answer_md: The traveling clock is younger at reunion.
examples.check_md: A smooth finite turn can replace the ideal turn and its actual proper time can be integrated; the endpoint comparison does not rely on signal-arrival ambiguity.

examples.title: Recover free-fall acceleration from clock time
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. In a weak uniform field, vary a vertical path y(t) between fixed endpoint events. Derive its equation from stationary proper time to leading order.

steps.why: Combine gravitational and kinematic rate corrections consistently.
The constant term has no variation and multiplying by $-mc^{2}$ does not change stationarity.
Apply the Euler–Lagrange equation to the Newtonian action.
Solve for the acceleration.

examples.answer_md: The usual downward free-fall equation is the weak-field, slow-speed limit.
examples.check_md: The mass cancels, consistent with universal free fall; both time corrections were needed to obtain the correct path.

practice.question_md: Would keeping only gravitational clock gain but omitting the speed penalty predict the correct thrown-ball trajectory?
hints: The path could gain time by going arbitrarily high without cost.
The kinetic term restrains that change for fixed endpoint times.
Both terms produce the Newtonian action.
practice.answer_md: No. The speed penalty is essential; dropping it removes the competition that produces a finite free-fall trajectory and the equation $\ddot y=-g$.

14.5.title: Twin paradox revisited
14.5.summary: Reunion ages depend on complete clock paths, and gravity can reverse a naive “the moving clock must be younger” guess.

prerequisites.refresher_md: For a slowly moving clock in a static weak gravitational potential $\Phi$, relative to a coordinate clock at $\Phi =0$, \(d\tau/dt\simeq1+\Phi/c^2-v^2/(2c^2)\). Keep only first order in $|\Phi |/c^{2}$ and $v^{2}/c^{2}$. For a small vertical height y in nearly uniform gravity, $\Phi =gy$.

An event is one occurrence at one place and time. Write its coordinates in a named frame. A time interval can involve two different places; it is not automatically one clock’s elapsed time. Coordinate times already account for signal travel delays.

parts.title: Ordinary spaceflight twins need no gravitational theory
parts.body_md: For an inertial twin and an out-and-back accelerated traveler in flat spacetime, integrate each proper time along its worldline. The traveler cannot use one inertial frame for the whole trip. Changing simultaneity at turnaround accounts for the mismatch in a piecewise comoving description; there is no contradiction in the reunion readings.

parts.title: The gravity version changes which path is free
parts.body_md: Compare a supported ground twin with a freely thrown twin who rises and returns. The thrown twin has a kinematic clock slowdown but also spends time at higher potential, where clocks run faster. In the weak uniform-field example, the height effect wins: the freely falling twin returns older. The supported twin feels a normal force, whereas the thrown twin’s accelerometer reads zero during flight.

parts.title: Equivalence and its limits
parts.body_md: The correspondence with an accelerating rocket is local or approximate over a weak, nearly uniform gravitational region. A large real gravitational field has tidal curvature, while the exact rigid accelerated frame has a position-dependent proper acceleration. Use the full appropriate metric and worldlines if those variations matter. Neither “who moves on the page” nor “who feels acceleration at one instant” alone replaces the complete proper-time calculation.

examples.title: A thrown clock returns older than a supported one
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. A clock is thrown vertically with initial speed $u\ll c$ in nearly uniform gravity g and returns to its launch height. Another clock stays supported there. Ignore launch and catching durations. Find the leading age difference.

steps.why: Use the Newtonian trajectory inside the already small relativistic correction.
Subtract the supported clock’s elapsed time at potential zero.
Integrate the gravitational clock gain.
Integrate the kinematic clock loss.
The height contribution is twice the speed loss.

examples.answer_md: The freely falling clock returns older by $u^{3}/(3gc^{2})$ at this order.
examples.check_md: The dimension is time, and the difference vanishes for $u\to 0$. The result assumes weak potential over the trajectory and negligible drag.

examples.title: A ship reverses under constant proper acceleration
examples.setup_md: Original worked example. In an inertial observer’s frame a ship passes at speed u, then maintains proper acceleration of magnitude g opposite its initial motion until it returns to the observer with speed−u. Find the elapsed times.

steps.why: The ship’s rapidity changes from $+\eta _{0}$ to $-\eta _{0}$.
Integrate constant proper acceleration through that rapidity change.
Integrate $dt/d\tau =\cosh\eta$ across the symmetric trip.
$\sinh\eta$ exceeds $\eta$, so the inertial observer ages more.

examples.answer_md: The accelerated ship is younger at reunion.
examples.check_md: The total displacement is zero because the integral of $\sinh\eta$ over symmetric limits vanishes. At small u, both leading trip times reduce to $2u/g$.

practice.question_md: For the thrown-clock example, double u while keeping g fixed and the weak-field approximation valid. What happens to the leading age difference?
hints: The duration doubles and the typical height and squared speed quadruple.
practice.answer_md: The leading age difference grows by 8. Both the explicit formula and the duration-times-rate scaling agree.
